Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu has declared three days of national mourning after a military aircraft crashed in southern Ondo State, killing 32 people.
Authorities say the plane was on a routine mission from Benin City to Lagos when it came down near a naval base on Monday morning.
A resident told the BBC that the plane had crashed near a swamp and that clothes and shoes had been found at the site. Smoke could be seen rising from the area.
Tinubu offered his deepest condolences for the 25 passengers and seven crew members on board and has ordered a full investigation.
The president also ordered national flags to be flown at half-mast across the country as a mark of respect for those who died.
"This is a painful moment for our Armed Forces and for the entire nation," Tinubu said.
"Our Air Force personnel put their lives on the line every day to secure Nigeria. Their sacrifice will never be forgotten," he added.
Aviation Minister Festus Keyamo earlier said he had been informed "of the disappearance of a military aircraft with tail number NGR 931, enroute Lagos from Benin at 0913 hours earlier today".
He said "efforts to raise the aircraft on radio proved abortive" before subsequent confirmation that it had crashed near a naval base in Igbokoda, Ondo state.
He said search and rescue efforts were ongoing.
The crashed plane, described as an ATR-42 aircraft, carries between 30 and 50 passengers, according to its manufacturers.
Tinubu has ordered the Air Force to immediately begin a thorough investigation into the cause of the crash to help prevent similar incidents in the future.
The identities of those who died have not yet been released. Authorities say the names of the officers will be published after their families have been informed.
The Nigerian Air Force plays a key role in the country's military operations, including efforts to tackle armed groups and insecurity in several parts of the country.
The accident is one âof the deadliest air disasters âin â Nigeria in recent years.
In May 2021, Nigeria's army chief, Lt-Gen Ibrahim Attahiru, was killed in a plane crash alongside 10 other officers in the north-western state of Kaduna amid bad weather.
In February of the same year, seven people died after a military plane crashed short of a runway in the capital Abuja.

Every morning at 6am, 10-year-old Rafeef and her younger brother get ready for school, putting on their cream and brown uniforms.
She always looks forward to seeing her friends and learning about everything from maths to Arabic and Islamic studies. She can't wait to start studying English next year.
But for Rafeef, the journey to school involves far greater risks than crossing roads or missing the bus.
Her school in Taiz, south-western Yemen, stands on a mountain at the edge of a valley known as no-man's land - a heavily contested front line in the civil war between forces supporting Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia, and the Iran-backed Houthis.
On one side of the school is government-held territory, on the other are Houthi sniper positions.
Rafeef's home is further down the mountain.
Every time she goes to school, she has to walk uphill with her back towards the snipers. "I'm afraid," she says.
According to Unicef, roughly 3.2 million children in Yemen were out of school even before the war escalated last month.
It says thousands of children have been killed or maimed since the war began in 2014, while thousands more have been recruited by armed groups on both sides.
Yet despite the risks, Rafeef says she does not want to stop going because she loves seeing her friends and it is her only chance to be with them. She begins naming the children in her classroom.
Going to school is the only time Rafeef's parents let her go outside. They say they are keen for her to get an education and have the chance of a better life. Rafeef hopes to become a doctor.
'A mortar came out of nowhere'
Rafeef's family moved to Taiz from the coastal city of Hudaydah nine years ago, seeking safety when Houthis took control there.
But Taiz has also endured fighting.
Rafeef says that two years ago there was a mortar attack outside her new home.
"Everyone was out except for me and my brother. Then a mortar came out of nowhereâ¦ shrapnel blew through the door and into the house." Her arm was broken and there is still a scar where she was hit.
And in recent days the conflict has intensified. On Sunday the Houthis cut off a vital supply route linking Taiz to Aden, which meant they were able to effectively encircle Taiz. Control of that route has kept shifting.
Residents have told the BBC they are afraid the Houthis could seize the city at any moment.
Government forces have made gains in other areas this week, they say, retaking control of strategic points on the Bab al-Mandab Strait - a key shipping chokepoint - and launching an offensive to try to regain control of the capital, Sanaa.
Homes in Taiz are mostly scattered across the slopes, but many have been abandoned by families fleeing the fighting.
Twice, we try to visit the neighbourhood where Rafeef and her family live, but a community leader advises us it is too dangerous.
On the first occasion, residents of the neighbourhood tell us that three people have been shot by snipers. On the second, we are told of another shooting.
At Rafeef's school, one of the teachers, Abdel Raqeeb al-Obaidi, 45, takes us on to the rooftop to show us what he says are Houthi military camps, barracks and sniper positions in the mountains.
Standing on the rooftop, a Yemeni security adviser accompanying us suddenly tells us to go back inside. We are visible from these positions and could be shot, he says.
Abdel Raqeeb laughs, acknowledging the danger. He says the school has been fired on before.
"The situation may explode at any moment while we are sitting in class or sleeping or we are in school or we are out on the street. We do not know how our future is and how tomorrow is."
For Abdel Raqeeb, the risk has become routine. His familiarity with it is unsettling.
Taiz has long been a major battleground in the country's devastating civil war. After ousting the government from the capital Sanaa in 2015, the Houthis attempted to also seize control of Taiz but were driven out of most of the city by local militiamen.
Seizing Taiz would give the Houthis full control over the country's north. Now, in their latest offensive, Houthis are making extensive use of drones alongside other weapons.
Sometimes civilians are collateral damage in the fighting.
Later that evening, we get a call from a hospital about a five minute drive away from the school. Two children have been badly injured by a mortar strike.
When we arrive at Al-Rawdah Hospital, we see a nurse standing outside the intensive care unit, holding a tiny pair of beige, rubber sandals that are splattered with blood.
They belonged to Ahmed, a three-year-old boy who we learn was killed when a mortar struck a mechanic's shop in the city.
Shrapnel in the heart
When I ask about the shoes, the nurse, Ikram Shamsan, begins to cry.
"What did this child or his family ever do wrong?" she asks.
Ahmed was killed when a piece of shrapnel pierced his heart, entering through his back. The boy had been with his father, who was getting his motorcycle tyre pumped up at the mechanic's shop. The father was unharmed.
A doctor tells us the father had intended to leave his son at home, but the boy cried because he wanted to come too.
As he takes his son's body from the hospital, the father asks how he will face the boy's mother.
Completing a simple errand turned into the worst day of their lives.
Another boy, 11-year-old Amjad, was also at the mechanic's shop. He and his brother worked there with their uncle, sending money to their family in their home village.
Shrapnel has struck Amjad in his lung and abdomen. When we reach him, he is in intensive care, struggling to breathe. No relatives are beside his bed.
His doctor describes his condition as critical and fears he could die within hours. He hopes his mother will arrive in time to say goodbye.
Amjad was admitted at about 20:00 that evening. His mother reaches him at around 06:00 the following morning, delayed by the eight-hour journey from the village.

The unexpected mass withdrawal of America's heavy bombers happened so suddenly on Sunday that it has got everyone wondering what prompted it.
An "abundance of caution," says US Vice-President JD Vance, adding that Washington felt Iran was doing what it has "done for 49 years... which is engage in acts of terrorism against the US and against a lot of other people".
An abundance of panic is how others have seen it.
For the last seven months, America's B-1 Lancer bombers and other aircraft have been operating out of Fairford to strike the Iranian missile launch sites.
In July, Iran threatened any country that provided the US with such a facility would be considered a "legitimate target".
Then on 27 September, a major incident was declared when five British men were arrested and later bailed after being seen acting suspiciously with their three white vans in the dead of night close to the airbase perimeter.
At the weekend, a UK-Iranian dual national was arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts. He was also released on bail.
Twelve valuable and strategically important B-1 bombers have now departed en masse and seemingly in such a rush that, reportedly, the air-to-air refuelling aircraft needed to get them back across the Atlantic to their home bases in the continental US were still being fuelled up while the B-1 Lancer crews were being ordered to scramble to take off.
So something was considered urgent and dangerous enough to prompt this.
Speaking after his vice-president's remarks, President Donald Trump himself said the US had removed its bombers because of "some threats" to the base.
"Rather than tempting the enemy", he added, the US had moved the planes "around a little bit".
There was almost certainly a fresh piece of intelligence, whether true or not.
British officials would not reveal what it was, but they did say "there is an ongoing high tempo of threat from Iran to the UK, and it is logical that US airbases would be pretty high on any targeting list".
Iran has denied any connection with events at RAF Fairford. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has also played down any suggested link between this rushed evacuation and the arrests made on 27 September.
The context here is that while the UK is not at war with Iran, the US is - and that is a distinction Tehran has publicly challenged. As far as the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps is concerned, Britain is already a participant in America's war with Iran.
There is also a cost factor involved here.
The B-1 Lancer bombers which have now left each cost about $330 million.
The Americans have already suffered heavy financial losses from Iranian strikes on US bases in the Middle East.
In late March the Iranians hit Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia, destroying an E-3 Sentry Awacs early warning plane.
That aircraft alone cost over half a billion dollars.
General Sir Richard Barrons, who served in one of the highest ranks in the British Armed Forces, said: "We now live in a world where a Â£1,000 drone could wreck one of those aircraft.
"So, I don't know what the threat was but the most prudent thing to do would be to remove them to Texas given that they were not doing very much at the minute."
But how does the US ordering the bombers to leave RAF Fairford reflect on Washington's confidence in the ability of the UK to keep the base secure?
Britain remains an incredibly close ally of the US and there are still hundreds of American servicemen and women stationed at RAF Fairford, as well as at other bases at Mildenhall and Lakenheath.
Work will likely be ongoing in secret now to review security at the base on both sides of the perimeter fence.
But it is hard not to conclude that, despite efforts to play down the drama, this is an embarrassing episode for the UK.
Rubio said the US has "confidence in the security of all our bases" and said the administrations was working "very closely" with UK authorities, who "couldn't be more co-operative".
UK counter-terrorism police are still investigating what happened at RAF Fairford and are keeping an open mind as to what exactly was behind events there.
I have been told a large amount of data, CCTV and other information is still being trawled through while the men remain on bail.
Meanwhile, now that the bombers have left British soil, the US insists it can still deploy them from its domestic bases anywhere in the world.
That could be seen as putting a brave face on something which, for Iran, sees a major US strike force effectively driven back to its home base in the continental United States.

Kenya has confirmed its first case of Ebola - a Kenyan citizen who has been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo for the past seven years.
Health Minister Aden Duale said the patient, who fell ill a month ago, and was treated in several hospitals in DR Congo, died days after arriving in Nairobi.
Duale said the patient boarded a flight on Saturday and underwent normal public screening at the main airport in Nairobi before he was transferred by a relative to a hospital in the city.
More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak of the disease.
Shortly after DR Congo declared an outbreak of Ebola in May, it was also reported in Uganda, where two people have died. However, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared the county free of the disease in August.
Since then, all cases of the disease have been declared in DR Congo.
The current outbreak has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no known vaccine.
Duale confirmed that the Kenyan national had tested positive for the Bundibugyo species.
According to the minister, the patient first travelled by road from DR Congo to the Ugandan capital Kampala, where he boarded a flight to Nairobi
Duale said that after being taken to the Nairobi Hospital, the patient was transferred to an isolation facility which was built during the Covid-19.
It was there that the patient "developed fever, chills, intense fatigue and weakness, painful swallowing, muscle pain and bleeding under the skin".
"Doctors suspected a viral haemorrhagic fever based on his symptoms and travel history and collected samples for testing. The sample tested positive for Ebola Bundibugyo virus," Duale said.
The patient died at 23:30 (20:30 GMT) on Monday and his burial is planned for later on Tuesday in line with public health safety protocols.
At least 28 contacts, including family members and healthcare workers, have been identified, while health authorities are tracing a further 23 passengers and four crew members who travelled on the same flight.
So far, WHO has recorded 4,082 deaths out of 8,463 cases since the emergence of the Bundibugyo species of the virus.
There are currently no approved vaccines or treatments for the species, which is highly infectious.

e1c0724cecf6.text: The main super PAC supporting Republican Senate candidates plans to inject $5 million into the South Carolina campaign as an "insurance policy" to help GOP nominee Darline Graham , a source familiar with the move tells Axios. Why it matters: The GOP's concern that a Senate seat in blood-red South Carolina could be in play shows just how bad the political environment is for Republicans, who face a rash of troubles in states long considered conservative strongholds. "It's an insurance policy. We're going to be there for Darline," said a Republican briefed on the plans for the Senate Leadership Fund. The shift to spending in conservative South Carolina comes after Senate Republicans announced they no longer were financing ads in swing-state North Carolina, where the GOP's Michael Whatley is lagging behind former Gov. Roy Cooper (D) in polls. Democrats, meanwhile, are reallocating resources in a way that reflects their optimism four weeks before Election Day. Democrats' main Senate super PAC canceled roughly $1.1 million in ad reservations in North Carolina, based on their belief Cooper is well-positioned to flip the seat now held by retiring Republican Thom Tillis. Zoom in: Graham, the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, was appointed to her seat in July at the urging of President Trump , a friend of her brother's. Graham faces a host of challenges: She's a relatively poor fundraiser compared to her Democratic opponent, Annie Andrews, a pediatrician who is outspending and outraising Graham, according to the South Carolina Post & Courier . Unlike her brother, Graham shields herself from the press and has shown a relative lack of mastery of foreign policy, which tripped her up during a GOP primary debate. Graham won that primary over Rep. Ralph Norman with 52% of the vote after getting help from Trump. It left some bad feelings with Norman, who endorsed her but briefly suggested he would mount a write-in campaign for the Nov. 3 general election. Zoom out: Voter anger over high prices and Trump's sagging popularity have helped to create a political landscape in which the Senate Leadership Fund super PAC is having to play defense across the country. It's trying to shore up GOP incumbents and challengers from Alaska to Ohio to Texas, where it recently plowed in $131 million over 17 days to boost Ken Paxton's campaign against Democrat James Talarico. "We're not taking anything for granted. We won't be caught flat-footed in any of these races," the source said. The money for Graham will be spent mainly on TV ads to "remind voters that Andrews is a Democrat." Democrats haven't won a statewide race in South Carolina since 2006. By the numbers: Closer-than-expected polling from two firms that typically survey for Republicans sparked concern last week in GOP circles. A survey from Trafalgar showed Graham pulling 43% and Andrews 42%, a statistical tie. InsiderAdvantage also produced a poll showing a 1-point race that's essentially tied, with Graham at 46% and Andrews at 45%. Earlier in September, GOP-leaning Rasmussen Reports showed Graham up by 5 points. Catch up quick: Andrews' campaign has been under the radar compared to that of Jaime Harrison, the Democrat who challenged Graham's brother for the seat in 2020. Harrison raised $100 million for that race, but because he was the state's former Democratic Party chair, it was easier for Republicans to make the race a partisan contest. In contrast, Andrews is running as a "mom and a doctor." Her campaign was largely financed with $3.6 million in campaign contributions bundled by 314 Action Fund, a political committee founded to elect Democratic candidates with STEM backgrounds. What they're saying: "South Carolinians don't know who Darline Graham is or what she believes — she avoids reporters, avoids voters, and lies about Annie rather than doing her job," an Andrews spokesperson told Axios. A Graham spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment. Trump gave a preview Monday of the bare-knuckle attacks to come when he took to Truth Social and used a slur for transgender people to attack Andrews while accusing her of a host of liberal positions. "South Carolina must show, in the upcoming Election, that it is not for her," Trump wrote . The 314 Action Fund jabbed back at the president in a statement late Monday, calling Trump "perverted" and saying that he "has resorted to name-calling and juvenile insults because his candidate can't win on the issues." Axios' Hans Nichols contributed to this story.

3c988a9f99c9.text: LOS ANGELES — Bryan Johnson , the face of the longevity movement who believes he may never die, announced recently that he had an incurable autoimmune disease — and his critics cheered, he told "The Axios Show" in an exclusive interview Monday. "I mean, I think people really want me to die. Now I get it. It's funny. It's ironic. I push a lot of buttons that people don't like," he said. The big picture : As Johnson himself acknowledged, there's an irony in the founder of the "Don't Die" movement watching people celebrate his diagnosis. But Johnson sees his diagnosis as rocket fuel for his mission to promote longevity, rather than a setback. Catch up quick: Johnson, 49, has autoimmune gastritis (AIG), a chronic condition in which the immune system attacks healthy cells in the stomach lining. Johnson said "there was joy all around the world" after he announced his diagnosis in July. He spends millions of dollars a year on extreme health interventions, documenting the experiments for an online following that has ballooned to roughly 8 million across platforms including YouTube . When asked if any of his interventions could have fueled his AIG diagnosis, he said: "No. I got diagnosed with hypothyroidism when I was 21 years old. The thyroid and the stomach are very closely linked in immunology. I probably have had this thing for about 30 years." The intrigue : Johnson views the diagnosis, which might appear to undermine his campaign against aging, as just another test of it. In his view, his efforts to do more than manage the disease can help prove the efficacy of his ambitions. "I like the challenge. I'm up for it. I think it's good timing. I'm going to get diagnosed with something at some point. Why not this?" Friction point: Johnson, who calls himself the "most measured person in the world," spends over $2 million a year on his personal health and longevity treatments. He has an entire medical concierge team and a makeshift doctor's office in his home. Experts say the cause of the disease is unknown, and that Johnson's proposed effort to reverse it is experimental. Zoom out: Johnson made his fortune founding Braintree, which bought Venmo and was later sold to PayPal for $800 million. He now runs longevity businesses including Blueprint and Immortals, alongside neurotechnology company Kernel and venture fund OS Fund. Between the lines: One common critique of intensive health tracking is that more testing can uncover more abnormalities, not all of them meaningful. Doctors warn that false positives and incidental findings can trigger a "cascade" of follow-up tests and treatments that can bring added cost, stress, and in some cases, harm. Johnson is a full-throated fan : "I personally appreciate information. I want to know because when you find things early, you're much more likely to be able to address them." He also said his process doesn't feel addictive to him, adding that "the biggest addiction in the world is to make money." The bottom line: The face of the longevity movement sees the hit to his public health record as another potential achievement in his quest to live forever.

72bec67544eb.text: Data: NYSE/Intercontinental Exchange via the New York State Comptroller; Chart Emily Peck/Axios; Note: 2026 projected by the comptroller if first-half growth continues at current pace. First-half 2026 profits were $45.9 billion. Profits are for broker-dealer operations of NYSE member firms and are not adjusted for inflation. Wall Street profits are blowing past expectations this year, the New York State Comptroller's office finds in a new report. Why it matters: Profits are on track for an all-time record, a sign of how the AI boom is fueling dealmaking and how volatile markets are helping trading. By the numbers: In the first half of this year, Wall Street firms raked in $45.9 billion — that's 51.3% more than the same period last year, and already more than the $45.3 billion forecast for the entirety of 2026. If growth continues apace, annual profits could exceed $90 billion. Zoom out: That's far more than 2025's record $65.1 billion and rivals the 2009 record even after accounting for inflation, the report says. Stunning stat: The fees that firms earn from underwriting — helping companies sell new stocks and bonds — rose 68% in the first half of the year, compared with the first half of 2025. Zoom in: That tracks with a 76.5% increase in global equity issuance, a large chunk from the SpaceX initial public offering . Plus, there was also an 11.3% increase in debt issuance, with the AI hyperscalers among the biggest borrowers. Yes, but: It's anyone's guess as to whether the second half of the year looks like the first. There are plenty of market headwinds blowing: the Iran war, higher inflation and interest rates, the potential for the AI bubble to burst among them. The intrigue: Wall Street appears to be thriving despite fears over the city's democratic socialist mayor, Zohran Mamdani. The big picture: The securities industry makes up a big and growing share of the city and state's tax revenues, but local business and politics aren't significant profit engines. Those instead are driven by national and global markets — it's been a huge year for stocks, the SpaceX IPO was the biggest ever, M&A hit a record and war-driven volatility juiced trading. What to watch: The big Wall Street banks are set to release third-quarter earnings numbers next week — that's the first big test of whether the pace is holding up.

5f705dc37ddb.text: A national Latino civic engagement group is turning to an AI app to help voters cut through an increasingly complicated election system — in English or Spanish. Why it matters: Nearly 39 million Hispanics can vote in this year's midterms, and their political loyalties are increasingly up for grabs. Hispanics have added 5.25 million eligible voters since 2022, more than any other racial or ethnic group, according to Pew Research Center. The Latino electorate remains highly fluid: About 1 in 7 Latino voters who backed Trump in 2024 now say they want Democrats to control Congress, according to a new NBC News/Telemundo poll . How it works: Mi Familia en Acción launched Nubi last week, a bilingual AI-powered app that answers questions about voting, voter registration, citizenship and Know Your Rights information. Users can ask questions in English or Spanish about where and when to vote, early voting, mail ballots and registration. Nubi operates in all 50 states and can tailor information to the local or district level. Unlike a general-purpose chatbot , Mi Familia en Acción president and CEO Héctor Sánchez Barba tells Axios that Nubi doesn't search the open internet for answers. The organization feeds it information from sources it considers reliable, with human review and guardrails around what the AI can answer. If Nubi doesn't have an answer, Sánchez said, it is designed to say so and direct the user to a trusted source or partner rather than invent a response. State of play: Nubi represents a five-year effort to marry Mi Familia en Acción's traditional organizing with technology. The organization launched a more basic chatbot about two years ago before developing the current AI version. Mi Familia en Acción financed development itself, Sánchez said, though he declined to disclose the cost, calling it a "very big investment." The organization says it plans to keep updating Nubi as voting rules, court decisions and government policies change. Zoom in: The goal is to turn a complicated search across election websites into a conversation. A voter could ask whether they're registered, whether they can vote by mail, where their polling place is or what early-voting options exist. Nubi then walks the user through basic questions before giving a locally specific answer. The tool is updated regularly and eventually could expand its answers on questions involving immigration enforcement or problems a voter encounters at a polling place. What they're saying: "People don't need to be a constitutional lawyer to find information about how they need to vote," said Sánchez, adding that the goal is to put reliable information in one place. He stressed that Nubi is nonpartisan and doesn't recommend candidates or causes. Sánchez also said the technology won't replace door-knocking and other traditional organizing, but could extend civic information into rural or overlooked communities that organizers rarely reach. Zoom out: Nubi arrives as Latino voters play an increasingly large — and less predictable — role in American elections. Pew projects Hispanics will account for 16% of eligible voters in 2026, nearly double their 9% share in 2006. Latino voters are also fragmenting into competing political identities rather than moving uniformly toward either party. In May, 52% of registered Latino voters surveyed in 17 competitive House districts said they were undecided or could change their minds.

6d4264f88579.text: Everytown for Gun Safety , a group that advocates for stricter gun laws, is teaming up with House Democrats on a $10 million ad campaign to boost former gun safety advocates now running for Congress, Axios has learned. Why it matters: That's a significant sum at a moment when Democrats are raising alarm bells about being outgunned financially in the midterm elections. The candidates boosted by the campaign are all former volunteers for another gun safety group, Moms Demand Action. The candidates include: JoAnna Mendoza of Arizona, Pia Dandiya of Florida, Christina Bohannan and Lindsay James of Iowa, Christina Hines and Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet of Michigan, and Paige Cognetti of Pennsylvania. "For nearly two years, a MAGA House has rubber-stamped the Trump administration as it tore up federal gun safety laws, and flipping these eight seats is how we put a stop to it," Everytown president John Feinblatt said in a statement first shared with Axios. "There's a Moms Demand Action volunteer on the ballot in every one of these districts, and we're partnering with House Majority PAC to turn them into majority makers." Mike Smith, the president of House Democrats' main super PAC, House Majority PAC, said in a statement: "Every seat on this map is a chance to put a check on a Trump administration and a MAGA House that have spent two years putting the gun lobby ahead of American families." Between the lines: The money will go to fund TV and digital ads focused broadly on "public safety," referencing not just gun control but drug trafficking, immigration, crime, and police funding. The Bohannan ad says she is "running for Congress to put public safety first. That means working with both parties to secure our border, hire more police officers and keep illegal guns and fentanyl off our streets." The Cognetti ad mostly focuses on her broader anti-corruption message but lauds how "she got millions for police and cut violent crime by 80%" as mayor of Scranton. The other side: "House Democrats have fully embraced the radical socialist agenda of abolishing prisons, releasing criminals back on the streets, and defunding the police," NRCC spokesman Mike Marinella told Axios in a statement. "Voters won't buy their lies about Republicans who have fought to protect our communities."

763254a521ed.text: President Trump's newly minted "Super Intelligence" task force faces a daunting mandate: reconcile fiercely divided cabinet factions to forge a tech policy that keeps pace with the blistering AI race. Why it matters: The task force brings the administration's scattered AI work under one roof, but it also makes it likely that any new rules will be forged in the crossfire of competing internal camps. In an interview, Task force co-chair Scott Kupor rejected the assertion that the administration is asleep at the wheel on AI policy, arguing that rigid, static legislation would risk becoming instantly obsolete. What they're saying : "The worst thing for us to do would be to assume a static set of knowledge that allows us to put a regulatory schema in place that then has unintended consequences," said Kupor, a Silicon Valley veteran who is currently serving as director of the U.S. Office of Personnel Management, akin to an HR director for the federal government. "Look, we live in D.C.," he said. "There's nothing that's not political in this town. People have different views and that's totally fine. Our obligation is to demonstrate to the American people that this is good and also that we take the anxieties and the concerns seriously." "At the end of the day there is no daylight between the president and anyone else, which is we need to win," he said. Kupor was the first employee hired by venture giant Andreessen Horowitz. Between the lines : The group's makeup highlights the competing fiefdoms driving Trump's AI strategy , with some working on model approval and coordination and others continuing to voice deep skepticism about pro-regulation forces in the industry. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Trump Chief of Staff Susie Wiles have worked behind the scenes to encourage some oversight, including through the voluntary model-review process that already exists. Managed within the Commerce Department, the reviews have already been used for top models at Anthropic, OpenAI and now Google, sources tell Axios. On the other end of the spectrum, figures like David Sacks and the Pentagon's Emil Michael represent an approach that is wary of the potential for a slowdown in model development or new regulation to reduce competition for frontier companies. Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence and the new AI czar , is expected to bring cohesion to the group's collective work, much as he does with the myriad intelligence agencies. The entire committee is set to operate under Trump's explicit marching orders: Innovation cannot be bottlenecked, and America must stay ahead while finding a safe path forward, Kupor said. Kupor suggested one outcome may be that AI regulation is divided among different federal agencies, although it is too early to know what the group — which will do its work over 120 days — will ultimately recommend to the president. His primary area of focus initially will be to seek input from stakeholders in the energy, manufacturing, security and financial services industries. Kupor said he expects Clayton will keep close tabs on the intelligence community and the committee will continue to stay in close touch with the AI companies. Zoom in: The administration is leaning hard into corporate self-policing to manage the risks. Kupor and other officials believe that third-party audits and direct reporting to corporate boards carry severe securities law implications that rival traditional government oversight. The bottom line: The task force's goal isn't to draft a bureaucratic "PhD dissertation," in Kupor's words. But it remains to be seen whether streamlining existing efforts without new legislation will satisfy Americans who are increasingly anxious about AI safety.

8e5e9be04724.text: The 2026 midterms are shaping up to be the most intensely observed, recorded, dissected and challenged election in American history. Why it matters: A small army of partisan and nonpartisan observers will show up. So will a surge of Justice Department monitors, organizers looking for signs of ICE and citizen journalists broadcasting their search for illegal voting in real time. Between the lines: More nonpartisan observation can bolster confidence in elections, studies show . But officials worry that activists expecting to find wrongdoing could misread routine events. Election officials have been raising concerns that "vigilante citizen journalists" could interfere with the election, said Andrew Walchuck of Common Cause, a nonprofit organization that's also recruiting nonpartisan election observers. "I worry that people are going to go in and claim they're seeing things that they aren't," said Andrew Garber of the Brennan Center. "Just minor, innocuous things that are going to happen as millions and millions of ballots get cast and counted, then it gets spun into something nefarious or untrue," Garber said. The intrigue: After the 2020 election, claims from observers and activist sleuths helped fuel challenges to the results. It was then channeled into numerous lawsuits from the Trump campaign. The cases were almost all dismissed or denied relief in court. Influencers and online activists can turn real-time claims about wrongdoing into national controversy before officials can weigh in or push back — including while votes are being cast or counted. "What gives me concern is that we have an administration that is trying to spread conspiracy theories and spread lies about our elections and... [then] having more people out there with that purpose behind their work troubles me," Walchuck said. The other side: "Despite extreme Democrats and the media claiming it never happens, the evidence of voter fraud continues to pile up. Anyone who illegally votes in our elections will be held accountable," Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman, said in a statement. This year there have been more than two dozen federal charges against people for voting when they're not eligible and about 160 arrests, according to the Justice Department . A review from the Center for Election Innovation & Research, a nonpartisan organization, says instances of illegal voting are "extremely small." Zoom in: The DOJ plans to train 1,000 election monitors to deploy across the country, one of the largest-ever efforts from the agency. It builds on a significant increase in observers in 2024 . The Senate Democrats have spun up their own arm of election observers, using office staff to monitor the polls. That's in addition to a new 50-state-plus-territories recruitment program by a coalition of Democratic state parties, aiming to recruit at least 10,000 election watchers. The Republican National Committee is building on its election watch network set up in 2020 to counter perceived voter fraud. GOP partisans have signed up in record numbers to be poll workers and the party is hosting virtual and in-person trainings for observers and challengers. A network of anti-ICE activists is transitioning ICE watch trainings into poll watching trainings, responding in part to the Trump administration saying ICE could make arrests at the polls. When asked in September about deploying agents, Trump told TIME magazine he hadn't thought of it. Zoom out: These efforts will coexist with a slew of nonpartisan observing efforts, ranging from voter protection groups to international election observers. There will also be state party and campaign staffers who regularly monitor the polls for concerns. These are typically more mundane, including monitoring accurate opening and closing times for polling locations that can be remedied with quick litigation. The rules and terminology for observers vary by state laws , which also govern how close an observer can be to voting machines or tabulation processes and how to document concerns about malpractice. The bottom line: "Having questions and wanting to understand more about the election process as a sort of curious citizen is a good thing," said Avery Davis-Roberts of the Carter Center, which monitors elections internationally and will have volunteers in five states in November. "And we hope that people will use observation and the findings of our observation as a way to better understand how the process works and maybe have some of those questions answered."

34cfce1b69cb.text:
When Lori Baute first learned about precautionary full-body MRI scans, she dismissed the idea.
“ I heard Kim Kardashian got one, and some other wealthy people,” Baute said. But at 59, she was worried about her long-term health. She has a family history of cancer, and she’s a critical caregiver for her aging mom and her adult brother with special needs.
After a close friend was diagnosed with bladder cancer, Baute decided to make an appointment with a clinic that offers full-body scans near where she lives in Ocala, Florida. Her results came back a week later. One major finding: She has lesions on her pancreas. “When I got that, I was really petrified,” she said.
Worried about pancreatic cancer, Baute shared the results with her gastroenterologist, who ordered a targeted MRI scan as a follow-up. That test showed the lesions were benign cysts.
Baute’s experience is becoming more common as companies pitch body scans directly to consumers as a way to detect cancer and other diseases early. But no major medical association — including the American Cancer Society and the American College of Radiology — recommends these scans for people without a very high risk of certain cancers.
And even medical screenings that doctors do recommend can carry some of the same reasons for caution.
The QTip:
Before saying yes to the test, ask about the risks and benefits — even if your doctor recommends it.
Here’s what to know:
1. Every Test Comes With Costs and Risks
At a minimum, a medical test will cost you time — and could mean a hefty medical bill. Many tests marketed directly to consumers, like full-body scans and at-home blood screening kits, are not covered by insurance, and some tests can cost several thousand dollars.
Some laboratory tests might involve only the discomfort of a blood draw or the awkwardness of collecting a urine or stool sample, but others carry the possibility of physical harm. For example, a small percentage of people who get CT scans each year will develop cancer because of the radiation exposure from the tests, according to estimates from the National Institutes of Health. Relatively simple procedures like a biopsy or an endoscopy come with the risks of pain, infections, tearing, a reaction to anesthesia, or further serious complications.
Plus, testing can cause anxiety and stress — as patients wait for results and if the results are inconclusive. “I see patients every week in my office who are tortured by the results of tests that they really didn’t need to ever have,” said Rita Redberg, a University of California-San Francisco professor and cardiologist and an advocate for less medical testing. For example, if you discover a cyst, then “you’re living for the next year, two years, three years getting repeated tests to figure out whether it’s benign or a cancer,” Redberg said. She cautions patients against testing unless they have specific symptoms.
2. Testing Often Leads to More Testing — And More Risk
A reality of getting a medical test is that the results often lead to additional, and potentially more invasive, testing. Doctors call this “diagnostic cascade.”
Baute, for example, plans to continue monitoring her pancreas with annual scans. To her, she said, the financial cost and anxiety are worth it if she can feel “like I’m in control of my health and I have knowledge.”
But Redberg points to a worst-case scenario, documented by JAMA Internal Medicine in 2011: After starting an exercise program, a 52-year-old woman experienced chest pain and went to see her doctor. Her exam suggested that her pain was muscular and she had a low risk for heart disease. Still, her doctor ordered a scan of her heart to reassure her. The results led her doctor to order another test, during which her artery was ripped. She had emergency bypass surgery, experienced complications, and ultimately, Redberg said, “she ended up with a heart transplant — all from this unnecessary scan just to reassure her.”
3. A Few Simple Questions Can Help You Decide
Before saying yes to the test, it’s important to know about the risks and benefits — even if your doctor recommends it, Redberg said. She suggests asking a medical provider and yourself questions like:
- What am I going to learn from this test?
- How is this test going to help in my care?
- Could I improve my health without doing this test?
She said many test results, especially in her field of cardiology, end up pointing patients back to the basics of a healthy lifestyle, like eating well, exercising, and not smoking. And those, she said, could be advised without a test.
People and Policy
If your health insurance covers a medical test, that means the test has most likely met vetted, scientific standards that demonstrate benefits to patients. Insurers must cover evidence-based services that have a rating of A or B from the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force. Private insurers, as well as Medicaid and Medicare plans, must cover the full cost of recommended preventive screenings. Many medical tests marketed directly to consumers are not covered by insurance.
Emily Siner at Nashville Public Radio contributed to this report.
HealthQ is a health series from reporters Cara Anthony and Blake Farmer, approachable guides to an unapproachable healthcare system. It’s a collaboration between Nashville Public Radio and KFF Health News.

Witnessing the Failed Execution of Christa Pike: ‘We Could All Hear Her Breathing’
On Sept. 30, I was one of the seven media witnesses who observed Tennessee fail to execute convicted murderer Christa Pike, the first woman to face the death penalty in the state in almost 200 years.
From our previous reporting, each of us had an inkling that the lethal injection process might not go according to plan. Pike’s attorneys had asked the Tennessee Supreme Court to allow her to be hanged instead, citing concerns that a platelet disorder and small veins would make the actual injection not only painful but ineffective.
And Tennessee had already botched an execution attempt in May, when healthcare workers failed to establish complete IV access into Tony Carruthers, who was sentenced to death after being convicted for his involvement in the kidnapping and murders of three people in 1994.
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee said after the failed execution of Carruthers, who has maintained he is innocent, that the state wouldn’t try again to kill him for at least a year. After Pike left the execution chamber in an ambulance on Sept. 30, Lee announced he would suspend lethal injections for the rest of the year.
The morning of Pike’s scheduled execution, I and the other media witnesses arrived at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville by 8:30 a.m. and waited to be ushered into the prison with nothing but our driver’s licenses in hand. The plan was to wait inside until Pike began her journey to the death chamber at 10 a.m.
But we didn’t make it that far.
Before the Department of Correction’s staffers began moving us away from the outdoor media tent and our belongings, the reporters’ phones all went off. A federal circuit court had stayed the execution. This was my fifth stint as a media witness to an execution, and I’d never seen a stay issued. We didn’t know what that would mean.
It turned out to mean waiting for nine hours at the prison, barred from leaving the grounds. We spent most of it in the boardroom where parole hearings take place.
Hours of Waiting. Then, ‘It’s a Go.’
Throughout the wait, the victim’s family often came up in conversation. In 1995, Pike, then 18 years old, killed Colleen Slemmer, who was 19. Slemmer’s family in Florida traveled to Tennessee for the execution with money raised through crowdfunding. It’s unclear where they waited while the last-minute legal wrangling played out.
Sometime around 6 p.m., the prison system’s communications director, Dorinda Carter, told us: “It’s a go.”
Tennessee had asked the U.S. Supreme Court to lift the stay, and it did. Carter read the ruling aloud to us.
For unknown reasons, it took another hour or so for the security team to usher us into the witness bay, an all-white cinder block room with black pleather chairs in two rows and a big window overlooking the death chamber. A loudspeaker pipes sound into the room from the chamber when the microphones are on.
A black curtain hangs in front of the window inside the death chamber. Department of Correction workers open it once IV lines are inserted into the condemned prisoner.
The curtain is there to obscure the workers who place the IVs, in order to shield their identities as required by state law. That process is enshrined in the “Lethal Injection Execution Protocol,” which is the guidebook the Department of Correction writes for itself. There is no other regulation over executions in the state.
My employer, the Nashville public radio station WPLN, is a party in a lawsuit challenging the state’s concealment of the IV insertion. When executions are botched, it’s often due to something going wrong while IVs are placed — or with the subsequent step if IVs fail, placing a central line in a deeper vein through the chest, neck, or groin.
A lower court ruled in favor of WPLN and other media plaintiffs in January, but the state appealed the order, and it has been halted while higher courts consider the case.
The Death Chamber
The American Medical Association officially bars doctors from participating in executions, and many other health professionals also consider assisting an execution to be unethical.
Outside of prison staffers and the execution team, only the prisoner’s spiritual adviser and attorney are allowed in the room with the prisoner while the IVs are inserted. So generally, attorneys’ descriptions are the only account of the procedure.
Under normal circumstances, witnesses sit in the bay for 10 or 15 minutes with the curtain closed. That’s how long it tends to take for the IV team to place a line and start running saline, to prepare for the 5 grams of the sedative pentobarbital that will be pumped in to kill the prisoner.
Once the lines are set, the execution team enters an adjacent, concealed room. The IV lines run through the wall into that hidden chamber, from which the drugs are administered.
But at Pike’s execution, we sat in the bay for 45 minutes with the curtain closed and the microphone turned off.
Until Carruthers’ failed execution, the Department of Correction kept the lights off in the witness bay during the wait. Witnesses at his execution said they sat in a dark room for an hour and a half as the execution team tried and failed to place an IV line. This time, the prison kept the lights on.
The clock we use to give a minute-by-minute account is in the death chamber, so we can’t see it with the curtain closed. John North, a reporter with the television station WBIR in Knoxville, was the only witness wearing a watch. The rest of us asked him over and over what time it was.
After half an hour, it was clear the IV team must have been struggling.
We wondered whether Pike’s execution would unfold similarly to Carruthers’. That time, the governor called and ordered the execution halted before the curtain ever opened.
But at 7:27 p.m., we heard the curtain being drawn away.
We saw Pike in profile, lying on the gurney, facing the window for the other bay, where the victim’s family and

Drinking water costs spiked faster than inflation, grocery prices and median household income, researchers at nonprofit Food & Water Watch outlined in a first-of-its-kind report released Tuesday.
The average community water system increased household drinking water prices by 62 percent between 2015 and 2025—with costs in Louisiana, Maryland and New Hampshire having particularly steep rises, according to the 17-page report. California also stood out in the data when it comes to seeing expensive water bills.
Kristin Dobbin, an assistant professor of Cooperative Extension at the University of California, Berkeley, who was not involved in the report, called the analysis “extremely important.”
The finances behind drinking water are “not something we’ve had a big picture view on across the country before,” Dobbin told Inside Climate News on Monday, noting that broad trends are much easier to review for national electricity rates.
“We need to situate the water conversation within these broader concerns about affordability,” she said. “Certainly, it’s striking that they found just how quickly water costs have risen in the decade.”
Food & Water Watch gathered and analyzed 2025 water billing data for the nation’s 500 largest community water systems, which serve more than 155 million people, or 45 percent of the country. The nonprofit compared that data to household water bills from 2015.
The new report—“Surging Water Costs amid the US Affordability Crisis”—notes that last year, the average U.S. water system charged households $531 a year for 60,000 gallons of water, an estimate of annual average water use per household.
Eleven years ago, water systems typically charged about $336 a year per household, which is about $457 in 2025 dollars when adjusted for inflation.
While water bills vary greatly nationwide, a corporate water system in San Jose, California, had the highest price for water in the report, charging $1,416 annually in 2025.
Fifty-two percent of the 25 most expensive systems reviewed by Food & Water Watch were in California, despite the state’s systems representing just 18 percent of the 500 systems in the dataset.
In Louisiana, Maryland and West Virginia, water bills grew about twice as fast as state median household incomes, the report found.
In New Hampshire, bills grew nearly five times faster.
Mary Grant, the water policy director at Food & Water Watch, said West Virginia jumped out in the report.
Many water utilities claim that their bills are largely still affordable for median-income households, she said.
“But in some places like West Virginia, water bills are becoming unaffordable for a typical household at the median income, and that’s really a warning sign,” Grant said. “I think that we really need to have federal action to stop this crisis before more people suffer from unaffordable water bills.”
This story is funded by readers like you.
Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.
Donate Now
Affordability “is a legitimate challenge for many households,” said Jenn Kocher, a spokesperson for the National Association of Water Companies, which represents regulated, private water companies, which serve nearly 40 million U.S. customers.
Due to a publication embargo, Kocher could not review Food & Water Watch’s full report.
Still, after reviewing some of the findings Kocher said any assessment of water rates should also consider system performance, including reliability, water quality compliance and long-term infrastructure conditions.
Rising water bills “reflect sector-wide cost pressures, not ownership models,” Kocher, whose group has also fought for a permanent federal water-assistance program, said Monday. “In addition, rate comparisons should account for actual household usage and customer assistance programs, rather than posted rates in isolation.”
Why are water bills so high nationwide?
Dobbin, of UC Berkeley, said factors including inflation are having a big impact on the drinking water sector, which relies on specialized materials like treatment chemicals, a supply chain that was stressed during the COVID-19 pandemic and water infrastructure that is deteriorating nationally.
The Environmental Protection Agency recently found drinking water systems across the U.S. will need $625 billion in upgrades over the next twenty years to meet existing water quality standards. The American Water Works Association placed that figure closer to $960 billion.
In Maryland, a vast majority of customers receive water from municipal water systems, with rates set by city, town, or county governments instead of the Maryland Public Service Commission, which affects affordability, said David Lapp, a lawyer and policy analyst with the Maryland Office of People’s Counsel, an independent state agency that represents residential and noncommercial utility customers.
“Water service is an essential public service, but small privately-owned water systems in Maryland typically lack the customer base and financial resources necessary to provide that service reliably while maintaining affordable rates: of the 22 private water companies in Maryland, most serve fewer than 1,000 customers and some serve as few as ten,” said Lapp, who could not review the full embargoed report on Monday.
“In recent years,” Lapp said, “we have seen rates for customers of some of these private water companies, mostly in rural communities including in western Maryland, increase substantially.”
Other findings from Food & Water Watch’s report:
- Water bills increased at 1.6 times the overall inflation rate and more than 2 times the rate for groceries
- Water bills increased 19 percent faster than the U.S. median household income
- Water bills were considered unaffordable for low-income households in 93 percent of the analyzed water systems

The cryptocurrency industryâs leading network of super PACs is under scrutiny after revealing it will back 19 House Republicans but only 13 House Democrats.
Fairshake, which emerged as a kingmaker last election cycle, said just three members from each party would receive $1 million ahead of November. But it did not provide a breakdown for the rest of its spending, even as skeptics pointed out that its list contained more Republicans than Democrats in tough races.
âThe absence of [North Carolina Democratic Rep.] Don Davis is the most dangerous thing, because thatâs a Dem whoâs in a swing seat whoâs not getting love,â despite backing the industryâs top legislative priority, one cryptocurrency executive told Semafor.
Last cycle, âthere was at least the argument that Dems had driven them to this; this time, itâs been two years of going hard in on [President Donald] Trump.â
Know More
Hill Democrats privately grumbled about Mondayâs announcement and the groupâs decision not to support Democratic backers of cryptocurrency legislation like Davis and Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet, D-Mich., who represent swing districts and stood to benefit from outside spending.
The vast majority of lawmakers on Fairshakeâs list represent safe districts, facing only token opposition in their general elections. And the three Democrats named by Fairshake as receiving $1 million represented districts that have been competitive in previous elections but who are expected to win re-election this year.
Fairshake, which a spokesperson noted âhas always been and always will be an issue-focused organization,â spent more in Democratic primaries than Republican ones this cycle. As AI adoption spreads across the US workforce, new polling suggests that its benefits have so far been concentrated among those likely to hold upper-level positions.
Twenty-eight percent of US employees say they use AI at least weekly, according to a two-year study from Jobs for the Future, The Families & Workers Fund, and Gallup, while 54% say they havenât used it at work.
Use of the technology on the job is much more common among those with college degrees and those in managerial roles.
Speed is the most common benefit that AI users point to, with 63% saying the technology helps them do their jobs faster.
Among those in the highest paid positions â people earning $10,000 or more a month â seven in 10 say itâs accelerating their work, while fewer Americans who earn less say the same.

NY-17: The third in a series on the environmental stakes behind one of the nation’s most fiercely contested congressional races.
At 8, on her walk home from elementary school, Sylke Jackson would drop sticks, leaves and nut shells in Nyack Brook. They would soften and float along beside her, as if companions.
At 10, as Nyack Plaza was built to provide low-income housing, she remembers how the stream disappeared into a pipe. Her companions were replaced by the acetone fumes out of a budget cosmetics factory nearby. So, as a child, did she watch development force a change to her local landscape.
Today, at 56, she said years of large development projects, benefiting from tax exemptions while impacting the local environment, have fatigued residents and bred mistrust.
Now, in the closely watched U.S. House race in New York’s 17th Congressional District, which includes all of Rockland and Putnam counties and parts of Westchester and Dutchess counties, data center development has become a political flashpoint between U.S. Rep. Mike Lawler, Rockland’s Republican native son and a former New York state GOP leader, and his Democratic challenger Cait Conley, a decorated Army combat veteran who served on the National Security Council during the Biden administration.
Jacqui Drechsler, a Clarkstown resident, thinks industrial development is out of hand. “We’re sick of it,” she said. “Many of us feel our taxes are being abused.”
With Republicans controlling the U.S. House of Representatives by a narrow 218-213 margin, Democrats see the district—one of eight held by Republicans that Democrat Kamala Harris won in the 2024 presidential election—as one of their best opportunities to flip a seat.
Lawler, a former New York state assemblyman, lives in Orangetown, home to the Orangeburg data center hub. In the 2024 election, Lawler won Rockland County by an 18-percentage-point margin, crucial in helping offset his Democratic opponent Mondaire Jones’ margins in Westchester. Harris beat Trump by less than a point in the district.
Now, as Rockland residents contend with the consequences of development and question who benefits from it, the issue could shape how they view Lawler and his party this November. Healthcare, government ethics and reform, and cost of living—with data centers clearly linked to energy affordability—are top of mind for voters heading into the midterms, according to polling.
Data centers have become a leading issue in this race, with both Lawler and Conley mining each other’s remarks, campaign donations and records for political ammunition.
Lawler has sought to position himself as a check on the costs data centers impose on ratepayers and a supporter of local control over their development. He was a sponsor of the Ratepayer Protection Act, which passed the House last month before falling short in the Senate, and would require states to consider making data centers bear the full cost of any infrastructure upgrades needed to meet their growing energy demands.
Conley, meanwhile, blames Lawler for the growth of Rockland County as a data center hub and supports Gov. Kathy Hochul’s one-year statewide moratorium on new data center development.
“Unlike Mike, I support a data center moratorium. In Congress, I’ll ensure these companies don’t pass utility costs on to families, harm our environment or exploit our communities,” she wrote on X.
For Lawler, the politics are not straightforward. His labor coalition includes particularly strong backing from the building trades, whose members can benefit directly from the construction jobs generated by new development. Seven building-trades unions have endorsed his re-election campaign. He has noted that the county’s data-center industry predates his tenure, with many facilities serving financial services rather than AI.
In this critical midterm election year, moratoriums on development have taken effect across Rockland County.
In August, Lawler’s hometown imposed a six-month moratorium on new data centers and battery-energy-storage systems. Orangetown hosts four data centers, with one, a 20-megawatt facility owned by DataBank, seeking expansion. The 30-megawatt expansion was exempt from the town’s moratorium but has been paused after the local Planning Board voted unanimously to subject it to a more extensive environmental review, and the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation determined that the project is subject to Hochul’s statewide moratorium.
Clarkstown, north of Orangetown, has taken a broader approach, recently announcing a six-month building moratorium that temporarily halts certain major development applications, such as AI data centers, while officials assess the effects of future growth on infrastructure, transportation, the environment and public safety.
The backlash that prompted that moratorium has centered in large part on Cedar Corners, a proposed warehouse complex on a 41-acre forested site in Congers, one of several hamlets that make up the town. The site lies within a state-designated disadvantaged community, an area identified as facing environmental, public health and economic burdens.
The project would clear 27.6 acres of woodland, shrubs and groundcover, and create 627 parking spaces around the warehouses, with an additional 72 loading bays for commercial trucks. Brooklyn-based Vanta Developers has already secured $6 million in sales and mortgage tax exemptions for the project from the Rockland County Industrial Development Agency.
Mistrust has grown as public financial records show the campaign to re-elect Supervisor George Hoehmann received upwards of $8,500 from parties associated with the Congers project. The Clarkstown Planning Board is appointed by Hoehmann, who is effectively the town’s chief executive and has served as Supervisor since 2016.

Two Democratic senators want answers from Trump administration officials on industry influence on the still-unreleased AI regulatory framework, part of the AI executive order President Donald Trump signed earlier this year, according to a letter shared first with Semafor.
âWe are concerned that the Trump administration is accommodating the interests of Big Tech CEOs rather than addressing the safety and security risks posed by increasingly sophisticated AI systems,â Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., wrote in the letter addressed to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, White House cyber adviser Sean Cairncross, and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, among others.
The letter cites reported industry influence over what eventually became the executive order. It also highlights Meta CEO Mark Zuckerbergâs central role in shaping the more recent White House AI accord, pointing to the administrationâs âcozy relationshipâ with and âdeference to industry executives.â
The letter is the latest indication that Democrats are not giving up on a sustained push for answers from the administration on what is still a mysterious, voluntary framework for AI companies to submit their highest-level AI models to the government before release. Should the party gain power back in Congress, its demands will have more teeth.
âThe American people deserve strong guardrails set by democratically elected officials, not a toothless framework shaped in secret by a handful of billionaires,â Warren and Blumenthal wrote Monday, pressing for answers to five questions by Oct. 19.
They asked for details on meetings and correspondence between industry and government officials leading up to the release of the executive order in June. They also want to know whether independent evaluators or other stakeholders beyond industry were consulted, and demanded a description of the pre-deployment testing process established under the framework.

The Scoop
The White House has formally sent Congress proposed legislation that would impose mandatory minimum sentences on those convicted of fraud involving federal benefit programs, according to a copy of it seen by Semafor.
The proposal, sent to House and Senate leadership on Sunday night, follows President Donald Trumpâs call over the weekend for lawmakers to crack down on âfraud in Medicare, Medicaid, and Social Security programs.â
The administrationâs language would establish a range of mandatory minimum sentences based on the amount of loss involved in fraud schemes, according to the document. The proposal would also bar courts from placing those sentenced under the provision on probation or suspending their sentences.
People found responsible for less than $40,000 in losses would face at least one year in prison; those responsible for between $40,000 and $250,000 in losses would face at least two years in prison; and violations involving $100 million in losses or more would result in at least 20 years in prison. All violations would carry a maximum sentence of life in prison.
Itâs unlikely that Congress would be able to take up and pass the legislation during its post-election session after the midterms. With Democrats poised to take the House majority next month and the Senate also in play, the proposal also faces a steep climb in 2027.
Also included in the administrationâs legislative proposal is language that would hold âany officer or employee of the stateâ personally liable if they knew about alleged fraud and âwillfully, intentionally, or recklesslyâ ignored it. Such officials could also be financially liable for damages up to the âamount of all loss resultingâ from the fraud, or if that loss exceeds $1 million, up to three times the amount.
Know More
Trump in recent months has empowered Vice President JD Vance to pursue fraud across the US, as he and other Republicans have sought to campaign on a familiar message of stopping waste, fraud, and abuse.
The administration has pursued a number of high-profile fraud claims, most notably in Democratic-led states such as Minnesota and California.
This is the latest crime-related push from Trump, who won his presidential election in part on a law-and-order message. The proposal now sits with Congress, where lawmakers will have to decide whether to take it up.

President Donald Trump is expanding access to tax-exempt diesel while simultaneously pledging a swift end to the Iran war, an implicit acknowledgment that his administration is running out of ways to significantly stem the conflictâs economic fallout.
âItâll end very quickly, and prices are going to come down very sharply,â Trump said at the Nebraska rally Monday night, where he signed the executive order on so-called red-dyed diesel. âYou might say, âPlease, please, sir, itâs going down too fast.ââ
Later, he again promised to pay every American $5,000 if Republicans come out ahead in the midterms, warning of a â1929 South economic depressionâ if Democrats win.
Republicans are cool to the checks idea, and despite Trumpâs promises to wrap up the war, his administration has no clear way out of the conflict.

Lionel Messi is about to play his last match for Argentina.
On what will be his 208th appearance, the country's most-capped player and record goal scorer will bid an emotional farewell in a friendly against Benin at the Monumental in Buenos Aires.
Arguably Argentina's greatest ever player - only Diego Maradona comes close - announced his retirement from the national team on 31 August, six weeks after the World Cup final defeat by Spain, saying he had nothing more to give.
Coach Lionel Scaloni insists that if Messi ever wants to carry on, he can, and there is no embarrassment in changing one's mind. But that chapter seems closed.
His club career though goes on. The contract with Inter Miami runs to the end of the 2028 season, but it is reviewed year by year, and nobody close to him expects him to walk away a day before he has to.
In fact, it is quite likely he will renew it if he feels, mentally and physically, up for it.
Ask the people around him what comes after that and they smile, because Messi has never really planned beyond his next game.
Even so, the shape of what lies ahead is already in front of us. He will stay inside football, because he would struggle to live without it, but his other business interests stretch far outside the game.
An owner who wants to be involved in everything
Messi used to like the idea of being a sporting director or an adviser to the president, close to the decisions without all the travelling and the phone calls.
And asked recently whether he would rather be a coach or an owner, Messi chose owner.
A coach lives and dies by every Saturday and has to worry about far too many things for Messi's liking.
An owner shapes the direction of a club from a little further back. Having said that, he would be an owner who does not stop at approving the appointment of a manager and stepping away. He would want to be involved in everything.
The groundwork is being laid in Spain. UE Cornella, on the edge of Barcelona and in the fifth tier, is the nursery where young players grow. He bought it in April.
CD Eldense, in the second division, announced Messi as its new owner on 1 October, subject to authorisation from the Spanish sports council, the CSD.
Eldense will be the club that leads his football operation, but the target this season is not to get relegated, so former Villarreal boss Javi Calleja got the job with the arrival of the new owner.
The plan is to run both through people he trusts, who will act as a link between Messi and the clubs until the day he can give them his full attention.
For now he follows every Eldense match closely on his computer. After Eldense beat Real Oviedo by four goals to one, his first message as owner was an Instagram post that read "Aupa Deportivo".
The pull of his name has been felt as well. Around a dozen sponsors came forward within a couple of days, some of them brands that had been talking to the previous owners without ever closing a deal, and some that already have a relationship with him.
In Uruguay he and Luis Suarez founded Deportivo LSM in May 2025, and they won promotion to the country's third tier in its first season.
A network of more clubs was discussed at the start. But the sums needed to lift them up the divisions have cooled that idea quickly, and it is not on the table today. Messi's focus is to see whether Eldense can establish itself in La Liga.
There is a link to Miami as well. As part of his contract with Inter Miami, he will have some shares in the club when he retires. A franchise of his own is not part of the plan.
Could he go home to Newell's Old Boys, the club where he played as a child in Rosario? The idea has never been formally discussed.
It may have crossed his mind while drinking mate with Suarez, in the way a return to Barcelona or a spell at Napoli, the club of Maradona, might have.
Nobody close to the player expects it though. Everything is built around Europe and Miami, and the perfect home is waiting for the family in Castelldefels, close to the sea and Barcelona.
A growing business empire and love for youth football
Newell's will still be close, because the club is one of the sixteen academies at this year's Messi Cup.
If owning clubs is one love, youth football is the other, and his regular presence at his son's games and the Messi Cup are the proof.
He puts his money and his time into a tournament for Under-16 academies, which began in 2025 with eight teams.
Last year, the organisers expected him to come to one or two games, perhaps only the final, but to everyone's surprise, he sat through every match on every day.
This year the teams doubled to 16, from 25 October at Inter Miami's facilities in Florida, including Atletico Madrid, Chelsea, Barcelona, Inter Milan, Arsenal, UE Cornella, and others.
Away from the pitch, Messi has built a portfolio that helps explain why Forbes put his net worth at about $1.1bn, external in June, with earnings of around $140m over the previous year split between football and business.
His best known endorsement is the lifetime Adidas deal he signed in 2017.
The most visible piece is MiM Hotels, six boutique properties from Ibiza to Andorra, which Melia has run under a rental agreement since 1 November 2025.
MiM takes its name from Messi and the Majestic hotel group, and runs the hotels inside its Melia Collection.
In Rosario, his family firm invests in Carrasco M, a development of 24 homes by the Parana river, with Ãngel Di MarÃa's property agency handling the sales.
He is also a partner in the restaurant chain El Club de la Milanesa which plans to open five branches in Catalonia, the first in Castelldefels.
He has a mate collection with the drinkware giants Stanley, the brand's first multi-year deal with an athlete, and he gave his opinion on materials and colours.
