At least 15 people have died in overnight strikes across central and eastern Ukraine, in what Volodymyr Zelensky has described as one of Russia's "most vile" attacks.
Ukraine's president said a residential building in Pryluky in the Chernihiv region was destroyed as a "birthday 'gift' to Putin", who turns 74 on Wednesday. Strikes also hit Kyiv, Dnipro, Kremenchuk, Zaporizhzhia and Oleksandriya.
Zelensky said Ukraine had struck targets in attacks on Russia's Perm, Samara and Astrakhan regions in the past 24 hours, adding there was "also a response in the Black Sea", without providing further details.
Moscow is yet to comment on the latest strikes.
"The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively," Zelensky said, adding that 70 missiles were fired in total.
In the social media post on Wednesday morning, Zelensky said five people had been killed and 26, including five children, injured in a strike on a five-storey apartment building in Pryluky.
He added that people could still be trapped in the rubble.
Chernihiv Oblast police later reported that the death toll had risen to nine after the bodies of three children were recovered, with emergency workers continuing a search operation.
Two people were also killed and eight injured after Russian missile strikes damaged five apartment buildings in Dnipro and four high-rise buildings in Kremenchuk, said Zelensky.
Two people were also killed in the capital, Kyiv, and two others in Oleksandriya, he added.
Ukraine's national police posted pictures online showing what it says is an unexploded Russian Iskander missile in the middle of a Kyiv district. BBC Verify has confirmed the images are genuine and the apparent missile fragments came down in an area of open land surrounded by high-rise apartment buildings.
A video posted by the police shows people digging through collapsed remains of a residential building in Pryluky. Another verified video shows damage to cars and what appears to be rubble and a fallen tree in an area surrounded by apartment blocks in Kremenchuk.
Zelensky renewed a call for allies to provide air defence support packages to Ukraine, saying its military only managed to shoot down "some" of the missiles launched by Russia overnight.
According to Zelensky, one of the "key targets" of the attack was the country's energy infrastructure, which Moscow earlier said it would intensify strikes on following Ukraine's strikes on Moscow's energy facilities.
In a separate post on Wednesday, Zelensky said Ukraine had struck four targets in retaliatory attacks in the past 24 hours, including two oil facilities and a training ground in the Perm, Samara and Astrakhan regions.
"There is also a response in the Black Sea," the Ukrainian president wrote.
On Tuesday evening, footage emerged showing a huge plume of smoke engulfing an oil tanker off the coast of Sochi, along the Black Sea in southern Russia.
The Russian transport ministry later said unmanned boats had attacked the Liberian-flagged Aframax Rio oil tanker. Authorities claim the crew was rescued.
Separately, Bulgaria has halted a search for the missing crew of a ship that sank after being hit by a drone on Tuesday, Vice-Admiral Rumen Nikolov from the Maritime Administration Executive Agency said, as reported by Bulgarian television network Nora TV.
Tracking data shows the ship was anchored at the southern end of the Bosphorus strait until Monday when it entered the Black Sea heading north. Its last reported position on ship-tracking site MarineTraffic was at 23:43 GMT on Monday in what is known as the Bulgarian exclusive economic zone of the Black Sea.
Bulgarian specialist news outlet Maritime.bg reported the Alfa Watan was attacked by a drone and sank 70nm (130km) east of Byala.
As well as the civilian cargo ship, a second vessel - carrying grain - was also hit within Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone, its Prime Minister Rumen Radev said on Tuesday. The 18 crew members on the second vessel were rescued.
Bulgaria has not said who it believes was behind the attacks.
It comes as Russia intensifies strikes in the Black Sea, particularly the eastern side, as part of its war against Ukraine.
In an evening address on Tuesday, Zelensky claimed Russia was responsible for the attacks.
Moscow has not commented on the latest incident.

The News
Ruben Gallego isnât sure if heâs running for president yet, but he still has big plans for his Democratic Party once itâs back in power.
The Arizona senator is launching a huge, wide-reaching policy agenda on Wednesday thatâs aimed at confronting a labor market â and workforce â getting reshaped in real time by the AI boom. He wants to raise the minimum wage and boost overtime pay while imposing taxes on data centers and automated jobs, in addition to creating a federal public works program to ensure US workers can cope with AI.
Itâs a big move by the first-term senator as his party wages a pitched fight for control of Congress in next monthâs midterm elections. He said he recognizes that the public needs to start hearing about what Democrats intend to do with control in Washington, if they wrest some of it from GOP hands this fall.
âPeople that are working right now donât feel like their hard work is actually bringing them anything in return â¦ and going into election season, people want to know where Democrats stand,â Gallego told Semafor in an interview this week.
âWith AI becoming more and more prevalent in peopleâs lives and fears, I think itâs also important that we have a real forward-leaning policy that deals with AI and the workforce,â he added.
Gallegoâs sweeping proposals certainly look like the policy engine undergirding a 2028 presidential campaign. He said heâs ânot naiveâ about his work furthering that speculation, though he demurred on his future aspirations.
âNo matter what,â Gallego said, âIâm going to be involved inâ policy debates after the 2028 race.
âIâm not in the space right now to make a decision,â he added. âA lot of conversations have to happen between me and my wife, especially when it comes to raising kids and potentially running for office.â
Know More
Gallegoâs plan, which he pitches with a personal touch by invoking his upbringing in Arizona and the stateâs recent run of rapid growth and economic change, touches almost every aspect of the American economy.
But heâs chiefly concerned with evident public views that wages are not keeping pace with rising prices â that the American âdream is slipping away from millions of Arizonans,â as he writes in his proposal.
On top of raising the minimum wage to $20 per hour and pegging it to inflation, his agenda would promote sectoral bargaining agreements to establish labor standards for entire industries, require companies to provide paid leave, and raise overtime pay for eligible workers from time-and-a-half to double pay.
Heâs got equally ambitious plans for the AI industry, calling for a 10 percent excise tax on data center revenues and an end to tax incentives for those projects, a ârobot taxâ to discourage job losses due to automation, and consideration of a tax on AI tokens.
He wants to use that money to help fund a âNew Deal-styleâ public works program to ensure the US wonât experience âmassive unemploymentâ from the adaptation of AI.
âData centers and AI companies cannot just be operating untouched and also unbothered in terms of what they do to our labor markets, to our communities. They need to be part of the solution and not just be a problem,â Gallego said in the telephone interview.
He also wants to prioritize reclassifying certain so-called gig workers as employees rather than independent contractors and require companies to give workers more notice ahead of mass layoffs.
Gallego said heâs ready to maximize Democratic authority to get it done. He proposed putting as much of his proposal as he can in a party-line budget reconciliation bill that Democrats can pass with a simple majority if they control the House, Senate, and White House come 2029.
He added that Democrats should not listen to the Senate parliamentarian if, for example, a minimum wage hike gets ruled ineligible for reconciliation (as it was in 2021).
âWe shouldnât be afraid to push the limits on reconciliation, on overruling the parliamentarian,â he said, arguing that Republicans have âalready kind of blown up the parliamentarian primacyâ anyway.
Burgessâs view
The rising class of Democrats has big ideas, and you can already start to see the party nearing a big debate about its agenda ahead of 2028. Gallegoâs plan is one of the most expansive yet, but he isnât the first to jump in.
Sens. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland and Cory Booker of New Jersey have tax cut ideas. Sen. Andy Kim of New Jersey wants his party to give kids universal health insurance coverage.
This bold flurry is a stark contrast with Democratic leaders, who would like to start really shaping their agenda â¦ after the midterm elections.

Yorkshire Water has admitted a Â£1.5m scheme to reduce storm overflow discharges into a North Yorkshire river has not performed as expected.
When the investment was announced in 2024 for the River Ure in Ripon, the water company said the scheme would reduce the issue by about 75%.
But it said the number of recorded discharges from its Clock Tower combined sewer overflow (CSO), near the Ripon by-pass bridge, fell from 75 in 2021 to 43 in 2025, a reduction of about 43%.
The company has described the result as "disappointing", but stressed that comparing individual years was complicated by rainfall levels.
"[2025] was a particularly dry year, which will have further contributed to a decrease in discharges," a Yorkshire Water spokesperson said.
"As such, whilst there has been a reduction, the scheme did not perform as expected, which is disappointing."
Combined sewer overflows are designed as pressure-relief points on sewer networks which carry both wastewater and rainwater.
During heavy rainfall, they can discharge into watercourses to prevent overloaded sewers backing up into homes, businesses and streets.
Such discharges can be permitted by the Environment Agency under specified circumstances.
'Deeply disgusting'
Recent testing by campaign group Stop Ure Pollution and the Yorkshire Dales Rivers Trust further upstream has raised concerns about bacteria and other pollution in the river, the Local Democracy Service reports.
The Skipton and Ripon branch of the North Yorkshire Green Party has now submitted an Environmental Information Regulations request, seeking information held by Yorkshire Water about the performance of the Clock Tower scheme and changes in discharges following work carried out in 2025.
Green Party councillor Andy Brown said the levels of sewage going in the rivers "is deeply disgusting" and called the latest testing further upstream "far from reassuring".
He said campaigners and organisations, including Ripon City Council, would continue pressing for improvements.
"Yorkshire Water must play its part," he said.
"It must act, and it must deliver the facts â straight-up and undiluted."
Yorkshire Water said it was investigating further projects in Ripon as part of a Â£1.5bn investment programme aimed at reducing storm overflow use.
"We know there is much more to do to protect local watercourses," the spokesperson said.

The News
Fourteen major mining companies in DR Congo paid at least $20 billion to ineligible subcontractors between 2020 and 2025, the countryâs subcontracting regulator told Semafor, citing recently completed checks.
These findings at mining businesses, among them subsidiaries of Swiss commodities giant Glencore, Ivanhoe Mines and Chinese-Congolese joint-venture Sicomines, have prompted the regulator to plan tougher inspections this month to tackle breaches of subcontracting rules. These include the longstanding use of Congolese figureheads to disguise foreign control.
Glencore declined to comment. Ivanhoe Mines and Sicomines did not respond to Semaforâs requests for comment by publication time.
The regulatorâs move comes as the country courts new mining investment, including from the US, and seeks to ensure that Congolese partners genuinely own and help run the businesses supplying its mines, in line with its laws.
âWe are open to partnership. But we donât want people to come just for an extractive economy and leave us with holes,â Juan Ted Beleshayi, head of the Authority for the Regulation of Subcontracting in the Private Sector, told Semafor.
In recent weeks, he has ordered miners to terminate about 1,800 subcontracts with suppliers lacking valid registration certificates. These include contracts with 1,540 suppliers at two subsidiaries of Glencore, alongside those involving Ivanhoe Mines, Eurasian Resources Group and Sicomines. âWe really only carried out a simple check,â said Beleshayi, who took charge of the agency just over three months ago. He said he had completed checks begun under his predecessor.
This monthâs inspections would be âvery detailed and rigorous,â said Beleshayi. Inspectors will check who owns the suppliers on paper, who calls the shots and who controls the bank accounts. Companies who fail to comply with the regulatorâs decisions could face closure, he said.
Know More
Subcontracting represents billions of dollars to the Congolese economy â in 2025, 167 major companies declared $3.7 billion in contracts. The regulatory agency registers mining suppliers, which typically handle transport, machinery maintenance and construction among other work, and enforces rules based on a 2017 law that requires Congolese investors to own at least 51% of those businesses, with foreign ownership capped at 49%.
Chinese companies dominate DR Congoâs copper and cobalt mines and have often faced criticism from the regulator for shutting Congolese businesses out of subcontracting work. Beleshayiâs predecessor, Miguel Kashal, accused Sicomines, in 2023 of keeping all its subcontracts in Chinese hands. Three years ago, Sicomines pledged to give Congolese suppliers its secondary work. A company representative said that a misunderstanding over subcontracting rules had been resolved.
Beleshayi told Semafor his own inspections had found the same pattern. Sicomines did not respond to this claim. âWeâre not saying foreigners have to leave. We just want a 49-51 split,â Beleshayi said. Limited financing and technical skills prevent Congolese suppliers from handling major mining contracts, researcher Fridolin Kimonge told Semafor.
Ownership checks and contract cancellations alone cannot address those weaknesses. âIt is not enough to cancel; there has to be a plan behind it,â Beleshayi said. Temporary exemptions would allow foreign suppliers to help Congolese businesses become partners or competitors, he said. âWe will look for Congolese who understand American culture or can adapt to it, to build companies together,â he said of incoming US companies.
Rubenâs view
Like many African countries, DR Congo struggles to enforce laws that exist on paper. Part of the problem with its subcontracting law is finding replacements for the suppliers who break it. Congolese businesses often lack the financing and technical skills to take over major mining contracts, limiting how far the regulator can act without disrupting operations.
Washingtonâs push to loosen Chinaâs grip on Congolese minerals could give the regulator more options. Beleshayi expects American suppliers to accompany new US mining investments and form businesses with Congolese partners. If those companies can deliver the work and meet the ownership rules, existing suppliers would face competitors capable of replacing them. âYes, absolutely,â he said when I asked whether that prospect could pressure companies already operating in DR Congo to comply.
Conflict in mining regions, disputed licenses, slow permitting, and unpredictable enforcement have long deterred Western investors, while Chinese operators have been better able to absorb those risks. DR Congoâs recent reforms and Beleshayiâs crackdown could help signal to the US and European companies it is courting that the country is becoming a more reliable place to do business.
Room for Disagreement
Transparency has long been a central demand in efforts to improve DR Congoâs mining governance and local ownership alone offers no guarantee that contracts benefit ordinary Congolese, say critics.
In a 2020 study of six mining companies, researcher Kimonge found that DR Congoâs subcontracting law required majority Congolese ownership but provided no mechanism to trace where the money invested in those businesses came from. He warned that gaps in the rules also allowed political and administrative officials to own suppliers and steer contracts toward their own businesses. âThe situation has not improved much,â he told Semafor.
Mining governance analyst Jean Pierre Okenda called repeated denunciations of figureheads as âpopulist rhetoricâ that does not go far enough and urged the regulator to publish suppliersâ real owners and their ties to officials. Otherwise, he warned, replacement contracts could go to another set of politically connected businesses.

Tropical Storm Isaias has formed in the Gulf of Mexico and looks likely to strengthen into the first Atlantic hurricane of this year.
It is expected to reach hurricane strength late on Wednesday or early Thursday with forecasts suggesting it could then intensify to a category two storm.
It has the potential to bring damaging winds, torrential rain and a storm surge to parts of the US Gulf Coast with landfall expected on Friday or Saturday. Parts of Mexico could also see gusty winds and heavy rain as the storm moves northwards and eastwards.
Isaias will bring an end to the lack of hurricanes that has led so far to a record-breakingly quiet Atlantic season with development suppressed by the historic El NiÃ±o that continues to grow in the Pacific.
How strong will Isaias get?
In its latest update, the US National Hurricane Center estimates that Tropical Storm Isaias will strengthen rapidly and is likely to reach hurricane strength during Wednesday night. It will intensify further to a category 2 storm by Friday morning.
Parts of Mexico will feel the first impacts as the storm swirls out at sea, with 4in (100mm) of rain possible around the Bay of Campeche and the Yucatan Peninsula, accompanied by strong winds.
Isaias will then make landfall on the Gulf Coast - probably in Mississippi, Alabama or Florida - late on Friday or early on Saturday.
Forecasters predict that 3-6in (75-150mm) of rain could fall across the Gulf Coast, from south-east Louisiana to the north-west of Florida.
A few places could see up to 10in (250mm) with possible flash flooding, especially in urban areas, and the risk of isolated river flooding.
Dangerous winds are anticipated with the chance of a storm surge which could inundate low-lying coastal areas.
The US National Weather Service says it expects to issue Hurricane and Storm Surge Watches later on Wednesday with Florida Governor Ron DeSantis declaring a state of emergency across 25 north Florida counties over concerns about potential impacts.
As the storm moves further inland and loses contact with its warm water fuel source it will weaken but it is still expected to bring some potentially disruptive wet weather.
Between 1-3in (25-75mm) of rain is forecast for large swathes of the south-east USA - as far north as the Tennessee Valley and the Carolinas - with isolated totals of 5in (125mm).
El NiÃ±o has lead to an eerily quiet hurricane season so far
Forecasters in the US predicted the 2026 hurricane season would be quieter than average due to the developing strong El NiÃ±o in the Pacific Ocean.
Eight to 14 named storms are forecast, three to six of which would become hurricanes, including one to three major hurricanes.
So far it seems this quiet forecast has come to pass.
Isaias is the ninth tropical storm of the Atlantic season, but will be the first to become a hurricane.
On 12 September the season set a new record for the latest date reached without a hurricane forming since the start of the satellite era in the 1960s. Almost another month has passed without one since then.
A major reason for this is the very strong El NiÃ±o that is continuing to intensify over the Pacific.
The heat released into the atmosphere by the very warm seas in the eastern tropical Pacific has weather impacts that ripple across the globe.
It can disrupt wind patterns above the Caribbean and the Atlantic leading to increased wind shear, meaning winds that blow at different speeds and directions at different levels in the atmosphere.
This can rip storms apart before they have time to strengthen.
However this is not the only factor that determines whether hurricanes will form. While it reduces the odds, it does not make it impossible - as Isaias proves.
Isaias has formed over the Gulf of Mexico where sea temperatures are currently 30-31C - around 2C higher than normal.
It is the warm ocean that gives hurricanes their fuel, providing energy and moisture allowing them to grow.
There is currently limited wind shear meaning the storm has chance to strengthen. However, wind shear is expected to increase dramatically in the 24 hours before Isaias makes landfall which may limit how intense it can become.
However the range of factors influencing hurricane development is complex and exact forecasts are likely to shift slightly over the coming days.

0ed177868d2c.text: Mark Zuckerberg's Biohub is partnering with Google and the federal government in its ambitious effort to use AI for generating vast quantities of biological data that can predict how cells behave. Why it matters: The ultimate goal is an AI model that lets scientists test potential experiments virtually, helping them identify the most promising ones before spending the time and money to perform them in the lab. AI is capable of understanding proteins and other pieces of biology, but modeling an entire living cell is orders of magnitude more complex — and researchers don't yet have enough of the right data to do it. Driving the news: Biohub, the Department of Energy, the National Institutes of Health, Google DeepMind, Isomorphic Labs, Meta and a collection of scientific organizations are collaborating to create and standardize data for what Biohub calls a "universal virtual cell." The big picture: The goal is to use AI to explore many more scientific questions in biology virtually, allowing scientists to reserve expensive lab work for experiments most likely to teach them something important. "If we can put more and more reasoning and intelligence into every single question that we actually ask in the lab, the value of those empirical results will be far greater," Biohub head of science Alex Rives told Axios. Much of AI's recent progress has come from combining better algorithms, more computing power and enormous amounts of data. Biology presents an additional challenge: Much of the information AI needs doesn't exist yet and has to be painstakingly measured from the physical world. "We're at the beginning of a new scientific paradigm with AI," Rives said. Yes, but: Biology is harder than many other AI domains because researchers need what Rives calls "empirical AI" — models that learn from biological evidence and can accurately predict what happens in the physical world. "The big challenge in biology is to bridge that gap between compute and the digital world and the real physical world of biology and life," Rives said. "The way to do that is through data." Such models could eventually help scientists investigate fundamental questions such as how aging and regeneration work — or medical questions such as which molecular mechanisms are responsible for Alzheimer's disease. How it works: The first phase will create a broad map of cellular biology, gathering different kinds of information about cells and how they respond to changes. Further out, Rives envisions models that could examine an individual's disease and predict its molecular causes and the best way to intervene. The intrigue: The commercial partners will have one year of exclusive access to the data they develop before it is shared publicly. Rives said the temporary advantage is intended to give companies a reason to contribute money while still ensuring the resulting data becomes an open scientific resource. "We have to have some incentive for commercial players to be a part of this, and the embargo period creates that," Rives said. "But it's a one-year embargo. So what that means is that very rapidly, data becomes available broadly to scientific efforts." Zoom in: The effort involves $1.8 billion in funding, data, computing and measurement technology. DOE plans to invest more than $500 million over five years in biological measurement, modeling and computing, while NIH is bringing datasets and other resources resulting from more than $500 million in previous federal investment. Google DeepMind, Isomorphic Labs and Meta are collectively investing another $300 million, while Biohub previously committed $500 million to the effort. Flashback: When Biohub announced its initial $500 million effort in April, Rives told Axios one of the biggest unanswered questions was whether cellular biology would exhibit the same kind of "scaling laws" seen elsewhere in AI — with models becoming predictably better as they are trained on increasing amounts of data. What we're watching: Rives thinks researchers won't have to wait particularly long to find out whether the bet is working. Within a year of having the first large-scale dataset, he said, researchers should be able to train models, measure their capabilities and determine which kinds of additional biological data make them better. "It's worked in every field, and it works in biology too," Rives said, pointing to AI's progress in protein biology.

When social and affective neuroscientist Naomi Eisenberger’s dad developed dementia, she knew the popular wisdom. Caring for him could shave years off her life. But Eisenberger, of UCLA, was skeptical. Caring for her dad, who died in January, was stressful but also meaningful, she says. “It gave me a lot of joy to bring him some happiness.”
Caregiving kills as an idea first emerged in the scientific literature almost three decades ago. Distressed caregivers were 63 percent more likely to die within four years than non-caregivers, psychiatrists Richard Schulz and Scott Beach reported in 1999 in the Journal of the American Medical Association. The finding has since been cited almost 5,300 times, including almost 300 times in the past two years.
But researchers have largely failed to replicate that finding, with considerable research showing instead that caregiving links with living longer, Eisenberger and colleagues report in September in Biopsychosocial Science and Medicine. Caregiving stress may be softened by humans’ hardwired propensity to help others in need, the researchers suspect.
Silence surrounding caregiving’s positives is probably well-intentioned. In 2025, almost one-quarter of all adults in the United States, some 63 million people, provided care to adults or children with a medical condition or disability, according to a 2025 report by AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. Almost 65 percent of caregivers surveyed reported experiencing moderate or high emotional stress and almost half reported financial difficulties. Yet financial and emotional support for caregivers remains limited, the report notes.
Highlighting caregiving’s pros could jeopardize what little help is available, says sociologist and gerontologist Rebecca Utz of the University of Utah in Salt Lake City. “I don’t like to take our foot off the pedal and say that caregiving is so positive because it’s hard, and people need support.”
But painting caregiving as wholly negative, rather than nuanced, erases insight into how caregiving might also protect health, Eisenberger and colleagues argue. Most stressors, such as work-related burnout, link with chronic inflammation. Caregiving is less likely to show that link. Understanding that caregiving paradox could reveal how the body can withstand stress, Eisenberger says.
Moreover, helping a loved one may bring unexpected benefits, Eisenberger says. She cites a 2003 study in The Gerontologist showing that adult children who did not care for a parent with severe disabilities experienced more depression than those who did, though the researchers could not show causation. “I’m not suggesting everyone go out and engage in informal caregiving,” Eisenberger says. “I’m trying to make informal caregiving [feel] a little less scary.”
Caregiving was labeled as life-threatening
In highlighting the need for researchers to take caregiver well-being seriously, the 1999 study was groundbreaking, Eisenberger and colleagues write. But it had design flaws.
Schulz and Beach, both of the University of Pittsburgh, compared mortality rates across a four-year period from over 800 individuals. Roughly half the participants had disabled spouses, with some serving as caregivers and others not; the other half had nondisabled spouses and served as the control. Caregiving spouses filled out self-reports indicating their degree of mental strain.
Over the next four years, 103 participants died. Schulz and Beach zoomed in on mortality rates among one subgroup — spousal caregivers reporting considerable strain. Of those distressed caregivers, 17 percent died during the study period compared with 9 percent of control group members.
But buried in the data was another finding, Eisenberger and colleagues note: Individuals not providing care to their disabled spouses still died at the same rate as caregivers experiencing distress. Individuals with sick and healthy spouses occupy different realities, largely invalidating comparisons between those groups, Eisenberger says. In this case, the findings suggest that having a sick or disabled spouse, and not caregiving status, increases one’s likelihood of dying.
A nuanced picture
More than 6,000 caregivers were asked to evaluate both the sense of purpose and emotional stress associated with caregiving. Their answers illustrate the role’s emotional duality.
The team is not the first to dispute the idea that caregiving kills. That list includes Schulz himself, who coauthored a 2009 Psychological Science study titled, “Caregiving behavior is associated with decreased mortality risk.” (Neither Schulz nor Beach could be reached for comment.) That study, though, has been cited less than 400 times, with just a couple dozen citations in the past two years.
“I … assumed that the field would have taken notice,” says evolutionary and social psychologist Stephanie Brown, an author on the 2009 paper and a similar 2014 review of caregiving in Social Issues and Policy Review. But “slam pieces on caregiving” remain on prominent display in doctor’s offices and other medical settings, says Brown, of the Renaissance School of Medicine at Stony Brook University in New York.
Caregivers are stressed. Biology may help compensate
More recent research hints at why caregiving, a tremendously stressful undertaking, may not kill.
It’s increasingly accepted that stress can trigger systemic inflammation that then compromises the immune system. In theory, stressed caregivers should be inflamed. They’re not, researchers reported in 2020 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. That study relied on data from more than 30,000 U.S. adults. In surveys taken in the early 2000s and the 2010s, participants indicated their caregiver status, type and intensity of care being given, and experiences of strain. They also provided blood samples.
The scientists zoomed in on roughly 250 people who became regular caregivers and analyzed their blood samples for six inflammation-related biom

Ten people who came into contact with a man who died of Ebola in Kenya have been quarantined, health officials in the East African nation say.
They are also trying to trace 57 other contacts of the Kenyan patient after he travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo, dying in hospital in Nairobi on Monday.
This is the East African nation's first-ever Ebola case and there is now growing concern about the country's screening measures.
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention chief has told the BBC that despite being sick for a month, the patient passed through multiple cities in DR Congo, driving to Uganda and eventually flying to Kenya without his sickness being detected.
"We know that he left Buta, a city in [northern] DR Congo, to drive to Kisangani. And from Kisangani, he took a flight to Beni. From Beni, he drove to Uganda. And from Uganda, he took a flight to Nairobi," Jean Kaseya told the BBC's Focus on Africa programme.
"What are symptoms he was presenting? Why was he not detected?" he asked.
The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
The current outbreak in DR Congo, which began in May, has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.
Kaseya said the Africa CDC was investigating the case, alongside the Congolese authorities. A team from the organisation was also due to meet the Kenyan health authorities.
Kenya's health ministry official Patrick Amoth said the patient might have passed screening after taking medications that masked his symptoms.
After arriving at the airport in Kenya's capital, he was transferred by a relative to a hospital in the city where he died, and was buried on Tuesday in line with health safety guidelines.
Kenyan authorities have urged people not to panic, with the health ministry assuring of heightened surveillance at airports and border crossings.
But Dr Dennis Miskellah, a representative from Kenya's main doctors' union, said the Ebola case did not come as a surprise to him and most health workers.
He told the BBC's Newsday programme that he had witnessed "lapses" at various border points, including with neighbouring Uganda and Tanzania, as well as at Kenyan's main airport.
"How could you have been sick for almost a month plus in DR Congo, come all the way to the country through not just any small border point, but the main entry point, the main gateway into the country and pass unnoticed?
"That's the question that most Kenyans are asking."
The health ministry says it has intensified measures to contain the spread, with a joint response involving county administrations, humanitarian partners and others.
President William Ruto has said that surveillance and rapid response teams are on the ground, building on the systems that the country adopted following the outbreak in DR Congo in May.
His spokesman said Kenya had the capacity to detect, isolate and manage suspected cases, adding that so far more than 650,000 travellers had been screened and 267 samples tested.
Facilities in four main hospitals have been designated for the management of Ebola patients, including at the Nairobi Hospital, where the first Ebola patient died.
In June, a US plan to establish an Ebola treatment facility at a military base in the central Kenyan town of Nanyuki sparked concern, with Kenyans reacting furiously about the risks of cross-border infection. The plan was halted by the courts.
On Wednesday, Health Minister Aden Duale told local television station NTV that pending the outcome of the court case, the government was considering turning the facility into the "first" infectious disease hospital in the region, to deal with outbreaks like Ebola.
More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak of the disease.
Shortly after DR Congo declared an outbreak of Ebola in May, it was also reported in Uganda, where two people died.
However, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared that county free of the disease in August.
On Tuesday, Uganda's health ministry emphasised that the country remained free of Ebola and was continuing to "maintain strong surveillance measures to protect public health".
It said the Kenyan Ebola patient had transited through the country for less than 24 hours and screening teams had "observed he had a normal temperature at the time of departure".
According to Africa CDC chief, his organisation was working with all the countries in the region to reinforce response mechanisms.
Kasiye said Kenya was "well prepared" and was therefore able to immediately receive the case, "but it is not the case for all other countries".
"It means the regional approach is more important today to stop this outbreak."
However, Kasiye said there was no quick testing available at border points and the taking of temperatures was unreliable as medication is able to stop a fever.
"I have to make it clear - we don't have diagnostics to test for Ebola. It's just about temperature," he said.
Dr Miskellah, from the Kenyan doctors' union, said he was concerned that governments were counting on the "honesty and full co-operation of the travellers to self-declare, to say the truth" about their health.
This was however undermined by a lack of proper health education to destigmatise the virus, meaning people often wanted to hide their symptoms, he said.

South Africa is facing growing pressure from labor unions and business groups to provide around $600 million in fuel relief, after the Iran war drove petrol prices to record highs in the continentâs biggest economy.
The calls heap pressure on the coalition government to loosen its purse strings, threatening to undermine its reputation for fiscal discipline just as Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana prepares to present his three-year fiscal plan later this month.
South Africaâs biggest labor federation, Cosatu, described the price shock, which sent a liter of fuel above 30 rand (almost $2) for the first time, as âa cost of living crisisâ because workers spend nearly a third of their wages on transport.
In response, the central bank has raised its main interest rate twice this year and warned in its monetary policy review this week that it has adopted a âfirefightingâ stance before energy prices spill over into broader inflation. The raised borrowing costs apply a secondary squeeze on households and businesses demanding fiscal relief.

Chinaâs competitor to the dollar-denominated system that zips money between global banks saw record daily volume in August. A spike last spring, as the Iran war sent sanctioned companies looking for a way around Washington, now looks less like a blip and more like a permanent, if small, leg-up for Beijingâs efforts to build a parallel system of financial plumbing.
This isnât the death of the dollar. New data from Atlantic Council researchers Jessie Yin and Lize de Kruijf shared first with Semafor, shows the greenback still underpins most global trade and foreign-exchange transactions. (Try converting Turkish lira to Indian rupees without going through the greenback.)
âThe top line numbers all remain stable,â said Josh Lipsky, the Atlantic Councilâs chair of international economics. âBut look underneath the hood and thereâs some worrying signs.â
Chinaâs efforts to dethrone the dollar have so far mostly been a curiosity. Renminbiâs place in global central-bank reserve coffers has actually fallen since 2022, despite Beijing shoveling its currency into developing economies through central-bank swap lines. But crises can reset the board: The number of direct participants in Beijingâs cross-border interbank payment system has more than doubled since Russiaâs invasion of Ukraine, and the resulting weaponization of Western financial networks to freeze Russian assets.

Lizâs view
The bull market of the early 2010s was called the most hated rally in history. This one may be a close second.
Back then, investors underestimated the power and determination of the Federal Reserve to prop up a flagging economy. Flatlining corporate earnings, European debt bombs, and runaway government spending disappeared into a sea of free money.
Todayâs problem is hyperscalers spending themselves into oblivion, spreading inflation well beyond Silicon Valley and obscuring problems nearly everywhere else. The S&P 500 hit another record yesterday, even as oil stays trapped in the Gulf and Europe tilts toward another debt crisis. The rally is driven by just a handful of AI companies. Some of them have the earnings to back it up â Goldman Sachs expects Nvidia and Micron alone to account for a third of the S&P 500âs earnings growth in the current quarter â but the return on their investments is far from certain, and far from now.
Alan Greenspanâs declaration that the Fed canât deflate a bubble without wrecking the economy is far from economic canon, but itâs holding up in the AI era. Mark Zuckerberg and Satya Nadella arenât slaphappy consumers who can be sobered up by higher rates. They are self-styled great men of history in an existential race and wonât stop spending until their shareholders make them. Their shareholders are very happy. You see the problem.

One thing was clear on Skydanceâs first day of life: Beneath David Ellisonâs velvet glove is Ynon Kreizâs iron fist. To earn his $40-odd million payout to help run the combined Paramount-Warner Bros., Kreiz will have to serve as a Tom Wambsgans-ian pain sponge â the executor and cost-cutter behind Ellisonâs lofty vision boards.
After Ellison told Skydanceâs assembled employees at a town-hall meeting Tuesday that âthere is something magical aboutâ movie-making, Kreiz stated plainly âultimately, our success will be determined by performance,â according to prepared remarks viewed by Semafor. Investors are warily eying Skydanceâs freshly downgraded debt, and layoffs are coming. Thereâs only so far Hollywood and Washington connections can take Ellison before the reality of managing a debt-laden media giant forces him to prove he can actually run one.

Scott Bessent isnât worried. The market is. The US Treasury secretary has been trying to reassure investors that economic growth and budget restraint can put the US governmentâs financial house in order. But heâs 0-for-3 on his 3-3-3 plan of increasing oil production, growing the economy, and cutting the deficit. His bond buyback program landed as a curious half-step â big enough to suggest concern but too small to make a difference. Tempers are flaring, WSJ reports.
Cracks are showing in the riskiest corners of the credit markets, always the first to surface confidence gaps. Take the loan market, where the amount of deeply distressed loans (those made to low-rated companies trading at 60 cents on the dollar or less) has ballooned to a level not seen since March 2020, as JPMorgan strategists pointed out this week. The biggest concentration of these highly distressed loans, of course, is in the technology sector, where SaaSpocalypse fears have eased among stock investors but not sandbag-packing credit investors. Rising global bond yields and Fed tightening havenât helped. If Bessent âis the house now,â investors are calling his bluff.

Elon Muskâs SpaceX is the in-betweener in the AI capex wars. SpaceXâs reported $40 billion debt raise to buy Nvidia chips shows it is stuck between mature tech giants like Google and Meta and startups like OpenAI and Anthropic, whose private status tends to forgive their inability to pay their own bills.
SpaceX carries five times more debt than Alphabet, and three times more debt than Meta, relative to their respective profits, and while money from Starlink helps prop up SpaceXâs cash-guzzling rocket business, it isnât nearly the cash cow that rivalsâ ad businesses are. It needs to borrow because itâs spending more on AI than itâs taking in from the rest of its businesses.
By going public in June, SpaceX locked itself out of the raise-and-pray venture capital world. But its stock priceâs sideways lurch since then makes it unattractive to issue new shares to pay for its growing AI tab. Its BBB credit rating is two notches below Meta and Alphabet, and a tougher sell with blue-chip bond funds; enter Apollo, which has a pot of money to match seemingly every risk out there (including cash-strapped governments!). Oracle finds itself in a similar position.

Susan Collins distanced herself from President Donald Trump during her first Maine Senate debate with Democrat Troy Jackson, arguing she has maintained her political independence by repeatedly voting against Trump's agenda and saying that she's "not exactly his favorite senator." Democrats are trying to flip the Maine Senate seat as they work to win control of the Senate. Trump lost the state in 2024, giving Democrats hope of defeating the five-term moderate Republican, who has been targeted by Democrats in previous elections and survived. READ MORE: Troy Jackson is racing against time in his bid to unseat Susan Collins During the hourlong debate, Jackson focused largely on attempting to connect Collins to Trump. He kicked off the night by pointing out she cast a critical vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a Trump nominee who eventually helped overturn the constitutional right to abortion. Collins supports abortion rights and said Kavanaugh assured her it was settled law, but she has said recently that she does not regret her vote to confirm him. Please check your inbox to confirm. "Would you trust her to pick the next Supreme Court justice?" asked Jackson, a former state lawmaker and logger. He also repeatedly brought up her procedural vote to advance the president's 2025 tax and spending bill — though Collins ultimately broke with her party to vote against it. READ MORE: Maine Dems hammer Collins over report of pay-to-play probe. GOP senator calls it 'completely false' Collins countered that she has voted against Trump more than she did Joe Biden when the Democrat was president, and has pushed back against Trump on tariffs, immigration enforcement and the war in Iran. "I voted against my party more than another other senator on either side of the aisle," Collins said. The attention on Trump comes as only 31% of U.S. adults approved of how the Republican is handling the presidency, according to a September AP-NORC poll. That's well below where his approval stood when he took office last year. The president has started holding rallies around the country in an effort to help GOP candidates win in November, telling voters to pretend he is on the ballot. At Tuesday's debate, a moderator noted Trump has floated the idea of campaigning in Maine, and asked Collins if she would stand beside him if he does. "I'm not exactly his favorite senator," she said, adding "I would say that he's not coming to Maine." Collins, who has said she didn't vote for Trump in 2016, voted to convict the president after his 2021 impeachment over his role in the Jan. 6 Capitol riot. In January, Collins joined a handful of Republican colleagues in backing a failed effort to limit the president's ability to unilaterally use force in Venezuela. The move prompted Trump to say on social media that they "should never be elected to office again." Collins argued that her seniority and experience in the Senate have resulted in money and resources for Maine, saying: "Leadership matters in Washington." WATCH: Gov. Wes Moore, GOP challenger Dan Cox face off in Maryland governor's debate She also spent Tuesday evening attempting to turn the focus of Maine's high cost of energy and housing on Jackson, arguing that he had a larger role in making a difference when he was the state Senate president and criticizing "Augusta's failed policies" as a way to connect Jackson's to the state's struggle to address affordability. Other moments showed how the two candidates were approaching their appeal to working class Maine voters. For example, as Collins touted her ability to remove certain items from Trump's trade war with Canada, including pulp, concrete and road salt. Jackson pushed back by quipping "we can't eat road salt." Jackson and Collins are scheduled to participate in three more debates later this month. Almost two-thirds of the population of chinstrap penguins have disappeared from a remote volcanic island near Antarctica, aerial surveys suggest.
Zavodovski Island was home to the largest penguin colony in the world, but researchers who carried out the surveys say it has now lost that accolade.
According to the study, there were 63% fewer occuplied nests of chinstrap penguins in 2025 than at the same time in 2011.
The research team say climate change is affecting the birds' food supply and survival, and the penguins may now be officially endangered.
Another species of penguin, the macaroni, also nests on the island and is thriving, which scientists believe is linked to their more varied diet.
Zavodovski is part of the South Sandwich Islands, a remote archipelago north of the Antarctic continent which is a UK overseas territory.
In 2011, it was hailed by the British Antarctic Survey (BAS) as home to the largest penguin colony in the world - with an estimated 600,000 chinstrap penguins and 90,000 macaroni penguins nesting on its bleak, rocky terrain.
BAS, which led this new research, says it is "one of the most extreme places in the world to undertake fieldwork".
A BAS team sailed for 15 days to reach the island and study its avian inhabitants, using drones, aerial photography and fitting tracking devices to 20 birds.
This research and satellite imagery suggested that - between 2011 and 2025 - the number of occupied chinstrap penguin nests declined by 63%.
Where did all the penguins go?
The researchers say the "alarming" fall in the chinstrap population is all about the food supply and rising ocean temperatures brought about by climate change.
Prof Norman Ratcliffe, who led the research, explained that the chinstraps' "specialist diet" and preference for cooler waters appears to have left them vulnerable.
"With waters warming, the krill [that the chinstrap penguins eat] have moved southwards.
"Sea-ice cover to the south and a lack of suitable islands for nesting prevents chinstraps from following the food," he said.
Hungry whales and active volcanoes
The team examined other possible threats to the penguins' precarious existence on their remote island. Birds here nest in the shadow of an active volcano - Mount Curry, also aptly known as Mount Asphyxsia.
Sites downwind of the volcano have been given names including Stench Point, Noxious Bluff and Asphyxia Plain, because of the smell of fumes emitted from the crater.
Dr Ratcliffe told BBC News: "When you add all the penguin guano on top of that, and you really do have one of the smelliest places in the world.
"It's like a penguin Mordor."
Mount Curry's last major eruption was back in 2016, but the penguin declines that this study analysed have been steady and ongoing since 2011, suggesting that something else was happening.
Another concern was competition for the krill that chinstrap penguins rely on - possibly from migrating humpback whales. But, while the humpbacks eat huge quantities of krill, they also help boost krill production by fertilising marine plants that the krill feed on (with their huge quantities of whale poo).
Researchers say a more fundamental, climate-driven shift in ocean food supplies is to blame.
There is an unexpected element of this story that also adds to the picture of how - and why - this region is changing: While the chinstrap population has been declining, the number of macaroni penguins on the island has increased dramatically.
Macaroni penguins, scientists say, are more adaptable, because they have a broader, more flexible diet.
Tracking data from the study showed that the macaronis foraged in warmer waters to the northeast of the island, where scientists say they were were likely to be supplementing their diets with fish and other crustaceans.
Dr Ratcliffe said this shift was "biggest change in community composition ever observed at a single location in Antarctica".
"Our data shows that the cold-adapted Antarctic chinstrap species are no longer thriving beside their sub-Antarctic neighbours," he added.
"It is further evidence of how rapid warming in the Antarctic is impacting unique and sensitive ecosystems."
As for the title of world's largest penguin colony, scientists say that is now held by a site more than 5,000km away - on the other side of the Antarctic continent - Cape Adare in the Ross Sea.
The research is published in the journal Current Biology, external.

The Scoop
Every Thursday afternoon, a cadre of state AFL-CIO leaders meets on Zoom to advance a shared project: the âContract with Working Americans,â a populist economic platform they devised independently of the national AFL-CIO.
These calls are a new organizing tactic for labor, which historically leads top down from Washington, and the goal is new, too: to mobilize not only workers who belong to unions, but the many more American workers who do not.
âWeâre trying to connect two segments of a group that, quite frankly, should be naturally aligned, but just havenât,â said Derrick Osobase, vice president of Communications Workers of America District 6, which covers Texas. âWe are actively talking to working-class people who are not affiliated with the union, and wrapping them into an agenda that they have said will make their lives different.â
The idea for the âcontractâ was born of a paradox: Union membership has declined from 20% of all workers in 1983 to 10% last year, even as union popularity hovers at 90-year highs. Seventy-one percent of US adults approve of unions, according to Gallup, including 52% of Republicans.
The widening gap between those figures is where organizers see an opportunity.
âFor years the labor movement, for understandable reasons, has fought for a narrower set of issues,â said Francis Eanes, executive director of the Maine Labor Climate Council. âBut I think itâs made it easy for some folks to say weâre just another special interest out there fighting for our own.â
Skeptics of labor, he said, say a union is âa private welfare state that provides benefits to its members and no one else. I think itâs an unfair characterization, but itâs not entirely unfair.â
The Gallup numbers suggest Americans of different political shades seem to be concluding that private welfare states arenât such a bad idea.
In a moment of declining trust in Congress, political parties, the media and many other institutions, labor activists believe a union-led movement whose stated aim is to agitate for the benefit of all workers could have real juice in setting a new national agenda as audacious as Newt Gingrichâs 1994 âContract with America,â which helped produce a sweeping congressional majority for Republicans that year.
âBoth political parties are wildly unpopular. Unions are more popular than ever,â said Matt Schlobohm, executive director of the Maine AFL-CIO. âIt is really important that we â working people, the labor movement â define and put out an agenda and demand it. Or somebody else will define it for us, and itâll be culture wars, or itâll be some mealy-mouth opportunity agenda.â
The main tenets of the âContract with Working Americansâ were born out of a series of canvassing surveys led by state AFL-CIOs and affiliates. But there is no single document; iterations of it vary somewhat from state to state, to account for local trades and industries. (The national AFL-CIO did not respond to a request for comment.)
The âcontractâ framework was inspired by negotiated union contracts and is meant to establish policy commitments from candidates in exchange for the movementâs support. All versions include a set of economic priorities: Signatories must support lowering prescription drug costs by expanding the governmentâs power to negotiate directly with companies, expanding healthcare coverage, capping childcare costs, bringing down the price of gas, and raising the minimum wage.
The contracts adopt a populist tone throughout. They include shared language demanding a congressional stock trading ban and a ban on lobbying by elected officials after leaving office; a tax on billionaires; and, in a time of rising AI anxiety, a ban on AI surveillance, to prevent ârobots deciding your paycheck, hiring and firing you, or monitoring your work.â The language does not include identity- or criminal justice-specific provisions, and largely steers clear of climate topics.
Several candidates with national profiles have signed on to versions of the contract so far this cycle, including in Texas, where Democrats hope that Senate nominee James Talarico and gubernatorial nominee Gina Hinojosa could make the state ground zero for a Blue Wave next month. Troy Jackson, the Democratic Senate nominee in Maine, delivered a public âPledge to Working Mainersâ adopting the demands in Maineâs contract.
Independent Alaska candidate Bill Hill, a commercial fisherman and teacher challenging Republican Rep. Nick Begich, told Semafor he supports the ideas in the contract, though there isnât an Alaska-specific version of the contract to sign.
âThis is about an agenda that delivers for the hardworking people of this country, by lowering costs, making sure hardworking people get the value of their hard work, and building a system where billionaires and big corporations play by the same rules we do,â Hill said in a statement.
Another state AFL-CIO, and its endorsed candidate for statewide office, have agreed to sign on as soon as this week, and more are circling.
No Republicans have backed one of these contracts. Organizers in North Carolina and Maine said that the campaigns for Republican Michael Whatley and Sen. Susan Collins had not responded to their outreach.
Still, organizers said they see progress. In interviews, most said they believe labor has long been too aligned with the Democratic Party, leading to a kind of âmutual malaise,â in the words of North Carolina AFL-CIO President Braxton Winston.
Eanes touted the contractâs potential to inject what he saw a bit of virtuous transactionalism back into the democratic process by energizing votes around specific policy demands, building back a kind of feedback loop that unions have down to a science.

Earthquakes frequently trigger rock falls. Now there’s solid evidence marsquakes can send boulders tumbling, too.
Scientists mined high-resolution imagery of the Red Planet taken shortly after a recent temblor and found hundreds of new imprints left by tumbling boulders, researchers report September 2 in npj Space Exploration. Such rockfalls can be used as a proxy for seismic data, which is difficult to collect across the solar system.
The data were collected with NASA’s InSight lander, which touched down on Mars in 2018. Over the next four years, its seismometer detected more than a thousand marsquakes. Many of those temblors originated in a region known as Cerberus Fossae, just north of the Martian equator. That’s a dynamic landscape riddled with slopes, cracks and rocks on the move, says Vijayan, a planetary scientist at the Physical Research Laboratory in Ahmedabad, India, who goes by a single name. “Thousands and thousands of boulders have fallen.”
Vijayan and his collaborators focused on one well-detected marsquake captured by InSight that occurred in July 2019 just a few tens of kilometers from Cerberus Fossae. By comparing images taken in June 2019 and December 2020, the researchers discovered 27 new linelike features. Each was composed of tens to hundreds of distinct marks. These structures were most likely tracks created by boulders bouncing downhill, the team concluded.
Using historical imagery, the researchers calculated that only about two such features form each year on average in Cerberus Fossae. “We have statistics of previous boulder falls,” says Bivas Das, a seismologist at the Physical Research Laboratory and a member of the research team. Recording 27 new structures over a span of just 18 months is wholly unexpected, Das says. “That’s a big increase.” The nearby marsquake recorded by InSight was probably the instigator, the team concluded.
Mysteries remain, however. All of the rockfalls occurred on the north side of a prominent valley in Cerberus Fossae, despite more boulders being located on the south side of the valley. “That puzzles us,” Vijayan says. The complex landscape of Cerberus Fossae might well alter how seismic waves travel, making it difficult to predict how shaking will impact different areas, he says. “The wave propagation is going to be complicated.”
Looking for such boulder falls elsewhere could help space exploration efforts, the team suggests. Human settlements would do best avoiding areas that are seismically active, and tumbling boulders can be the proverbial canaries in the coal mine, Vijayan says. “They’re like a proxy in the absence of seismic data.”

176685279873.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/russia-keeps-tight-lid-on-lab-workers-death-as-global-concerns-mount Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Russia keeps tight lid on lab worker's death as global concerns mount World Oct 7, 2026 10:57 AM EDT Russian authorities are keeping a tight lid on information about last week's suspicious death of a lab worker in Siberia that has been surrounded by secrecy and claims that it could have been caused by pneumonic plague. While the case has raised global concerns, Russian state TV and other national state-controlled media have steered clear of the subject. Some state-sponsored news outlets withdrew earlier reports about the case, which has topped independent online news outlets. READ MORE: What to know about a Russian lab worker's death and speculation about pneumonic plague Russia's public health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said Sunday the lab worker was diagnosed with "pneumonia of unknown etiology," meaning its origin was not known. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. In its official, tersely worded statements, it does not link the case to pneumonic plague, saying only that "extensive" testing found no evidence her illness was caused by any of the pathogens she worked with at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East. A state TV station in Irkutsk reported she died Oct. 2 in a hospital in Shelekhov, a town just outside Irkutsk. Officials have quarantined a hospital and are monitoring the contacts of the worker, who died of what unconfirmed media reports said could have been pneumonic plague — a less common but severe form of plague that can spread from person to person. READ MORE: How Russia and the world are responding to a possible case of pneumonic plague after lab worker death Moscow informed the World Health Organization that no case of plague has been registered in the Irkutsk region in southeastern Siberia. President Donald Trump said Tuesday he would speak about the issue "very soon" with Russian President Vladimir Putin and report about it "probably tomorrow." Wednesday is the Kremlin leader's 74th birthday. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Wednesday that a Putin-Trump call hasn't been set yet but could be organized quickly. Trump said the U.S. stands ready to help Russia. Asked what the U.S. intelligence community was saying about the case, Trump said the U.S. is in "very deep discussions" on the topic. The WHO prods Russia for more information In response to the WHO's request to clarify the situation in view of media reports alleging pneumonic plague as the cause of the lab worker's death, Russia has declared that no case of plague had recently been registered in Irkutsk oblast, the U.N. organization said. Russian health authorities reported a full range of preventive measures had been carried out — including tracing of the dead woman's contacts, medical monitoring and lab tests, WHO said Wednesday. The Russian note relayed to The Associated Press by the WHO said the test showed "no presence of dangerous infectious disease pathogens in any of the contacts." WATCH: Understanding pneumonic plague after Russian lab worker's death The Geneva-based organization said it has requested further information to clarify the cause of the severe pneumonia, the pathogen that prompted the public health measures, and media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause. The organization said it has remained in contact with Russian health authorities and offered technical support. The Kremlin and other officials stay tight-lipped Peskov has referred all questions to Rospotrebnadzor, which does not mention suspected plague in its reports. In its latest statement Tuesday, the agency said "the sanitary and epidemiological situation in the Irkutsk region, the cities of Irkutsk and Shelekhov is calm." It said authorities were completing a "complex of prophylactic measures and medical observation over contacts," adding that so far they have found two cases of COVID-19 and two cases of rhinovirus. "No other infectious pathogens have been found among contacts," it said. The lab worker who died was described as highly diligent The news outlet Lyudi Baikala — or "People of Baikal" — identified the dead lab worker as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova and said she first was hospitalized with cold symptoms Sept. 29 and died three days later. It quoted her colleagues as saying she was a highly qualified and diligent researcher. They also emphasized that security rules at the facility, established in the 1920s to monitor and study the plague that is endemic to southeastern Siberia, are extremely strict. The report quoted Shipilova's neighbors as saying a team of disinfection experts did several cleanups of her apartment, leaving a strong antiseptic smell. The hospital where she died was under quarantine, no longer admitting or discharging patients, although its outpatient clinic has continued operating, according to Mayor Maxim Modin. Irkutsk Gov. Igor Kobzev said she died of a "particularly dangerous infection" and everyone who came into contact with her has remained under medical supervision. The incubation period for pneumonic plague — the disease's most virulent form — can be as short as 24 hours, according to the WHO. The lung-based illness is a less common but severe form of plague that can spread between people via respiratory particles. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) introduced legislation Wednesday that would direct the Smithsonian to preserve and display artifacts he said reflect the rise of "governmental propaganda" under President Trump . Why it matters: The bill will almost certainly fail in a Republican-controlled Congress. But it could preview how Democrats would scrutinize the president's use of taxpayer dollars to promote his image if they regain control in November. Trump's drive to remake D.C.'s physical and cultural landscape in his image can be seen in banners bearing his face on government buildings and attempts to rebrand institutions with his name . The administration also unveiled a plan last month to post warnings accusing Smithsonian leaders of pushing "personal, radical ideologies." Driving the news: Raskin's bill directs the secretary of the Smithsonian to collect and display Trump's sprawling portraits hung outside of federal agencies at the Museum of American History. It also calls for preserving signage or "artifacts" related to Trump's planned warning signs accusing the museum of "Ideological Capture." The proposed new exhibit would also include narratives from Americans "who resisted and opposed the rise in authoritarianism." It also calls for signage stating, in part, "Donald Trump ordered the installation of these signs without any Congressional authorization as required by the Constitution." What they're saying: " Unlike President Trump's project of censoring, whitewashing and fictionalizing American history, my legislation will forever preserve his manifestations of authoritarian narcissism and his propagandistic assault on American history and American democracy," Raskin said in a statement. The White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Catch up quick: The Smithsonian has been caught in the crosshairs of the president's D.C. residency and his government-wide DEI purge that has targeted so-called "woke ideology." Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch announced his retirement after more than three decades at the world's largest museum, education and research complex. What's next: The Smithsonian's next leader will likely helm the institution through continued pressure under Trump — and through the fallout that follows. Go deeper: Lonnie Bunch is leaving. Canada says it will indefinitely suspend plans to expand its medically assisted dying law to people whose sole condition is mental illness, citing a lack of consensus on who would be eligible.
It comes after a parliamentary panel earlier this year recommended that medically assisted dying - known as Maid in Canada - should not be expanded.
On Wednesday, Canada's justice minister, Sean Fraser, said that "while there is not a perfect consensus on this issue, we believe this is the correct approach".
Supporters of extending the programme to those with mental illness alone argue that not doing so violates their constitutional rights and access to healthcare.
A federal case remains before the courts challenging the government's earlier decision to delay access to Maid for people with mental illness.
Wednesday's announcement means that Canadians with mental illness as their sole condition will not be able to access assisted dying by March 2027 as previously planned.
Fraser said the government will instead introduce a new law in the coming weeks that suspends that expansion indefinitely.
That proposed legislation will also to allow patients who have a progressing incurable illness to consent to assisted dying before their health deteriorates to the point where they are unable to do so. Advanced requests are not currently legal.
"These are not easy decisions but we believe they will be the correct ones," Fraser said.
Medically assisted dying became legal in Canada in 2016 for people with terminal illnesses, who still account for the vast majority of cases.
Following a court case in Quebec, it was expanded in 2021 to people with incurable conditions but whose death was not imminent. In Canada, that mechanism is known as "track two" Maid.
The expansion has been the subject of controversy, with disability advocacy groups reporting cases where assisted dying was offered to people with disabilities without a patient requesting it themselves.
Canada was first set to expand its assisted dying laws to people whose sole condition is mental illness in 2023, but it delayed doing so twice to allow for time to study its potential delivery.

cc9c75b2a65f.text: By — Josef Federman, Associated Press Josef Federman, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/scars-from-oct-7-fuel-deep-divisions-over-netanyahu-ahead-of-israeli-election Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Scars from Oct. 7 fuel deep divisions over Netanyahu ahead of Israeli election World Oct 7, 2026 12:19 PM EDT JERUSALEM (AP) — As Israel gears up for its first elections since Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attack, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his opponents are putting it at the heart of their campaigns. Nearly every poster, stump speech or televised debate seems to reference the attack, which has scarred the country and remains fresh in the minds of voters. Three years on, the worst security failure in Israel's history now threatens to end the career of its longest-serving prime minister. WATCH: Brett McGurk chronicles negotiations to free Oct. 7 hostages in 'Brink' "October 7 is kind of a framework for the entire political discussion that is going on," said Tamar Hermann, an expert on Israeli public opinion at the Israel Democracy Institute, a Jerusalem think tank. "All of us are post-traumatic in a way." Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Netanyahu's opponents want him to pay for the failures that led to the deadliest day in Israel's 78-year history and plunged the country into a series of inconclusive wars. His defenders say Netanyahu was betrayed by the military establishment and that he has led Israel through a dramatic rebound from its darkest hour. WATCH: Netanyahu faces pressure after report alleges he brushed off warnings ahead of Oct. 7 A loss in the Oct. 27 election would likely end the career of the soon-to-be 77-year-old Netanyahu. A victory would mark the greatest turnaround yet for a man who has defied naysayers for three decades. A deadly day that has shaken an entire region On the morning of Oct. 7, Hamas militants fired several thousand rockets into Israel and thousands of militants attacked through holes blown in the border fence or with boats or motorized paragliders. Some 1,200 people were killed and 251 others taken hostage. WATCH: Netanyahu government defies court, raising constitutional crisis fears as election nears Israel responded with a military offensive that has killed over 74,000 Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, according to local health authorities, left the territory in ruins and sparked an ongoing humanitarian catastrophe. Israel later went to war against Hezbollah militants in Lebanon, seized a chunk of Syria, attacked targets in Yemen and joined the U.S. in two wars against Iran. Hundreds of Israelis, mostly young soldiers, have died, and nearly every household has been touched by the violence. Netanyahu promised "total victory," but Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran's theocratic government all remain intact. A visual installation depicting bodies, on the third anniversary of the deadly Oct. 7 attack at a beach in Tel Aviv. Photo by Aviv Atlas/via Reuters Israel's international standing has plummeted, a number of foreign governments have accused it of genocide — a charge it vehemently rejects — and Netanyahu is now wanted by the International Criminal Court. After a string of resignations by top security officials, Netanyahu is the only senior figure from Oct. 7 still in office, making this month's election in many ways a referendum on his leadership. It's the focus of the campaign for both sides Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu attends a state memorial ceremony for the three-year anniversary of the Oct. 7 Hamas attack, in remembrance of Israel Defense Forces and security members in Jerusalem, on Oct. 5, 2026. Photo by Debbie Hill/ Pool via Reuters Netanyahu and his opponents have put Oct. 7 at the forefront of their campaigns — for different reasons. His opponents — from across the political spectrum — call his outgoing coalition "the massacre government." Netanyahu says he has led a "war of redemption." READ MORE: Pilot stabbing further unsettles region shaken by U.S.-Iran war His chief rival is Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief whose son and nephew were killed in battle in Gaza. The opponents have pledged to form a government of "repair and reconstruction" — beginning with the formation of an official commission of inquiry into Oct. 7. They also have vowed to end draft exemptions for ultra-Orthodox religious men, a long-standing policy that has outraged the secular majority at a time of war, and accuse Netanyahu of threatening Israel's democratic institutions. "The most fateful elections in the history of the State of Israel are between evasion and enlistment," Eisenkot wrote on X. "Between taking responsibility and fleeing from responsibility." Netanyahu has repeatedly rejected calls for a commission of inquiry while trying to shift the blame to security officials. He recently accused the then-head of the Shin Bet security service, Ronen Bar, of withholding information ahead of the attack. Bar has vowed to file a defamation lawsuit. Netanyahu has meanwhile denied reports in American media outlets that the United Arab Emirates and Egypt warned him ahead of Oct. 7. He insists the country is stronger than ever. "Our enemies expected us to collapse," Netanyahu said in a recent address to the United Nations. "Well, we didn't collapse. Instead, we rose and fought like lions." Rise up" on the third anniversary of the deadly Hamas-led Oct. 7 attack, in Tel Aviv. Photo by Avi Ohayon/ Reuters Eisenkot's new Yashar party list includes two parents who lost children on Oct. 7. Sir David Attenborough has promised to "venture even further" and uncover marine life that is "more precious than we ever realised" in Blue Planet III.
The broadcaster, who turned 100 earlier this year, narrates the new six-part series exploring the darkest depths of the world's oceans, produced by the BBC Natural History Unit in Bristol.
After almost four years of filming, the latest instalment in the franchise will air on the BBC later this autumn, marking 25 years since the first series premiered.
At a launch event on Tuesday, Sir David said: "When I narrated the first Blue Planet series, it didn't occur to me that I would be narrating a third series in my centennial year."
More from Bristol
The production uses advanced equipment including remote underwater cameras, drones, and manned submersibles to capture newly discovered animal behaviours.
Viewers are taken into some of the world's least understood marine environments, ranging from coral reefs and tropical islands to the darkest depths of the ocean.
In the newly released extended trailer, Attenborough promised to "venture even further" than ever before, describing the ocean as "an endlessly fascinating place".
"We will uncover life that is more surprising, more intelligent, and even more precious than we ever realised," he said.
"We will discover the extraordinary relationship we have with the ocean. One that has never been more important to understand."
Sir David said he was "proud and delighted" to be associated with the project.
The new series is accompanied by an original score from Hans Zimmer and Bleeding Fingers Music.
Zimmer, who also scored Blue Planet II, said the series was the "most important work" he has ever done.
"I think everybody who comes to Blue Planet comes to it with the knowledge that it is something that changes the world by making you fall in love," he said.
"It's not something where you're being lectured or cajoled about things, but it's something that just shows you how spectacular and beautiful our world truly is.
"How we need to preserve it and how we need to love it, and how whatever we love, we need to treat with great kindness and great respect."
It also features an original song, Into The Deep (Seas Cry) co-written by Jade Thirlwall - best known for being a member of the pop group Little Mix.
Thirlwall described herself as a "huge fan" of the franchise, praising Attenborough as "a true hero".
"Being part of Blue Planet III in this way feels incredibly special and a real privilege," she added.
The premiere launch event took place at Piccadilly Circus in London on Tuesday, with footage from the new series taking over the digital displays.
