As the sky began to lighten over Israel's border with Gaza on Wednesday, the people of Kfar Aza moved silently towards the armoury at the centre of the kibbutz.
It was there, shortly after 07:00 on 7 October 2023, that Hamas-led attackers killed half the community's 14-member civil defence squad. They were among 64 killed and 19 kidnapped from the community that day.
The pain of those attacks is still fresh here. But three years on, there are questions about who else should pay the price for Israel's security failure.
"I need my country to take responsibility," said Inbar Goldstein, whose brother and niece were killed, and four other relatives kidnapped from Kfar Aza.
The 7 October attack was the deadliest Israel had suffered since its creation in 1948. About 1,200 people were killed across southern Israel by gunmen who broke through the border fence and attacked communities there. Another 251 people were taken back to Gaza as hostages.
Three years on from Israel's biggest security failure, there is still no independent state inquiry into how it was allowed to happen.
And the man in charge at the time of that failure - Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu - is running for election again, with the same campaign promise: to be stronger and tougher than anyone else in protecting Israel from its enemies.
"Nobody investigated the roots [of the attack]. It didn't start or end on October 7th - it's a long process of abandonment," Goldstein said.
Aside from Hamas's responsibility for the attack itself, there are growing questions in Israel around what caused the country's intelligence failure, what information was passed to military and political leaders in the run-up to the attacks, and what Netanyahu himself knew.
For months beforehand, young female soldiers posted at bases along the Gaza border to watch for suspicious activity had warned their superiors about possible preparations for an attack.
Among them was Roni Eshel. She was killed with 14 other members of her unit when gunmen overran their base at Nahal Oz, just next to Kfar Aza.
"There are so many questions," her uncle Elad Levy told me. "Were the Egyptians warning the prime minister? The Emiratis? Were there no other warnings Netanyahu ignored? We need to find out what happened â not just on the day, but the year before, and five years before that."
"The truth should be clear," he continued. "If we don't inquire into this, it will happen again and again."
Over the past three years, there have been mounting reports of warnings being given to Netanyahu - by his own security chief, as well as by regional neighbours â which he denies.
Last month, Israel's Haaretz newspaper published extracts from a new book, alleging that the leader of the United Arab Emirates had called Netanyahu 10 days before the attack to warn of Hamas plans for a major operation.
Netanyahu's office has dismissed the report as "an absolute lie" and has said he will sue the newspaper.
Amir Ohana, a member of Netanyahu's Likud party, said in a social media video last month that it was "preposterous and absurd" to suggest that Netanyahu could have known about the attack when the former Hamas leader in Gaza, Yahya Sinwar, had only told a handful of people.
Israel's prime minister, he said, had since reshaped the Middle East and did not give up, "even when voices inside and outside Israel called on him to stop".
Netanyahu has blamed his own security chiefs for the failures that led to the 7 October attacks, accusing them of deliberately choosing not to wake him in the hours beforehand, for fear that he would order a massive deployment of the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) and escalate the situation.
"God forbid we wake up the prime minister and he says, 'Wake up the entire IDF immediately, scramble the air force!'" he told Israel's right-wing Channel 14 television network.
"What would have happened if they had woken me? This would not have happened," he said, suggesting that his response would have better protected Israel from the attacks.
Yaacov Katz, a journalist and author of several books on Israel's defence, has written about the growing concerns over Hamas activity that emerged in the hours leading up to the assault.
In his book, While Israel Slept, he describes calls between senior military figures and intelligence chiefs in the early hours of the morning, the sudden recall of commanders from leave, and the dispatch of an elite intelligence unit to the border.
He told me their expectation was, at worst, a small, limited incursion by Hamas fighters.
"So why would [Netanyahu] order a massive pre-emptive strike by the IDF, if every security chief is telling him this is not what this is going to be? Waking him would not have made a difference."
But he said Netanyahu faced other questions about his failure to spot what was happening.
"You were the prime minister, you set the policy," he said. "You created a doctrine and a policy of containment that trickled down to the last soldier manning the watchtower on the border with Gaza: contain Hamas, separate the Palestinians, and keep Hamas in power to prevent the establishment of a Palestinian state."
For years, Netanyahu oversaw a policy of containing - not confronting - Hamas in Gaza, during which Israeli governments allowed Qatar to provide hundreds of millions of dollars of aid for Gaza.
A month after the 7 October attacks, he told a German newspaper that claims he wanted to strengthen Hamas were "an absolute lie".
"On the contrary we wanted to continue to weaken Hamas as much as we could," he told Die Welt. "But the money was meant to avoid a civilian catastrophe - that is the only reason."
Months after the attack, the IDF's then-chief of staff, Lt Gen Herzi Halevi, publicly apologised for the failure to defend civilians, saying he carried that weight on his shoulders and in his heart.
He resigned. A raft of military commanders were later fired, and Israel's domestic intelligence chief left his position.

ab80b50c6ce5.text: The good news about the epic shifts in global bond markets is that they mostly reflect economic fundamentals, not the kinds of panicky swings seen in a crisis. The bad news is that there's a risk the disruptions metastasize into a broader crisis in an era of fractured politics across major democracies. The big picture: Turmoil in the streets this week in France is the latest sign of hazards that await elected leaders who try to address yawning fiscal deficits head-on. They are squeezed between voters who want to maintain public benefit levels and tax levels and a bond market that is resetting long-term interest rates higher — meaning that carrying on with wide deficits will come at a greater and greater cost to service debt. That's why even what has been a relatively orderly repricing so far carries risks that are bigger than just high mortgage or corporate borrowing rates. Driving the news: The relentless upward march of bond yields continued Wednesday morning. The French 10-year yield soared 0.18 percentage point, to 4.93%. French yields are also surging relative to other countries that use the euro, especially Germany — the kind of fragmentation seen in the eurozone debt crisis of the early 2010s that originated in Greece . But France is not alone. U.K. 10-year yields are up 0.12 point, to 5.49%, while the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield is up 0.08 point Wednesday morning, reaching 5.36%, the highest since 2002. Reality check: These are massive moves in markets that form the bedrock of global financial markets. And yet they don't appear to be driven by the kind of crisis dynamics and forced selling that fueled bond market volatility in the 2008 crisis, the 2014 Treasury flash crash and the March 2020 pandemic. Rather, they've been driven by bottomless demand for capital from AI hyperscalers and deficit-running sovereign governments, exacerbated by surging energy prices that increase inflation risk. What they're saying: "When you look at outright yield levels and/or spreads, a lot of this is still quite rational, and within the realm of what fair valuation should be, just given where nominal growth is and where we are in the cycle," Kunal Shah, the co-CEO of Goldman Sachs International, tells Axios. "At this point, I still wouldn't say that we're anywhere close to the point of this being a broad financial stability risk or issue," says Shah, who is also co-head of fixed income, currency and commodities. "What policymakers in Europe have shown us, though, is that when there's broader issues on contagion and/or disorderly functioning markets, that's when they can be quick to respond." "Whilst the move in spreads has been very quick and sharp, in the broader context, we're still nowhere close to where we had got to in that previous European crisis," he says. "Financial conditions are tightening, but it's still not, I'd say, flashing red to the point that you need a backstop from the policymakers." Yes, but: The European Central Bank has more powerful tools than it did in 2010 to address imbalances between European countries, and has shown willingness to use them. But it can't do much about the fundamentals of governments spending consistently far more than they raise in taxes. And the global nature of the yield surge shows the common fiscal challenge across major economies. State of play: In France, there have been violent clashes with police as teachers and students protest proposed wage freezes and school funding cuts. In the U.K., a central political dispute is over the future of the "triple lock" pension adjustment mechanism, which all but guarantees pension costs will grow faster than the overall economy. The U.S. Social Security trust fund is on track to be exhausted in 2032 . The rate adjustment of the last several weeks will increase already-onerous debt service costs for all advanced countries. Of note: Those forces can create destabilizing effects for business even apart from the impact on rates. Shah, for example, says that U.K. governments lurching from budget to budget has made it hard for businesses making long-term decisions. "I hope that at some point we'll be able to break out of this cycle, because it does stifle confidence and it just makes planning for the long term very hard," Shah says.

Boots, the High Street pharmacy and retail chain, has been sold in an $8.9bn (Â£6.7bn) deal to Canada's billionaire Weston family.
Wittington Investments, the holding company, confirmed it had agreed to buy 177-year old company on Wednesday from US private equity firm Sycamore Partners and the Pessina family.
Boots started as a simple apothecary in Nottingham but has evolved to become a familiar and trusted High Street presence, selling a vast range of health and beauty products, meal deals and travel accessories.
Galen Weston, chairman of Wittington, said Boots played "a vital role in everyday life across the UK and Ireland".
Boots has performed well in recent years despite challenges from rivals and changing shopping habits.
Its stores have also seen lower footfall as people switched to working from home rather than visiting town and city centre offices every week day.
It has closed hundreds of branches across the UK, leaving it with about 1,800 currently and 51,000 employees.
Its ownership status has also been uncertain, with several changes of ownership under discussion and sometimes completed over the last two decades.
But Weston, who will become chairman of Boots, signalled the new owners had fresh plans for the chain, including shop upgrades and an expansion of healthcare services.
"We see a meaningful opportunity to make a great business even better through stable long-term ownership, further capital investment, and the renewed operating focus required to serve customers with excellence for generations to come," he said.
Boots was established by John Boot, who opened the first herbalist store in Nottingham offering an affordable alternative to traditional medicines in 1849.
The Weston family will be buying Boots' retail operations in the UK and Ireland, Boots Opticians, No7 Beauty Company and its Thailand and franchised businesses. It is set be completed in early 2027.
The Weston family owns the Canadian grocery chain Loblaws, pharmacy business Shoppers Drug Mart, and previously owned the London department store Selfridges from 2003 to 2021, before selling it for $4bn.
The separate UK branch of the Weston family is the majority owner of Associated British Foods, the parent firm of Primark.
The Westons were ranked fifth on this year's Sunday Times Rich List with a combined fortune of almost Â£19bn.
Wittington will have operational control over Boots, it has secured ownership in partnership with Fairfax Financial Holdings, a Toronto-based holding company.
Sycamore Partners, in partnership with Stefano Pessina and his family, will retain ownership of The Boots Group's Farmacias Benavides in Mexico and Alliance Healthcare Deutschland in Germany.

dc4e078c4a70.text: By — Jamie Stengle, Associated Press Jamie Stengle, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/texas-set-to-execute-jamaal-howard-for-2000-fatal-shooting Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Texas set to execute Jamaal Howard for 2000 fatal shooting Nation Oct 7, 2026 11:52 AM EDT DALLAS (AP) — A Texas man who fatally shot a convenience store clerk is set to die by lethal injection on Wednesday in what would be the nation's 30th execution this year. Jamaal Howard, 46, was found guilty of capital murder in the 2000 killing of Vickie Swartout, 42, who was shot once in the chest. He is set to receive a lethal dose of pentobarbital in the first scheduled execution in the U.S. since Tennessee's failed attempt at putting Christa Pike to death last week. READ MORE: Christa Pike is conscious and speaking after failed execution attempt in Tennessee, her attorneys say Pike's attorneys said Tuesday that she was awake and speaking as she received treatment at a hospital. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Texas has executed six people so far this year, with two more scheduled after Howard. A killing caught on surveillance Swartout was fatally shot during the robbery at the store in the small, rural town of Silsbee, located about 100 miles (161 kilometers) northeast of Houston. Evidence presented at the trial included the store's surveillance video, which showed Howard shooting Swartout. Howard, who was 20 at the time, took $114 and a carton of cigarettes from the store, according to court records. READ MORE: Many states have backup execution plans, but failures still happen His attorneys have argued that Howard is intellectually disabled and his execution should be halted. The state said that he has not presented evidence that would show he meets the requirements for a claim of intellectual disability. He has an appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court pending to stop the execution. READ MORE: Christa Gail Pike wasn't Tennessee's first failed execution this year. Here's what to know The Supreme Court in 2002 had barred the execution of intellectually disabled people. But it has given states some discretion in how they determine such disabilities. Executions in the U.S. this year Florida has carried out 16 executions so far this year, the most of any state. Most states that allow executions use lethal injection as their primary method. As Mainers prepare to choose a new governor in November, climate and energy issues may not be top of mind for every voter—but they are having big effects on residents’ lives.
The average cost of heating oil recently soared to a record high of more than $6 per gallon, promising an expensive winter ahead for the half of Maine households heated by oil-powered boilers and furnaces. The cost of electricity has also risen steeply, at the third-highest rate in the nation over the past 10 years.
At the same time, the effects of climate change are harming the state. Boom-and-bust rain and drought cycles are making farming more difficult. Rising temperatures are putting pressure on many plants and animals, including economically important species such as lobster. Sea level rise and worsening storms are eating away the coastline and damaging infrastructure.
All three candidates running for governor agree that energy affordability is a priority. And all acknowledge the reality of climate change. But they disagree on whether these problems can be tackled together.
Democrat Hannah Pingree and independent Rick Bennett think energy affordability and climate action can go hand in hand. In a September interview with The Maine Monitor, Pingree said she would continue the work of the Maine Climate Council, which created a plan to meet clean energy and greenhouse gas emissions goals set by the state Legislature. Bennett said he also supports transitioning the state to clean energy.
Republican Bobby Charles said that the state government should focus squarely on affordability, and embrace both renewable energy and fossil fuels, including supporting new natural gas pipelines.
Maine is the only state, alongside Washington, D.C., that is currently ahead of pace to meet its 2030 goal of cutting greenhouse gas emissions by 45 percent, though some other states have more ambitious goals.
Much of Maine’s success so far has been thanks to the rapid uptake of heat pumps, an energy efficiency and electrification solution encouraged by rebates and embraced across party lines.
As the federal government stepped back from climate action during the first Trump administration, state governments stepped up to fill some of that gap, said Anthony Moffa, a law professor at the University of Maine who studies climate policy. Maine in particular has been a leader in that regard, he said.
The state Legislature established the Maine Climate Council in 2019, and the group created a climate action plan called “Maine Won’t Wait.” This comprehensive plan has been “a model document” for other states, according to Moffa.
Maine’s goals have ramped up over time, with the latest update in 2025 requiring the state to source 100 percent of its electricity from renewables or other low-emissions sources such as nuclear power by 2040.
The governor plays a crucial role in pushing forward this change, Moffa said. While the Legislature can set goals, the governor is the one who empowers state agencies to create policies and programs that actually implement the law.
Hannah Pingree
Much of the climate-focused work that happened during the administration of Gov. Janet Mills was led by Pingree, who was director of the Governor’s Office of Policy Innovation and the Future from 2019 to 2025. As part of that job, Pingree served as co-chair of the Maine Climate Council, overseeing two iterations of the state’s climate action plan.
“I would continue that work,” Pingree said. “To not do that is going to put lives at risk. It’s going to put public safety at risk and really risk the future of our economy.”
Pingree wants Maine to procure more clean energy through projects such as the Northern Maine Renewable Energy Program, which aims to develop utility-scale renewable energy projects and transmission infrastructure in Aroostook County.
Locals have raised concerns about these projects, and Pingree added that the governor should work with the Maine Department of Energy Resources, the Public Utilities Commission and the Office of the Public Advocate “to ensure that actual community voices are heard, there is public benefit and there is public savings.”
As the supply of clean energy grows, Pingree wants Maine to use less oil and gas, which largely come to the state from other countries.
“We have no energy independence,” she said, and “no control over these international prices of energy.”
That’s become apparent as first the war between Russia and Ukraine and now between the United States and Iran have disrupted the supply of natural gas and oil.
Roughly half of Maine residents’ electricity bills are for this supply side of the equation. The other half pays for transmission and distribution. To help control those costs, Pingree wants the Public Utilities Commission to oppose what she calls “excessive rate hikes” from electric utilities. She also wants to incentivize more people to weatherize their homes, reducing the amount of electricity they need to use in the first place.
Although Pingree played a pivotal role in the Mills administration’s climate policy, she disagrees with Mills on some key issues. Pingree supports Wabanaki sovereignty, which is a priority not just for the Wabanaki themselves but also for many of Maine’s environmental advocacy groups. She also supports a moratorium on large-scale data center development.
Pingree has been endorsed by the Maine Conservation Voters Action Fund.

Coco Gauff said she had a "draining" few days after receiving racist abuse online before her fourth-round China Open exit.
The American received an "insane" amount of racist comments and direct messages following an incident in her third-round win over 16-year-old Sun Xinran on Monday.
China's Sun thought she had hit a winner late in the first set, but Gauff raised her hand to halt play because of a flickering light in the side panels surrounding the court.
After a video review - which players are allowed to request - the point was replayed, with Gauff winning it and subsequently going on to clinch the match.
The 22-year-old posted a lengthy statement explaining what had happened and later condemned the racist abuse she received in response.
Gauff was beaten 6-3 6-3 in her next match against Elise Mertens on Wednesday.
Asked how she had felt over the past 36 hours, Gauff said: "It has been kind of draining, I'm not going to lie.
"I just turn off my phone and move on. I mean, there's nothing you can do."
A spokesperson for the Women's Tennis Association said it was appalled by the abuse. It said it was in contact with Gauff "to offer our full support".
A statement given to the news agency AFP said the governing body was "seeking action" against the abusive content.
Gauff, who won the title in Beijing in 2024, committed 34 unforced errors and eight double faults against Mertens.
"I was just a bit flat. That's the main thing," Gauff said.
"The level was there at some points, I just didn't sustain it the whole match."
Belgium's Mertens will play former world number one Iga Swiatek in the quarter-finals after the six-time major champion beat American teenager Iva Jovic 6-1 6-3.
Elsewhere, Britain's Arthur Fery beat Marin Cilic 7-6 (7-2) 6-1 in the Shanghai Masters first round.
Fery came back from a break down in the first set before dominating the former US Open champion in the second to claim his first ATP Tour win since August.
The 24-year-old will face Russia's 26th seed Karen Khachanov next.

Gears of War, one of the video games that helped Microsoft's Xbox to win over millions of fans, is back.
Prequel E-Day takes players back to where it all started, telling the origin story of humanity's conflict with The Locust - the series' horrifying enemy species.
The game's been well-received by critics and players, but it's also seen as a big test of Xbox's new direction.
Unlike recent flagship titles from the company's studios, which have been released on PlayStation 5 and, in some cases, Nintendo Switch, E-Day is being pushed as an Xbox exclusive.
The apparent goal is to draw players back to the brand, but critics have questioned whether that's realistic at a time when console prices are higher than ever.
BBC Newsbeat spoke to developer The Coalition - the makers of E-Day - about what staying exclusive means to them.
'Heart, blood and guts'
Gears of War has been one of Xbox's flagship series since it launched back in 2006.
Creative director Matt Searcy tells Newsbeat the sci-fi shooter is a "mix of war story with comic book-y monsters that come out of the ground".
"It's a video game with a lot of heart, a lot of blood and guts," he says.
First released on the Xbox 360, Gears helped to popularise "cover-shooter" gameplay, which encouraged players to shelter from enemy attacks.
It brought a strategic dimension to third-person action games, and also won fans with its co-operative multiplayer modes - a feature that's returned for E-Day.
But, 20 years later, Xbox finds itself in a very different position in the console space.
It's seen as a third-place competitor, behind both Sony's PlayStation and Nintendo's Switch consoles.
Previous CEO Phil Spencer had begun to take the division in a new direction, releasing some of its most popular games on rival consoles for the first time.
E-Day was widely expected to follow other high budget series such as Halo on to other companies' machines.
But new Xbox boss Asha Sharma, who took over the job in June, announced Gears of War would remain a "console exclusive", although a PC version has also been released.
Her strategy has been called into question by critics.
After taking six years to make and an estimated budget in the hundreds of millions, they argue that keeping E-Day away from other platforms could mean it's less likely to make back its development cost.
Coalition studio head Mike Crump says E-Day is a "natural choice to be an exclusive".
"Gears has been an exclusive franchise to Xbox for 20 years now. It's sort of entwined deeply with the brand," he says.
"And we're proud of that."
He says the series "carries the banner" for the console and gives people a "reason to be in the Xbox ecosystem" - something he says has been the company's mission since day one.
However, there will inevitably be discourse around E-Day's sales figures and engagement numbers.
When asked what would constitute success for the game, Crump admits the studio has financial targets and goals for the number of players it wants to reach, but insists it takes a "broader view" than that.
"We measure things like, are we showcasing the platform? Are we pushing the hardware to its limits? Are we showcasing what the Xbox is capable of?
"Our goal basically is to be the best-looking game on the Xbox and really show the industry what's possible with our hardware."
Crump also says it's important to drive players towards Game Pass, Xbox's Netflix-style subscription service.
For onlookers, it's harder to ignore the wider picture at Xbox.
The division has been carrying out mass layoffs and undergoing a wide-scale restructuring since Sharma's appointment.
In July, she told employees there would be 3,200 job losses across Xbox-owned studios over the current financial year.
Last month, the company said it was about three-quarters of the way through this plan, external.
The Coalition has mostly avoided cuts so far, although one of E-Day's narrative directors announced last month he had been let go.
Reports have suggested developers at the studio are worried they could be at risk now the game has been released, external.
When asked about this, Crump says: "What I say to myself, what I say to the team, is we just we need to focus on the things that we can control.
"For us that's about shipping a great game that people are going to love and I feel like, as a team, we've done that."
He says E-Day will provide a "great foundation" for future games in the series, and insists "the next game will not take nearly as long" to make.
Developers at other studios hit by layoffs previously told the BBC they were concerned about a loss of institutional knowledge - experienced staff who've been working on certain series for years and sometimes decades.
Crump says: "We've got a great team here.
"And the leadership team in particular has worked together for upwards of 20 years.
"So there's definitely a continuity of knowledge and experience."

âA flawless face is the fastest way for a character to read as generic AI,â a Higgsfield spokesperson told Semafor.

The race in the West to become the top open-source AI model shifted into higher gear this week, as both Nvidia-backed Reflection AI and French lab Mistral unveiled new models they hope will break Chinaâs open-source monopoly.
The challenge looming over Beam and Le Chonkâs debuts (immediately my new favorite model name) is that they lag the top Chinese models and the leading closed systems from OpenAI and Anthropic on prominent benchmarks.
But Reflection and Mistral boasted in their announcements that they do beat other open Western models, such as those from Thinking Machines and Nvidia, suggesting the companies care just as much about the race against each other as the one with Beijing â despite US and European companiesâ shifts to using more Chinese models over the past year.
Reflection CEO Misha Laskin told me his goal isnât necessarily to dismantle the foothold Chinese models have achieved among developers and large companies. Instead, he sees a market in entities that canât or wonât use Chinese models â think heavily regulated industries and governments â and might otherwise have no choice but to pay for closed American AI.
The timing of that pitch is opportune: Many businesses are heading into year-end budget reviews with eye-popping AI spend figures to account for. Governments are also bracing for sticker shock as $1-a-year pilot deals expire. New data from Ramp suggests companies are switching which AI providers they use more than ever.
The question that will determine the fate of these and other Western open-source players is whether businesses and agencies will tolerate less advanced models for some tasks in exchange for affordability and control.

Prick up your ears, and you can hear it â the sound of many different kinds of Democrats grabbing credit for midterm victories that arenât official yet.
Thereâs Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, assessing that when (not if) Abdul El-Sayed wins his Senate race in Michigan, the left will âbreak open the entire political calculus in Americaâ â i.e., that progressives like them can win the Midwest. Thereâs Pete Buttigieg, making sure we know how many states heâs campaigned in (37) and how many candidates heâd endorsed (more than 100).
At this time in any campaign cycle, groups, candidates, and strategists pepper reporters with early claims that they were right. The election, they say, will be a referendum on their issue, a validation of their spending strategy, proof that their ideas moved votes.
These takes arenât immaculate. Iâve never deleted the October 2017 email from a strategist who was ready to explain why Ralph Northam lost the election for governor of Virginia. In fact, Northam won easily, and that strategist got strategically quiet.
As preposterous as it is, though, the pre-spin cycle matters, because anyone not ready to contextualize what happened to their benefit will lose face.
It mattered in 2020, when centrist Democrats burst out to blame âdefund the policeâ activists for their party underperforming the final polls. It mattered after President Donald Trumpâs win in 2024, when Sen. Bernie Sanders instantly blamed defeat on the party having âabandoned the working class.â That quick analysis shaped the conversation.
Populism won. This is the Sanders project â progressivesâ entire project, really. The goal of recruiting swing-seat populists and getting them through primaries was to prove, as Ocasio-Cortez said, that their kind can win anywhere, which should matter for 2028.
This theory may be tough to sell. One of its proof points was supposed to be Maine, where Graham Platner humiliated the party establishment, then himself. Progressives won the insta-caucus that replaced him, nominating Troy Jackson to face GOP Sen. Susan Collins, and Sanders will campaign for Jackson this weekend after some internal grumbling about whether consultants not approved by the left were ruining his campaign.
Michiganâs the ballgame now. An El-Sayed win would, for progressives, be the story of the midterms. Most of the movementâs primary victories came in safe seats, but to take control of the 2028 story, they want to be talking about El-Sayed winning, Will Lawrence flipping back a mid-Michigan district, and Randy Villegas unseating Rep. David Valadao in California. They want to say that hand-wringing moderates were wrong, and pure populism can flip or hold swing seats.
But if El-Sayed becomes the first Democrat to lose a Michigan Senate seat this century, progressives will enter 2028 with empty hands. What to watch: MI-SEN, MI-07, CA-22

Marcy Kaptur, D-Ohio, is running the most critical ads about âtransgender ideologyâ of any Democratic incumbent.

Governments around the world are hardening their AI stances as more agentic hacks breach critical systems. South Koreaâs president noted âconsiderable public concern and anxietyâ following revelations that hackers used an AI system to execute recent cyberattacks against banks in the country.
And officials from OpenAI and Anthropic faced questions from lawmakers in Australia on Tuesday, after the ChatGPT maker drew criticism for not alerting Canberra fast enough after one of its models gained unauthorized access to a government health data portal during internal training and evaluation.
Tech companies are playing whack-a-mole around the world as their models get up to more hijinks and are used for malicious purposes. US and Chinese tech companies are taking differing approaches to bring AI agents to the masses, the industryâs latest fixation. OpenAIâs recently released dots and Metaâs Muse are built around the assistant first and then sent out to use other companiesâ websites and services.
Chinese counterparts, including Tencentâs Xiaowei âÂ which is built into super-app WeChat â can, for example, place orders from businesses that are already on the app. Itâs an obvious use for closed systems like WeChat and Alipay, which Chinese consumers already use for much of daily life.
Xiaoweiâs strategy may not translate into revenue, the Hello China Tech newsletter wrote: Tencent earns no new fees from purchases, and early tests show it making mistakes. f0c7e7265c39.text: Microsoft on Wednesday unveiled a new class of Nvidia-powered Windows laptops, its latest effort to tie the operating system more closely to the AI boom. Why it matters: Microsoft is trying to carve out a high-end laptop category for people who want to run demanding AI workloads locally, rather than rely entirely on the cloud. Driving the news: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and former White House AI official Sriram Krishnan were on hand in San Francisco as the company officially launched Microsoft Surface Ultra, a high-end laptop powered by Nvidia's RTX Spark chip that starts at $2,599. "We have reinvented the computer as we know it," Huang said. Microsoft previewed the laptop back in June but left out key details around price and exact availability. It said at the time that Nvidia-powered devices would also be coming from the likes of Asus, Dell, HP and Lenovo, among others. Those devices, and the Surface Ultra, will be available starting Oct. 16. On the software side, Microsoft unveiled a version of Copilot that can work using local models alongside those in the cloud, and the company also announced that Meta is bringing its Muse personal agent to Windows. The big picture: Microsoft's first push into AI-powered Windows machines, known as Copilot+ PCs, got off to a rocky start after the delay of Recall, its signature feature. Between the lines: Microsoft's pitch for on-device AI is that developers' appetite exceeds what their companies' AI budgets can afford, with the ideal being an approach that uses both frontier models in the cloud and local models when they can be effective. "Hybrid intelligence exists because people's appetite for intelligence is effectively unlimited," Microsoft executive VP Pavan Davuluri said. And before it even got to the hardware, Microsoft spent a fair bit of time outlining how it is making Windows more secure, ensuring that agents' actions are separated from those taken by humans and remain within preset limits.

e5ed4e0e6628.text: Data: Reuters/Ipsos ; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios Nearly nine in 10 voters say using taxpayer money to pay for election-related ads featuring the president or Cabinet members is inappropriate, including 80% of Republicans, according to a recent Reuters-Ipsos poll . Why it matters: The administration's decision to spend millions of taxpayer dollars on Trump-fronted ads weeks before the midterms is facing an uproar and overwhelming public opposition. While the administration insisted the ads were actually PSAs, Trump later announced that a super PAC affiliated with him would foot the bill for future ads (but not reimburse the taxpayer dollars already spent). Friction point: New polling suggests the TV spots, which the White House said "are a reminder for Americans to love their country," might not get much love from voters. The poll of 4,506 adults found that just 9% of Americans find it appropriate to tap taxpayer funds for election-related television ads featuring the president or cabinet members. Zoom out: A majority of Americans also panned other actions Trump has taken: 68% say it's inappropriate to block media outlets from entering the White House, and 72% say the same about naming federal institutions and buildings after a sitting president. Data: Reuters/Ipsos ; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios Zoom in: A White House official contended in a statement to Axios that the "PSAs are clearly not political," saying Trump "is not on the ballot and the ads don't have a call to action." But one is nearly identical to a 2024 Trump campaign ad, using the same footage and narration, with the campaign sponsorship tagline replaced with a disclaimer: "Paid for by the U.S. Government." Earlier this month, Democrats called on the Government Accountability Office and the U.S. Office of Special Counsel to investigate the use of taxpayer money to produce and air the ads. Between the lines: Axios' Alex Isenstadt scooped late last month that the ads released so far were "just the beginning" and that Trump himself — pleased with the war-room-style social media posts his digital team regularly pumps out — was hand-picking the ads himself. And it's not just the White House that's gotten in on promotional hype that blurs the lines with campaign content: The FBI's rapid response account released a video Tuesday applauding director Kash Patel — and criticizing Democrats, including Senate candidate Abdul-El Sayed. The bottom line: As an election approaches where cost-of-living concerns are paramount, Americans have strong feelings about how their taxpayer dollars are spent. Standing before the Acropolis in Athens, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio swept through the history of ancient Greece to the rise of American industry in a speech on Wednesday that portrayed western civilisation at risk of decline.
Rubio said the world was at an "inflection point". Nations, particularly in Europe, should return to ancient Greek values and "rebuild our institutions and our alliances to face these threats together".
"We believe that Europe can awaken from its long slumber and rekindle the fire that was here millennia ago," he said.
While he spoke of cooperation, Rubio also said "nations need not abandon their distinct identities in order to recognise their common interests".
Rubio, often mentioned as a possible presidential candidate in 2028, touched on what he considered dangers in the world, such as "radical mullahs" in Iran and suicide bombers.
But most of his speech focused on a broader threat, describing the current period as a crossroads.
"The course we take will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world, or resigns itself to a future of atrophy, and servitude, and decline," he said. "The next decade will write the story of the next century."
Rubio called for a return to the "classical understanding of politics and statecraft that the Trump administration hopes to reclaim - reclaim not just for our country, but for the whole of our civilisation".
That appeared to include renewed national pride, which he said the ancient Greeks had embraced, but the west had abandoned as "we felt embarrassed that our achievements set us apart from the rest of the world".
"The word 'nationalism' became a dirty word," he said. "So we tore down our monuments. We condemned our own history, and in too many places, we taught our children to be ashamed of the countries they would inherit.
"In the process, we opened our borders and outsourced our industry and allowed our militaries to wither and to decay."
Rubio's boss, President Donald Trump, has sought to carry out an "America first" agenda during both his terms in office, and taken a more confrontational stance toward traditional allies and in longstanding trade relationships.
Just six months ago, Trump again threatened to pull the US from the Nato alliance, which he has frequently criticised while pushing members to make larger contributions to defence.
Rubio's visit to the ruins of the Acropolis in Greece was part of his three-country tour of Nato allies that includes stops in Iceland and Portugal.

7f49183c88a0.text: By — Ryan Foley, Associated Press Ryan Foley, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/shock-gloves-purchased-by-ice-cause-pain-compliance-and-fear-army-study-found Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Shock gloves purchased by ICE cause pain, compliance and fear, Army study found Nation Oct 7, 2026 4:24 PM EDT The shock gloves immigration agents could soon use to control detainees and protesters worked so powerfully during a military exercise that participants felt intense pain, stopped fighting immediately and feared additional exposures, according to a previously unreleased Army study. Immigration and Customs Enforcement leaders were aware of the findings before signing a $16.7 million contract to purchase 6,000 pairs of shock gloves in August, according to records obtained by the watchdog group American Oversight and shared with The Associated Press. READ MORE: 'A perfect tool for abuse.' Why experts are concerned about ICE's $17 million electric shock gloves contract The shocks had a profound impact on Army employees who played the role of combative prisoners during the exercise, which took place at the military prison at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas in October 2024. The participants, several of whom were large-statured men, stopped resisting seconds after officers applied shocks by touching gloves to their skin, and were left with "fatigue, soreness and excessive apprehensiveness to being shocked again," the study found. "After experiencing the effects of the GLOVE, ... participants stated just seeing the GLOVE was enough to make them want to comply," the authors wrote. Watchdog says gloves cause pain and raise safety concerns ICE has called the gloves "distraction and de-escalation devices" that will be safer than other non-lethal options to subdue targets for arrest and deportation and protesters who create civil disturbances. The agency has argued the rapid compliance they cause will keep officers safer and prevent incidents from requiring potentially lethal force. But critics have warned the gloves will give ICE another weapon to intimidate and brutalize people even as the agency is under fire for excessive force that has left a trail of deaths and injuries across the nation. The gloves, they note, are easy to discharge, do not leave a mark and have not been extensively used in settings outside of jails. The manufacturer warns they should not be used on high-risk populations such as kids, pregnant women or disabled people. "The military assessment in ICE's own files shows that these gloves can cause 'intense pain' and force compliance. It does not establish that they are safe," said Chioma Chukwu, executive director of American Oversight. "Everyone should be alarmed that ICE is preparing to deploy a tool designed to inflict, at best, intense pain, without showing that it is safe for the people who will be subjected to it." ICE released the study and other documents to American Oversight as part of the group's Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against the agency seeking records related to its use of force. Army study found shock gloves triggered 'immediate' compliance The military prison study assessed whether the gloves could be used effectively to forcibly remove combative prisoners from their cells, to respond to disturbances in common areas and to transport uncooperative inmates. Role-playing employees conducted several scenarios with and without the gloves to test their impact, including violent encounters in which inmates were to fight as hard as they could. The study found the devices "increased the efficiency" of teams carrying out forced cell extractions and responding to disturbances by reducing the length of physical encounters, keeping guards from becoming exhausted and preventing injuries. They did not "significantly change" the time it took to control inmates during escorts but required less effort. The electric jolt does not cause the body to freeze like a Taser shock does, but instead "works by overloading the peripheral nerve endings" of the skin to cause pain, the study said. Participants who were wet or had oil on their skin described even more powerful shocks, with one reporting discomfort for 30 minutes afterward. Ozone pollution from fires, along with extreme heat and drought, is further weakening the Amazon rainforest’s ability to absorb carbon dioxide, new research shows.
The Amazon and other forests absorb more than a quarter of human-caused CO2 emissions each year, more than 11 billion metric tons. But in recent decades, increasingly larger areas of forests have begun releasing more CO2 than they absorb, especially during droughts and heat waves.
One study, published Monday in the journal Communications Earth & Environment, documents how smoke from wildfires, agriculture and forest-clearing burning contributes to leaf-damaging ozone formation far from the flames.
This means fires in the Amazon have a double impact on the climate. They directly release climate-warming CO2 as vegetation burns and reduce the ability of remaining trees to absorb and store CO2. The reduction is equal to about 24 percent of the carbon released by the fires.
That “hidden effect is a significant loss to the Amazon’s carbon budget that hasn’t previously been considered,” said lead author Flossie Brown, an atmospheric chemist at ETH Zürich, a university in Switzerland.
The second study, published Monday in the American Geophysical Union journal Earth’s Future, found that the extreme heat and drought that gripped the Amazon and other tropical forests in 2023 and 2024 during El Niño conditions could occur nearly every year within 20 to 30 years, cutting CO2 uptake severely and even disrupting the self-regulating forest-to-atmosphere moisture cycle.
Repeated extreme heat events can “trigger self-perpetuating rainfall losses,” warned
lead author Johanna Van Passel, an ecologist at Ghent University in Belgium. “You have this feedback loop,” she said. “If the forest is suffering, it will cause less rain to fall in other parts, and those forests will also start suffering.”
All tropical forests stayed unusually hot for an 18-month period overlapping with El Niño conditions, on average, and 80 percent of the forests were drier than average. The Amazon rainforest was particularly hard-hit. After a full two years of drought, water levels at the port of Manaus sank to the lowest level in more than a century of record-keeping. Globally, three-quarters of tropical forests endured extreme heat and drought simultaneously for an average of six months, the study found.
Even if human carbon emissions are eliminated or neutralized by 2075, extreme heat and drought will still be six times more likely across tropical regions by the end of the century than they have been over the past 25 years.
Under any higher-emissions climate scenario, the extreme, forest-damaging conditions seen in 2023 and 2024 are projected to become the annual norm across most tropical regions by the 2040s, with or without El Niño. It’s a “very striking” projection for the near future, Van Passel said.
Brown, the lead author of the ozone study, said the research offered a way to connect the often-invisible atmospheric chemistry of the atmosphere with real-world effects “that felt really relevant and important to me.”

Some of the data came from enclosed growth zones at TropOz laboratory “where we can control conditions like ozone concentration and really measure the trees,” she said. Other measurements used to understand ozone’s effects come from satellites that track vegetation reflectivity and from flux towers installed in the rainforest canopy that detect changes in the air’s chemistry.
One surprising result was that, during the 1997 to 2024 study period, there was “on the whole, a decline in ozone damage, coming from increasing CO2 concentrations,” Brown said. One reason is that, as the concentration of CO2 rises, trees can photosynthesize more efficiently, so they take up less air, and less ozone, through their stomata.
But the overall decline was outweighed by the effects of extreme events. Fires, smoke-driven ozone, drought and heat are becoming more frequent and more damaging, with impacts far greater than similar events would have had in a cooler climate.
The next cycle of extremes is already beginning, with a powerful El Niño driving drought in the region and the season for agricultural burning starting in the coming weeks.
The fires are not intended to become huge or burn the forest, but during droughts, they often escape control and release significant amounts of nitrogen oxides that can be carried distances and combine with other reactive organic molecules to form ozone.
Brown said ozone damage is just one of many pressures on the Amazon, as drought and high temperatures are “already moving the Amazon into conditions that it didn’t grow to withstand.” Limiting the damage requires changes in the way agricultural fires are managed, including using practices other than burning, and slowing deforestation and other degradation, she added.
Her biggest single concern is extreme drought. The Amazon evolved as an environment that is always wet, “and now, this isn’t the case,” she said. “A natural rainforest shouldn’t burn. It’s too wet. So even the fact that we create and see these fires that spread into the Amazon is already some kind of tipping point.”

The botched execution of Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike has thrust Tennessee's criminal justice system into uncharted territory.
After state officials administered two lethal doses of the drug pentobarbital on 30 September, Pike survived and was transported to a nearby hospital, where she was intubated. Six days later, her lawyers announced she was "conscious and speaking".
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered an independent investigation into what went wrong at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville and suspended all executions for the rest of the year.
The fate of Pike, who has been on death row for 30 years for murdering Colleen Slemmer, now lies in a mysterious grey area.
Doctor Joel Zivot, an anesthesiologist retained by Pike's defence team, says he suspects the deadly chemical spread under her skin instead of her bloodstream, and, because of the the large dose, it could take days or even weeks for a clear picture of her health to emerge.
At a hearing on Thursday, an attorney for Tennessee said the decision on scheduling a new execution date was up to the state's supreme court.
Pike's lawyers are seeking to have Pike's death sentence commuted to a lesser punishment of life in prison without parole. Lee, who has the power to pardon Pike or commute her sentence, has not indicated what the state will do in her case.
The BBC spoke to multiple experts to explore what could happen next.
Attempt to execute Pike by lethal injection again
The Tennessee Department of Corrections could attempt to execute Pike again by lethal injection, but the state would very likely run into legal challenges based on constitutional protections against cruel and unusual punishment.
"For the state to attempt to execute her again using the same methodology, they would have severe legal hurdles," Tennessee-based defence attorney Stephen Ross Johnson said.
Ross said Tennessee had botched two executions in one year - it also failed to kill Tony Carruthers in May - which could give lawyers the grounds to argue broadly against the constitutionality of its lethal injection protocol.
Pike's lawyers could also argue a lethal injection is what Ross called "unconstitutional as applied", meaning it is cruel and unusual specifically for Pike, due to her medical condition.
Pike's lawyers had warned before the execution attempt that she has small veins and thrombocytosis, a blood-clotting condition that would complicate the procedure.
Her medical condition combined with the state's botched execution would make it difficult for Tennessee to present a convincing legal argument for attempting lethal injection again, Ross said.
Attempt to execute her with a different method
But Ross, president-elect of the National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers, could see the state attempting an execution by a different method.
This would require "additional legal hoops", including approval from the governor's office and potentially the state legislature.
Since Pike's survival, political leaders in Tennessee have called for moving her death sentence forward through other means.
Senator Marsha Blackburn, the Republican candidate for governor in next month's election, said: "Bring back the electric chair."
Congressman Tim Burchett, posted on social media that he's already filed a bill to "bring back hanging".
Tennessee could be allowed to use the electric chair because Pike committed the murder in 1995 before the state changed its execution laws.
She would need to waive her right to lethal injection in writing, which means it would have to be her decision, Vanderbilt University law professor Chris Slobogin said.
Given Pike's exact medical state is unknown, Slobogin said there is a scenario where the state could be blocked from attempting to execute her again, regardless of method.
It is also considered cruel and unusual punishment to execute someone who is mentally incapable of understanding why it is happening, he explained.
Historically this has applied to prisoners with dementia or psychosis, but experts have said there is a chance that Pike has suffered brain damage.
Commute her sentence
Tennessee is taking a long pause on carrying out capital punishment.
Only one person was due to be executed this year after Pike, which the governor has now postponed. Earlier, in May, the Carruthers execution was suspended by a year after state officials could not find a vein to administer the lethal injection.
That means it will likely take a while for any movement in Pike's case.
"At a minimum there's going to be some significant delay while this issue is studied by the state", defence attorney Ross said, adding Pike's health would also need to be studied.
Slobogin suspects the governor will commute her sentence, especially if missteps by state officials are uncovered in the investigation he has ordered.
"If the investigation, in any way, shape, or form, suggests that the protocol was not followed, or is hard to carry out, that might be the easy way for him to go, given the complications with the execution and all the bad press," he said.
There is legal precedent for a death sentence to be commuted due to a botched execution combined with an inmate's poor medical state.
The execution of Alabama death-row prisoner Doyle Hamm was called off after more than two hours of attempts to establish an IV line failed.
The state gave up on executing him following a legal settlement that related, in part, to his health. He later died of natural causes.

In 1991, Random House published a picture book called “Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: ABC’s for a Better Planet,” in which the masked cartoon turtles trade in their signature nunchucks for signs bearing environmental slogans.
For “A,” the turtles explain the sources of acid rain. Under “B,” the concept of biodegradability.
“Don’t Pollute Dudes!” the turtles exhort under “D.” They designate the letter G for “Green Power!”
Then the book reaches the letter “M”—for meat.
“A lot of the world’s cereal crop is fed to cattle, when it could be used to feed to starving people instead,” the book says. “And cattle expel methane, a gas that makes the greenhouse effect worse.” Underneath is a drawing of one of the turtles, Donatello, eating a salad.
“What can you do?” Donatello says, instructively. “How about not eating so much meat in the first place?”
This message and its potential to harness the power of early-’90s “Turtlemania” did not sit well with the meat industry. Its top lobbying group, then the National Cattlemen’s Association, now the National Cattlemen’s Beef Association (NCBA), publicly called for Random House to cease publication.
This example of meat industry pushback is one of many that Jennifer Jacquet, a researcher with the University of Miami, and her colleague Loredana Loy unearthed while researching the association’s influence, much of it in archives at the University of Wyoming. On Wednesday, they published a new paper in the journal PLOS Climate, in which they document a string of instances of the NCA attempting to tamp down messages and distort facts about the climate impacts of livestock, the researchers say.
“What we found in the archives really reveals the lack of concern about global warming,” Jacquet said, “and yet an incredible concern about the public’s view of the role of livestock in global warming.”
Jacquet and others have long researched the industry’s attempts to downplay its greenhouse gas emissions. Some of Jacquet’s recent research documents that the industry knew about its climate impacts long before the public became broadly aware of them, but worked to obstruct policies and campaigns meant to reduce emissions and consumption.
If those dietary or policy shifts had happened, they could have significantly lowered emissions: Jacquet and her colleagues calculated that lowering meat consumption in the United States by 50 percent per capita could have been up to 80 times more effective in reducing methane emissions than all the efforts to limit methane from the oil and gas industry over a 30-year period, starting in the early 1990s.
The latest paper adds details to the record, citing more examples of the industry’s efforts and specifically homing in on the National Cattlemen’s Association.
The NCBA did not respond to requests for an interview or for comments.
Jacquet said she wanted to look at the period immediately after 1986, when researchers published a major paper estimating the significant emissions of methane from enteric fermentation—the burps of ruminant animals. In 1988, NASA’s James Hansen famously testified about the “greenhouse effect” before a U.S. Senate subcommittee, saying that “non-CO2” gases, including methane, were also warming the atmosphere.
In the years that followed, as a new wave of environmental action arose and governments across the world started to act on climate, influential books advised people to eat less livestock-based food for both health and planetary reasons. “Diet for a New America” by John Robbins advocated a shift toward vegetarian diets and “Beyond Beef: The Rise and Fall of the Cattle Culture” by Jeremy Rifkin traced the long history of beef production, railing against intensive factory farms.

As these books became popular, NCA began strategizing its rebuttal. After the actors Lisa Bonet and River Phoenix appeared on the Phil Donahue Show in support of Robbins’ book and vegetarian diets, the NCA asked researchers at Texas A&M University to refute its main points. When “Beyond Beef” was published in 1992 and Rifkin launched a related campaign urging 16 countries, including the U.S., to reduce beef consumption by 50 percent, the NCA launched the “Food Facts Coalition” to fight “anti-cow” arguments.
F.M. Byers, a researcher at Texas A&M, became the go-to scientist the NCA called on to challenge the mounting evidence behind livestock emissions from cattle. “Cattle are not a significant source of greenhouse gases,” Byers wrote in an opinion piece for USA Today.
Livestock are estimated to produce about one-third of all human-caused methane, and in the U.S. are the biggest source.
As the NCA worked on the public relations front, its members were sufficiently concerned about the growing awareness of livestock methane, to the point that some attended a workshop on “Methane Emissions from Ruminants,” held by the Environmental Protection Agency in 1989. That same year the NCA published its “Strategic Plan on the Environment,” outlining how the industry should respond to growing concerns about its environmental and climate impacts.
At that time, the NCA said climate change was a real threat and was concerned that incoming Republican President George H.W. Bush would enact policies to address it.

86a6a057d305.text: President Trump threatened Wednesday to fire two of his top political consultants if he finds a conflict, after reports that they advised a Russia-aligned government ahead of local elections there. Why it matters: Chris LaCivita and James Blair are leading Republicans' midterm election strategy, putting their foreign consulting work in tension with their prominent roles in Trump's political operation. What they're saying: Trump called the pair "outside consultants" in a Truth Social post Wednesday. "They do not work for me, other than as outside consultants. They most likely have numerous clients, but for that, you would have to ask them. They are allowed to do work for others, just like all consultants in Washington, D.C." "I do not have any idea who else they work for but will, on reflection, ask them and, if there's a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!" The other side: A source familiar with both consultants and the trip tells Axios that it was "a normal weekend full of calls and texts on the various races and our strategy/tactics in each." Context: The nationalist party warned that new voting machines could threaten its hold on power, echoing Trump's repeated attacks on voting machines in the U.S. A national election commission required the territory to use the new equipment. The source said Blair and LaCivita were there for about 48 hours to give "strategic advice on Election Integrity and what to look for to spot and avoid potential election fraud, because it was the first election where Republic of Srbska was forced to use new ballots and Smartmatic voting equipment…which obviously made them nervous." Between the lines: Caroline Wren, a registered lobbyist for Srpska, said the republic's abiding interest is in gaining stronger relations with Trump's administration. "It's not about Russia. It's not about Putin. It's about Christians who want their freedom and autonomy," Wren said. "The Trump Administration has made a huge priority of protecting and promoting Christians around the world and there is no better place to do that than the Pro-Trump Christians in the Republic of Sprska who have been demonized by the Europeans and Brussels for their Western values," she said. Blair and LaCivita were "maybe on the ground for 36 hours," she said, observing that she saw Blair constantly on the phone discussing elections back in the U.S. "Chris and James work around the clock to deliver wins for President Trump and Republicans here at home," she said. Zoom in: Blair , who previously served as White House deputy chief of staff, left the administration earlier this year to work for MAGA Inc., a super PAC affiliated with the president. He was also a senior adviser on Trump's 2024 campaign. LaCivita , the former co-manager of Trump's 2024 presidential campaign , is a senior adviser at MAGA Inc. Catch up quick: LaCivita and Blair visited Republika Srpska, a semi-autonomous entity in Bosnia and Herzegovina, ahead of local elections, according to the New York Times. The two were reportedly recruited to advise the government on voting-related issues. They were hired to work for the government, not the nationalist party that controls it, though the party dominates the territory's government. Yes, but: American political consultants have a long history of taking on foreign clients. Zoom out: Trump's family businesses have expanded their foreign dealings since he returned to office. The Trump Organization and its partners have more than 20 Trump-branded projects planned, under construction or opening abroad — more than triple the number of overseas properties operating before his return. His administration accepted a luxury Boeing 747 from Qatar slated to eventually go to Trump's presidential library, while a UAE royal-linked firm bought a 49% stake in the Trump family's cryptocurrency business. Donald Trump Jr. had his wedding bankrolled by a Putin-linked Russian oligarch and later repaid him after public outrage. Go deeper: Trump's presidential profit machine bursts into the open

08b5264d8236.text: Saudi Arabia and Syria are discussing sending Syrian troops to Yemen to join the counteroffensive against the Houthi rebels, three U.S. officials told Axios. Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa is seriously considering it, but hasn't decided. Why it matters: While the discussion is mostly between Saudi Arabia and Syria, the Trump administration has been consulted by both countries and is not opposed in principle to such a move, the U.S. officials said. But sending Syrian troops could inject a religious dimension into the Yemen war and exacerbate the conflict. The troops could include Islamist Sunni foreign fighters who participated in the rebellion against the Assad regime. They would be fighting against the Houthis, who follow Zaydi Shiite Islam. Driving the news: The Yemeni government forces backed by Saudi Arabia launched a massive ground operation over the weekend against the Houthis. The offensive was designed to retake territories the Houthis control, including the capital Sanaa and the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait. A U.S. official said the issue of sending Syrian troops to Yemen came up during the meeting between Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) and al-Sharaa in Riyadh earlier this week. The Saudis want al-Sharaa to send troops in order to boost the Yemeni forces that are less trained than the Houthis. While al-Sharaa hasn't signed off on the decision yet, the U.S. official said it is highly likely the Syrian president will accept the Saudi request. Behind the scenes: The U.S. doesn't oppose sending Syrian troops to Yemen. It would provide more support for the Saudi-backed operation against the Houthis without the U.S. having to get deeply involved, a U.S. official said. Trump administration officials also believe that deploying Syrian troops to Yemen would strengthen the relationship between two U.S. allies, Saudi Arabia and Syria. Two U.S. officials said U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) has been consulted on how Syrian troops could be deployed. The White House and CENTCOM declined to comment. Spokespeople for the Saudi Embassy and the Syrian Foreign Ministry did not respond to requests for comment. Zoom in: A source with knowledge of the discussions said the Syrian military could send 10,000 to 20,000 troops to Yemen. The units under consideration are the 90th division near Damascus and the 84th division based in southern Syria near Sweida. The 84th division includes thousands of Islamist foreign fighters who came to Syria during the civil war to fight against the Assad regime under the umbrella of the HTS rebel group.

(AP) — Farmers, truckers and economists say a move to cut taxes on diesel will provide little relief from record-high fuel prices that have soared since the U.S. attacked Iran months ago. Industry groups said they appreciate President Donald Trump's executive order expanding the use of a diesel now reserved for off-road work, but farmers already have access to the fuel and many have already wrapped up harvest. Truckers will struggle to navigate differing state rules. WATCH: Trump campaigns with Ricketts in Nebraska, signs order on red-dyed diesel "In the context of diesel prices that are over two dollars more than they were last year, it just doesn't come close to closing that wound," said Matt Perdue, president of the North Dakota Farmers Union. With less than a month to go before the November election, diesel prices continue to hit record highs as some farmers transport their crops for processing and others rush to complete their fall harvest. Many have been feeling the squeeze as costs for inputs like diesel, fertilizer and seed have soared thanks to refinery constraints and supply disruptions amid the Iran war. The executive order defers the $0.24 federal tax per gallon of regular diesel, used for road projects, until the end of the year. Most states also levy their own tax on diesel. "Dyed" diesel is the same as regular diesel, except for its red dye to help law enforcement enforce penalties for on-road use. It's already allowed for off-road purposes like farming equipment, such as tractors and combines, as well as construction and heating uses. Who will see benefits Savings can compound if states take similar actions; many have eased restrictions or waived taxes on dyed diesel, including South Dakota and Iowa. Perdue said North Dakota has waived the tax on regular diesel. But where the state decision is focused on farmers, he believes the federal decision would largely benefit those on other levels of the supply chain. Farmers who will see the most benefit are those who haul their own product, like livestock or fresh produce, on public roads. Those who have already wrapped up harvesting won't see savings. "Most of our diesel use is behind us," said Perdue, who grows spring wheat, durum and canola on his family farm. The effect is likely to be negligible for big trucking companies because the order is on a federal level and states make their own rules, Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, wrote in a social media post. "The largest diesel users are the least likely to use dyed diesel," he wrote. "A national carrier crossing five or six states in a day faces enormous risk with a patchwork of rules, legal in one state, and subject to fines in the next." WATCH: How the diesel price spike is rippling through nearly every part of the economy Many states exempt road diesel from sales tax but apply sales tax to dyed diesel instead, he said. Easing limits on red-dyed diesel will likely have a minimal effect for small truckers, who pay for fuel up front, said Todd Spencer, president and CEO of trade group the Owner-Operator Independent Drivers Association. He estimates every $1 increase per gallon in fuel costs independent truckers about $400 more per week. Increased demand for dyed diesel The savings will be small, but it could still increase competition for dyed diesel, said David Ortega, food economics and policy professor at Michigan State University. "I think there's a real chance this could backfire and make the situation worse for farmers," he said. "Basically anybody that's running a truck on the highway on regular diesel can now be using this off-highway diesel. Even someone that owns a diesel pickup truck potentially has access to this other type of diesel." Perdue in North Dakota said he expects a "rush for dyed diesel, and we'll see how the supply responds." READ MORE: Trump calls on Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian diesel fuel, saying attacks are causing a shortage But not all dyed diesel pump stations are set up for larger trucks like semis, said Paul Mitchell, a professor of agricultural and applied economics at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. "It's going to come down to infrastructure ability to get your vehicles to a place that you can use and fill them up with," he said. Supply shortages persist Henry Hanscom, American Trucking Associations chief advocacy and public affairs officer, pointed out that the executive order directs temporary penalty relief and potential tax deferral for using red-dyed diesel, not outright tax forgiveness. He said the ATA would review the Internal Revenue Service's implementing guidance of the policy when it is available. Last month, Trump had threatened a diesel export ban, though he later said it is off the table. On Friday, G7 countries agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and fuel products. b0eda7d0422f.text: By — Matthew Lee, Associated Press Matthew Lee, Associated Press By — Derek Gatopoulos, Associated Press Derek Gatopoulos, Associated Press By — Farnoush Amiri, Associated Press Farnoush Amiri, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/watch-rubio-urges-europe-to-defend-western-values-and-strengthen-u-s-alliance-in-greece Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH: Rubio urges Europe to defend Western values and strengthen U.S. alliance in Greece World Oct 7, 2026 5:22 PM EDT ATHENS (AP) — Secretary of State Marco Rubio, in a sweeping speech against the backdrop of the Acropolis in Athens, called for the nations of the West to return to their civilizational roots and restore the values that drove the rise of Europe and North America to global dominance for centuries. 4b169566f692.text: By — Annie Ma, Associated Press Annie Ma, Associated Press By — Heather Hollingsworth, Associated Press Heather Hollingsworth, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-administration-proposes-a-70000-fee-for-international-students-to-work-in-the-u-s Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump administration proposes a $70,000 fee for international students to work in the U.S. Politics Oct 7, 2026 5:16 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — The Department of Homeland Security on Wednesday proposed a $70,000 fee for international students seeking to work in the United States, the latest effort from the Trump administration to crack down on foreign enrollment. A proposed rule would require schools to pay the fee for every student who participates in the optional practice training program, known as OPT, which allows students to work in jobs related to their major during or after their time in school. Students are generally eligible for one year of work post-graduation, though certain science, technology, engineering and math majors are eligible for an additional two years. Change would be a blow to higher education and some businesses American colleges and universities heavily recruit students from overseas as a source of tuition revenue. Tech companies and other industries also hire many international students for technical roles. The OPT program allows international students to gain hands-on experience and fill labor shortages in high-demand STEM fields, said Fanta Aw, CEO of NAFSA, an association that represents international education. WATCH: Study finds Trump administration cut legal immigration far more than illegal crossings "Driving away the talents, perspectives, and aspirations of international students will only hurt American innovation, economic growth, workforce development, and global leadership," Aw said in a written statement. In a statement, DHS described the fee as a response to fraud and abuse of the visa program, which it called a "pipeline for cheap foreign labor." The public has 60 days to comment on the proposal before DHS can finalize it and put it into effect. The proposal also could face legal challenges from higher education groups or business associations that could delay it. Trump administration puts pressure on international students The proposed rule is part of its wider efforts to crack down on immigration and reshape higher education. Last year, the Republican administration began suddenly terminating the legal status of thousands of international students, detaining and deporting many of them. This summer, the administration finalized a rule that sought to prevent international students from staying in the U.S. for more than four years without approval from the federal government. The move drew swift backlash from higher education leaders who said it would increase the burden on schools and noted that many programs are longer than four years by design. A federal court prevented the rule from taking effect in September. WATCH: How college communities are reacting to funding threats, international student arrests Doug Rand, a former senior adviser at U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services during the Biden administration, predicted that the fee would be struck down in the courts, as was a $100,000 fee for the H-1B work visas that many tech companies and universities rely on to fill openings for skilled jobs. The Trump administration is now trying a different way to raise the fee for the visas to more than $100,000. Rand said fees are not the answer. "When we educate international students at our universities, and they want to work and apply their talents here after graduating, of course we should embrace them -- not use an exorbitant fee as a pretext to send them packing," Rand said in an email. Enrollment concerns mount among education groups Sarah Spreitzer, vice president at the American Council on Education, which represents college and university presidents, said international enrollment has suffered. Last fall, the number of new students entering the United States for the first time fell by 17%, the sharpest decrease since the COVID-19 pandemic. "We know that OPT is one of the reasons that international students choose to study in the United States because they're able to have that post-graduation work experience," she added. New guidance from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement that the program, Curricular Practical Training, should only be authorized when the work experience is a degree requirement led to a lawsuit Monday. Education groups, including the Association of American Universities and NAFSA, said that in the past that program was allowed if it was "directly related to the student's major area of study." The groups also said ICE was threatening college university officials with criminal prosecution if they did not comply. "We know the administration has been trying to hinder legal employment-based immigration through numerous means," said Steven Brown, a Houston-based immigration lawyer.
