Some blind people can now find a doorway or spot an object with the help of an experimental treatment and custom goggles.
Participants in a new study had blindness caused by a genetic disease called retinitis pigmentosa, which progressively kills off light-sensing cells in the retina. The treatment improved seven of 10 people’s light sensitivity, researchers report October 7 in New England Journal of Medicine. The findings build on a 2021 report that the same approach helped one blind man see and count objects.
The treatment is based on optogenetics, a technique that uses genetic instructions to make cells respond to light. Rather than repair the retina’s damaged light detectors, it gives that ability to retinal ganglion cells that normally relay visual signals to the brain.
“This is a proof of concept that optogenetics can bring back some visual activity [and] object sensitivity,” says Botond Roska, neuroscientist at the Institute of Molecular and Clinical Ophthalmology Basel in Switzerland.
Pioneering work on optogenetics snagged the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine on October 5.
Scientists have been experimenting with optogenetic therapies to rewire the eye and restore vision to people with degenerative eye diseases for more than a decade. Just as in the 2021 study, in the new work Roska and his colleagues injected genetic instructions for ChrimsonR, a light-sensitive protein derived from algae, into participants’ worse-seeing eye. The treatment made retinal ganglion cells in that eye sensitive to amber light. A camera in the custom goggles detected changes in brightness in what was in front of a study participant, and the goggles projected those changes onto the retina as pulses of amber light, activating the treated cells.
Four of the eight study participants who completed behavioral testing after treatment were able to find a doorway or follow a line while wearing the goggles. No patient gained the ability to read visual words or see faces, but Roska and his colleagues hope to tackle that next.
But there’s a limitation to this work. The approach requires a working optic nerve to carry signals to the brain, says study coauthor José-Alain Sahel, an ophthalmologist at the University of Pittsburgh. It relies on cells in the retina communicating to the brain, so it cannot restore vision when that connection is damaged.

d85b981b13f9.text: By — Ellen Schmidt, Associated Press Ellen Schmidt, Associated Press By — Gene Johnson, Associated Press Gene Johnson, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/fbi-says-it-stopped-a-mall-of-america-terror-attack-by-a-teen-after-agents-sold-him-an-assault-rifle Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter FBI says it stopped a Mall of America terror attack by a teen after agents sold him an assault rifle Nation Oct 7, 2026 4:56 PM EDT MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — FBI agents thwarted a terror attack by a teenager on the Mall of America after monitoring him for nearly two years and ultimately supplying him with the assault rifle he planned to use, authorities said Wednesday. The 18-year-old had been on the FBI's radar since December 2024, when he began trading messages with a confidential informant. A criminal complaint says he initially expressed an interest in traveling overseas to fight for the extremist group al-Shabab. As his plans to instead attack the mall solidified, it says, agents sold him an AK-47 and ammunition on Tuesday and arrested him on the spot. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "This was a radicalized young man who needed to be watched," U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen said. Agents "were able to detect a threat, and disrupt it, before the defendant carried out his intention to kill, in his words, maybe 30 to 60 people." Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud was arrested Tuesday in a public park in Richfield, several miles northwest of the Mall of America, after he paid $600 to an undercover FBI employee posing as a member of ISIS for the rifle and 200 rounds of ammunition, the agency said. Mohamud appeared in a yellow jail uniform for his initial appearance Wednesday in federal court in St. Paul. He told the judge he did not have a job, own a house or a car, or have any money in the bank. He was represented by Siri Carlson McDowell, a federal public defender. Carlson McDowell and relatives of Mohamud declined to comment after the hearing. READ MORE: FBI gives employees a classified 'Patel Report' about times the agency 'fell short' According to an FBI agent's sworn complaint, Mohamud repeatedly affirmed in chat messages to the informant that he intended to attack and kill non-Muslims at the mall on Oct. 24, the date of a scheduled Hmong arts celebration. When the informant asked if he was serious about committing the attack, Mohamud replied, "yes i am 100% sure," the complaint said, and added: "I would have backed out by now if I wasn't sure." Rosen said Mohamud is an American-born U.S. citizen of Somali descent. The agent wrote that Mohamud's messages expressed admiration for recent terror attacks as well as an interest in traveling to Somalia to join ISIS. Ultimately he decided he couldn't afford to travel there and would attack the mall instead, the complaint said. The teen first came to the FBI's attention in December 2024, the same month the source began exchanging messages with him, the complaint said. By May 2025, agents were concerned enough that they went to his home. His mother told them he wasn't home from school yet and called the boy's father, who declined to speak with them and said he would give their contact information to his lawyer, the complaint said. "What I would say to parents all over Minnesota, and all over America: If you get any indication — especially if you hear from federal law enforcement — that your son or daughter is being radicalized, to the point where federal law enforcement wants to come and give you that warning, those are warnings that ought to be heeded," Rosen said. Tens of thousands of people of Somali descent live in Minnesota, dating back to when refugees began arriving in the 1990s. Over the years several have been charged with attempting to join ISIS or other terror groups. Johnson reported from Seattle. Associated Press reporter Philip Marcelo in New York contributed. An elderly woman whose eviction sparked nationwide protests over Spain's housing crisis and a political row that triggered early elections has died, according to Madrid's tenants union.
Maricarmen Abascal, 87, was forcibly removed on a stretcher from her apartment of more than 70 years on 23 September after she was unable to afford rent increases.
The company that owned the flat later offered to allow her to return at a lower rate - but she was unable to sign an agreement as she had been admitted to hospital.
"We regret to announce that Maricarmen passed away today," the Madrid Tenants' Union said in a statement, adding her situation marked "a turning point in the history of this country".
Union spokesperson Alicia del RÃo said: "Speculation costs lives, and today rentierism has finished killing our colleague Maricarmen" but "her memory lives on with us".
Abascal became a symbol for Spain's housing crisis following her eviction.
Her father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a cap on the rent.
However, UrbagestiÃ³n, which bought the property in 2018, increased the rent from â¬500 per month (Â£428; $572) to â¬2,650 (Â£2,280; $3,020).
The company later offered to reduce this to â¬1,650 - still â¬300 more than Abascal's monthly pension.
Three previous attempts to evict her were blocked by the courts and the case has received increasing media attention.
Anger over the situation grew, leading to protests and putting pressure on the coalition government to approve emergency housing legislation - but it was rejected in Congress last week.
That led to further protests, with tens of thousands of people taking to the streets in cities across the country over the weekend.
Referring to the rejected bills, the Madrid Tenants' Union said: "While a historic agreement was reached that would have allowed her to return to her home, this solution has come too late. An absolutely avoidable situation after a torturing process."
It said the events surrounding her eviction represented a turning point in the country's history, but added that the cost to get to this point had been "too high".
"Above all, we will fulfil what she always asked of us: 'fight, keep fighting for what is yours,'" it said.
In a video recorded from her hospital bed following her eviction, Maricarmen said: "I haven't managed to defend my home, but I have fought so that others can learn to fight for what's theirs."
"All my love goes to Maricarmen's family and loved ones," Spanish Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez said. "A hug as well to everyone who today feels this loss as their own."
Protesters gathered at one of Madrid's main squares, Puerta del Sol, following the announcement of Abascal's death. The site has become a protest encampment for protesters over the last two weeks.
Photos show demonstrators lighting candles and holding posters of Maricarmen at the housing protest camp on Wednesday evening.
Earlier on Wednesday, unions had called a general strike to take place on 11 November, demanding housing reforms.
The public outcry over Abascal's situation has led to political turmoil in Spain.
On Monday SÃ¡nchez, who leads a leftist coalition that does not hold a majority in parliament, called an early election for 29 November. It followed his failure to get the emergency housing legislation through Congress.
The political right had argued that the government's attempt to intervene in the housing market would have led to fewer homes being rented and would have raised prices further.
Speaking on Monday, SÃ¡nchez said he needed "a broader progressive majority" that can "overcome the resistance of the elites" to push through reforms.
Other issues not relating to housing, such as numerous corruption scandals linked to his party, and pressures relating to the cost of living and immigration, have also caused him problems.
Most opinion polls suggest the conservatives are likely to emerge as the largest party in the next election. However, they would be expected to need the support of the hard-right Vox party to form a government.
Additional reporting by Tom McArthur

OpenAI's ChatGPT for Teens was designed to promote healthier use of the artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot, but new research has found its important safety features fall short.
The major AI firm rolled out many teen safety guardrails in August, including curbs on emotional dependence and new parental alerts for problematic use.
On Wednesday, OpenAI said it found average teen use of ChatGPT to be relatively limited and tended toward "learning" activity.
However, research released the same day from non-profit Common Sense Media found that ChatGPT still poses an "unacceptable risk" for teens as safety features, including notifying parents of self-harm conversations, often fail.
When OpenAI this summer released what it called ChatGPT for Teens, external, it said users identified as being between the ages of 13 and 17 would be opted into "features to promote healthy use and additional controls for parents".
Those features include preventing teen ChatGPT users from engaging in romantic or other language that could encourage " emotional dependence," including preventing the tool from implying that it was in any way conscious. There are also blocks on sexualized imagery and "reminders" for teens if they were to share an image that was "sensitive."
The features are also meant to enable parents to receive notifications, if they had linked to their children's ChatGPT account, about chats that included discussions of self-harm or disordered eating.
OpenAI said those features have caused an uptick in teen use focused on learning, from study help to advice on their school work.
In addition to seeing the average teen user on ChatGPT for less than 15 minutes a day, OpenAI said that for longer stretches of use, automatic reminders to take a break work well. Almost half of teen users quickly stopped using ChatGPT after such a reminder.
The company added that, for teens who are seen to have used ChatGPT for three consecutive hours or more, their prompts included something related to learning in more than 80% of such cases.
But Common Sense Media's new research, external determined that ChatGPT for Teens was an "unacceptable risk" for young people and parents, and said OpenAI should ban people under 18 years old from using the platform until teen guardrails were proven reliable.
An OpenAI spokesman said a review of Common Sense Media's methodology found that much of the testing may have begun and concluded before activation of parental controls was complete."
"We welcome rigorous independent evaluation, but we do not believe Common Sense Media's testing accurately reflects how ChatGPT's teen safeguards work in practice or expert perspectives on how AI can support teens," he said.
While the firm's research, done through multiple accounts registered as belonging to a teen and conversations before and after the teen guardrails were put in place, found that ChatGPT was good at avoiding "sexual roleplay" with young users, other OpenAI guardrails failed, including for discussions of suicide.
The research found that even an hour of teen-ChatGPT conversation about "suicidal ideation, self-harm, or disordered eating on newly created, parent-linked accounts" resulted in "zero" alerts sent to parents.
It was only older ChatGPT accounts with "weeks of accumulated conversation history on sensitive topics" that would result in a parental alert.
In such conversations, ChatGPT also "failed to reliably recommend that teens in crisis connect to a hotline or professional," the report found.
The tests also showed that ChatGPT for Teens continues to do school work, and that the bot still will engage in anthropomorphised language or "talk like it's a friend," despite OpenAI's promise to curb that behaviour.
"ChatGPT for Teens could give parents false confidence in guardrails and safety alerts that frequently don't work," Tom Siegel, who leads the Youth AI Safety Institute within Common Sense, said.
The way young people interact with online platforms has become a major issue in recent years as self-harm and suicide among children has become more common.
This year has seen several lawsuits looking to hold companies like Meta, TikTok and others responsible for harming the mental health of children end in unprecedented losses for the firms.
OpenAI, too, has come under increased scrutiny and legal pressure over the way young people use ChatGPT.
The Tumbler Ridge mass shooting in rural Canada in February was carried out by an 18-year old who had for months prior been discussing gun violence with ChatGPT.
OpenAI has previously apologised for failing to flag the shooter's account with law enforcement, and is facing several lawsuits over the incident.

A Chinese fitness influencer has been dropped by her sponsor after she apologised for riding a bicycle during the Berlin marathon.
Sun Yuanyuan, known as Abeeeer on Chinese social media, had claimed a personal best during the event which was held in September.
But an Instagram page dedicated to monitoring inaccurate or misleading race times posted by influencers published a picture which appeared to show Sun on a bicycle between the 35km and and 40km marks.
Sun apologised and admitted to "breaking the rules". Brooks, the running shoe company, has ended its sponsorship deal with her and her finish time has been disqualified by the marathon organisers.
An Instagram account calling itself the Official Marathon Time Integrity Unit (OMTIU) posted a photo of Sun apparently on the back of a bike being ridden by another person during the marathon.
The page also posted a grid of Sun's "splits" - which are the times taken to complete different 5km segments of the race.
The grid appears to show that she sped up between the 35 and 40km marks, when she was allegedly on the bike.
Sun posted an apology on the Chinese social media platform Rednote, which was shared by OMTIU, admitting that she had broken the rules.
She wrote: "I won't make any excuses for this behaviour.
"I was feeling physically unwell on the course, [but] that is absolutely not an excuse for breaking the rules.
"My attempt to take a shortcut was disrespectful to the fairness of the competition and the spirit of the marathon."
Sun, who has 520,000 followers on Rednote, also said she "deliberately concealed" her actions, adding: "I feel deeply guilty about this."
Brooks confirmed to BBC News that it had dropped Sun.
A company statement said: "Brooks believes running should be grounded in integrity, fairness, and respect for competition.
"After verifying the facts, Brooks China terminated its relationship with the individual and publicly addressed the matter."
OMTIU was set up to highlight "the growing trend of GPS-based fabrication, selective Strava displays and false PR claims" among marathon runners, particularly fitness influencers. Strava is a fitness tracking app.
The page's mission statement says: "We exist to protect the integrity of the sport by ensuring that the times athletes share publicly reflect the times they actually ran."
Its Instagram bio describes it as "satire".
BBC News has contacted the Berlin Marathon for comment.

Memorial events have taken place in Israel on the third anniversary of the devastating Hamas-led attack there that sparked the war in Gaza.
Families paid tribute to their loved ones at some of the sites where about 1,200 people were killed in the assault and 251 were taken hostage.
"The nation unites on this day in the longing for our dear ones," said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faced calls from protesters for an independent state inquiry into security failures that day.
In response to the attack, Israel launched a military offensive in Gaza which has killed more than 74,200 people, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are seen as reliable by the UN.
Violence has continued in Gaza despite a ceasefire agreed almost a year ago and living conditions for the 2.1 million people living there remain dire.
On Wednesday morning, bereaved families and survivors gathered at a memorial for the 378 people who were killed at the Nova dance festival in southern Israel on 7 October 2023.
The festival site was near Kibbutz Re'im and not far from the border with Gaza, from where Hamas-led gunmen launched their dawn attack.
Witnesses have described how festival-goers were shot, sexually abused and tortured by gunmen during the raid.
Forty-four people were kidnapped, of whom 25 were brought back from Gaza alive.
Ahuva Yavin Mayze, whose 21-year-old daughter Adi was shot and killed at Nova, told the BBC what happened at the site was "dystopic, unimaginable".
"Today is a difficult day, not only for me but for a large part of the nation," said Shlomo Sharf, a former Israeli footballer, in comments reported by Channel 12.
He paid tribute to his granddaughter, May Naim, 24, who was also killed at the festival.
Former hostage Yarden Bibas, whose wife and two young sons were kidnapped from their home in Kibbutz Nir Oz and later killed in captivity in Gaza, was quoted by the Times of Israel as saying: "Shiri, Ariel and Kfir. Sorry. Sorry that you are up there and I am here."
Crowds also filed into the small cemetery at Kibbutz Kfar Aza, where 64 residents were killed and 19 were taken hostage on 7 October.
Zion Regev, a community leader, said most surviving residents had yet to return to their homes because of the trauma of what happened.
"This is the first time we are doing all the things here in the kibbutz," he told Reuters news agency. "It's a very emotional day, it's a very difficult day for our community, three years after 7 October."
A man who reportedly helped to fend off Hamas attackers at Kibbutz Magen praised IDF troops who "fought so bravely" during the raid.
Speaking to crowds at the national memorial event at Tel Aviv's Yarkon Park on Wednesday evening, Ido Yakir said Israel would remember everyone "who knew that they had to give their lives in order to save others".
In a statement released by his office on Wednesday afternoon, Netanyahu said he had lit a memorial candle commemorating every victim of 7 October.
"We will complete the mission: we have settled the score and will continue settling the score with all the murderers," he added.
At a ceremony on Monday marking the Jewish calendar's anniversary of the attack, the prime minister said Israel had killed 4,000 out of the 6,000 Palestinians who infiltrated Israel from Gaza that day.
In Tel Aviv's Dizengoff Square, Israeli anti-government protesters dyed the fountain red to mark the anniversary of the attack.
The fountain has been used as a memorial site for those killed, with pictures, flowers and messages laid around the basin wall.
Protesters also briefly blocked one of the main highways in the city to hold a moment of silence on Wednesday morning.
They held banners that read, "the people will remember their sons and daughters", along with others that said "a complete failure" and "guilty" next to an image of Netanyahu.
Many senior Israeli defence and security officials have resigned or been fired since the attack took place. But there has not been an independent commission of inquiry into Israel's worst security failure.
The prime minister has rejected any personal responsibility and has refused to establish a state inquiry led by Israel's Supreme Court, arguing recently that the country's judiciary would be biased against him.
Einav Zangauker became an outspoken critic of the Netanyahu government while her son, Matan, was in captivity in Gaza. He was released last October as part of the ceasefire agreement.
"They're trying to make us forget what happened on 7 October," she told Army Radio. "We won't forget, we will demand the truth."
Memorial events were organised in other countries around the world, including in Germany, where the Jewish students' union held a vigil at Berlin's Brandenburg Gate.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the Hamas-led attack marked a "profound rupture".
"We commemorate the victims, we share their pain," he said, adding that antisemitism must be confronted with "even greater resolve".
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham told Britain's Jewish community: "We stand with you."
"The impact of the attacks has been felt not just in Israel, but in Jewish communities across the world who still bear the burden of the tragic events that day," he said.
Outside Downing Street, a vigil was also held to commemorate British-Israelis killed in the initial attack, later as hostages, or in fighting with Hamas.
Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, said: "The unspeakable savagery and terror of 7 October must never happen again."
She also said that the European Union "remains ready to help turn today's fragile ceasefire into a durable peace, based on a two-state solution."
Speaking to reporters outside the White House on Wednesday, US President Donald Trump said he had spoken to Netanyahu and wished the people of Israel well.
"That was a horrible day, a horrible tragedy," he said.
This is the first anniversary of the 7 October attack with no hostages remaining in G

aa8328bf4079.text: By — Maura Carey, Associated Press Maura Carey, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/tropical-storm-threat-churns-planning-for-georgia-alabama-game-with-trump-set-to-attend Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Tropical storm threat churns planning for Georgia-Alabama game with Trump set to attend Nation Oct 7, 2026 6:04 PM EDT Tropical Storm Isaias could make landfall on the U.S. Gulf Coast as a hurricane this weekend, hours before No. 2 Georgia plays at No. 6 Alabama in a major college football game on Saturday night that President Donald Trump is planning to attend. Forecasters say Isaias could become a hurricane by Thursday and make landfall late Friday or early Saturday somewhere along the Alabama-Mississippi-Florida coastlines before moving north. The storm could prompt schools to cancel games, change kickoff times or even move games to other locations. The Southwestern Athletic Conference moved Florida A&M's game at Alabama State from Saturday to Friday morning. LIVE MAP: Track the path of Tropical Storm Isaias Trump, who attended Texas' win over Tennessee in another Southeastern Conference game on Sept. 26, was asked Wednesday about the storm. "I love Alabama. I've got to go to the game," Trump responded. Trump said he didn't want to do "anything to take the focus" away from "all of the great people that work on those things," including first responders and police, adding "We'll have to see" about his travel plans. WATCH: How a super El Niño is fueling extreme weather patterns Georgia and Alabama have not disclosed backup plans for the game scheduled to kick off at 7:30 p.m. Eastern in Tuscaloosa, 200 miles inland from the coast. Alabama issued a statement saying "at this time there are no plans to alter the contest" but officials at the school and the SEC will continue to monitor conditions. The SEC ultimately makes the decision. "It's uncertainty beyond my control," Georgia coach Kirby Smart said. "I'm focused on trying to prepare our team and game plan and scheme." Smart said Georgia went through similar preparations last week with the threat of severe weather surrounding its game against Vanderbilt. The weather turned into a non-event in the Bulldogs' 38-14 win. "We had that same prep last week with the threat of those things," he said. "You can't really practice conditions. You can't simulate them, so you're much better off to educate, learn from the past of other people that have played in them, and prepare your team to play and not make it about that." READ MORE: What Florida's extreme drought means for the upcoming hurricane season The storm could trigger flash floods with dangerous winds, heavy rain and tornadoes. Events in Alabama have already been canceled. Alabama meteorologist James Spann told AL.com that moving the game to Sunday night would be the best choice. Smart and Alabama coach Kalen DeBoer said they were being updated but didn't outline contingency plans. "I'm not really involved in too much, just updated on kind of where things stand," DeBoer said. "If there's anything that would need to be adjusted, but you know, I haven't heard anything recently." In 1988, Alabama postponed a Sept. 17 game at Texas A&M to December because of Hurricane Gilbert. Georgia's 2016 game at South Carolina was pushed to Sunday due to Hurricane Matthew while the LSU-Florida game that same Saturday was postponed to November. c07c2018d01c.text: By — Fatima Hussein, Associated Press Fatima Hussein, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trumps-90-medicare-rebate-rolls-out-but-millions-arent-eligible-critics-see-a-political-stunt Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump's $90 Medicare rebate rolls out, but millions aren't eligible. Critics see a political stunt Politics Oct 7, 2026 5:53 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump says his administration will make one-time payments of $90 per person to help more than 20 million Medicare enrollees pay for their Part B premiums. It will cost about $2 billion. Less than one-third of all Medicare recipients are eligible for the payments, which are expected to be sent out this week. Not eligible are roughly 35 million Medicare Advantage enrollees, millions of other people with disabilities and low-income Medicare recipients. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The election-year promise that the Republican president made over the weekend comes as the Nov. 3 midterms are fast approaching, with the cost of living and healthcare expenses among the top issues for voters. Some questions and answers about the payouts: Who will benefit? Some 20.8 million people in the original Medicare Part B who are living in the United States, not receiving premium assistance from Medicaid or not paying an income-related monthly adjusted amount. Medicare Advantage enrollees, who make up more than half of the eligible 64.2 million Medicare beneficiaries, will not receive a payment, according to KFF, a healthcare research nonprofit. Nor will 12 million low-income older adults and people with disabilities who get premium assistance. READ MORE: Trump promised $5,000 checks if Republicans win the midterms. How would that work? The Part B program covers expenses such as doctor's visits, ambulance services and lab tests. Total monthly costs generally start at about $200 and vary with income. Allison Schuster, a White House spokeswoman, said in a statement that the administration "is enabling Americans to take control of their health by putting money directly back in the hands of Medicare patients." When will the payments go out and how will they be disbursed? According to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services website, eligible beneficiaries will receive one $90 rebate this month, with most getting a direct deposit on or around Friday. Others will receive a paper check from the Treasury Department later in October. Juliette Cubanski, director of KFF's program on Medicare policy, said the payment will be automatic. WATCH: Trump floats tariff 'dividends' for Americans, but experts question the math "As far as a benefit goes, people don't have to call or sign up — it's just money they receive directly, but not everybody on Medicare will receive this money." A White House fact sheet says people can call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227) to check on their eligibility for the premium rebate. To check on payment status, people should call the Social Security Administration at 1-800-772-1213. What is the source of the money? Payments will come out of the Medicare Improvement Fund created by Congress in 2008 and intended to make improvements to the Medicare fee-for-service program. The fund was created to improve program management and conduct oversight of contracts and contractors, according to the Congressional Budget Office, but its purpose has expanded after various legislative changes. READ MORE: Fact-checking Trump's promise to give Americans $2,000 payments from tariff dividends This is not the first time the fund has been used. Democratic President Barack Obama's administration, along with Congress, redirected $20 billion to expand healthcare coverage through the Affordable Care Act. But under Trump, it is the first time that the fund has been used to directly pay recipients. What are critics of the plan saying? Critics of Trump's promise characterize the $90 payments as a preelection stunt designed to sway voters rather than address structural problems in healthcare costs and administration. The top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden, said in a statement that "this is another desperate attempt by a failed president to escape Americans' revulsion with his failed agenda, amounting to one tank of Trump-inflated gas." WATCH: Trump's vow of $5,000 payments to Americans faces bipartisan criticism Trump recently promised $500 rebate checks to an estimated 1 million Obamacare enrollees across 30 states whom the White House alleged were overcharged by the Biden administration for some fees. Cubanski said the Medicare rebate payments were being doled out when Americans were feeling the bite of higher food, energy and gas prices. Surging healthcare costs are only compounding those pressure, she said. "This might be helpful for people but it might not go very far." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. A lawyer for convicted murderer Christa Pike says that she woke up in hospital "angry and confused" after she survived a botched execution attempt last week.
Her first words were to ask "Where am I?" and "Who are you?", her lawyer Randy Spivey recalled during a news conference.
Pike, who was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend in 1995, survived two lethal injections on 30 September in Tennessee.
Experts and her legal team say her apparent recovery is unprecedented, and that no other US inmate has survived a lethal injection from executioners.
A court on Wednesday ordered the state of Tennessee to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution.
Pike, 50, continues to receive critical medical care and is being restrained at her hands and feet in her hospital bed, her lawyers said at the news conference after a court hearing on Wednesday.
Spivey said that her legal team believed for days that she was brain dead, and expected her to be taken off life support at any moment.
However, in a "shock to everyone", she began to talk on Tuesday, while recalling only limited details about the execution attempt.
Pike, he said, had helped the execution team find a vein in her arm, and she was kind and polite while she was being injected.
Then she woke up in a hospital with a tube down her throat and people she didn't know. Both of her arms, he said, are now "tremendously swollen".
"We don't know the toll all of this will take" on her mental health, Spivey said, noting how she was left "angry and confused" by the ordeal.
He added that she also has a blood clot in one of her arms, pneumonia, and is not able to swallow.
Pike is believed to be the only person to survive an execution attempt by lethal injection.
After it became clear Pike would not die, following two rounds of the drug pentobarbital, she was taken to hospital, where she remained unconscious for days as medical staff cleared her body of the injected chemical.
Earlier on Wednesday, lawyers appeared before a judge for an emergency hearing, where her team requested that all evidence from the botched execution be preserved.
That evidence could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state.
Luke Ihnen, one of Pike's lawyers, began by describing the "roadblocks" that have made it challenging to communicate with his client.
"Up until yesterday our client was unconscious, and unable to communicate," he told Judge Chancellor I'Ashea Myles. Pike is now "speaking limitedly", he said.
Tennessee Assistant Attorney General Will Ayers called attention to the "unusual procedural position here", prompting agreement from the judge. He argued that an emergency motion was unnecessary because the state is already compelled to preserve evidence.
Still, Judge Myles ordered that "anything that was in the actual room needs to be preserved and maintained," including IV lines and syringes, as well as waste, like packaging, inserts, and labels.
The judge also demanded documentation on Pike's psychological condition prior to, during and after the 30 September execution attempt.
She advised the state to take "special care" not to misplace or accidentally delete any information that may be pertinent to the case.
Asked by the judge whether the state intended to reschedule execution for Pike, Ayers said he did not know the answer.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered a pause on all executions in the state for the rest of the year, and has said he wants answers about what went wrong. The state's prisons chief said he is resigning after the failed execution.
Ihnen asked the judge to allow Pike access to a phone so she can call her lawyers, and they can have "continuous liberal access to Ms Pike". He said they were kept waiting for over two hours during a recent attempt to visit her in hospital.
Ihnen added that Tennessee prison officials are keeping her "shackled" to her hospital bed, despite requests from medical staff that the handcuffs be removed.
Her lawyer also requested that the Tennessee Department of Corrections be required to notify his team 48 hours before she is transferred from the hospital to any state hospital or other government-run facility.
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for troubled teens.
Shipp was 17 years old at the time, meaning that he was spared the death penalty for his part in the attack because he was not yet legally an adult at the time. He remains in prison.

Flight Attendants Association-CWA President Sara Nelson said the 250-foot (76 meter) arch compounds multiple safety concerns that she said have gone unaddressed from a deadly January 2025 crash over the Potomac River that killed 67 people. Nelson also criticized Trump's plan to turn the arch into "a top grade military complex" able to host drones and snipers while storing ammunition. "DCA is already stretched to its limit, we do not need an obstacle taking up space in our flight path," said Nelson. "Nor should commercial aviation have to dodge military drones, missiles or snipers while attempting to take off or land at Washington National Airport. Safety first always." WATCH: Retired general calls Trump's proposed arch near Arlington a 'sacrilege' Nelson's statement on behalf of the union, which represents 55,000 flight attendants across 20 airlines, joins the voices of an assemblage of veterans' groups, Congress members and others with safety concerns and complaints about the memorial's threat to historic and symbolic sightlines between different landmarks in Washington, D.C. Though the arch has received early approval from the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts, whose members were all tapped by Trump, a group of three veterans and an architectural historian sued, saying the project needs to be approved by Congress. Last month, the Republican president said in a social media post that he had agreed, at the "strong request" of the military, to convert the planned 250-foot-tall (76-meter) memorial arch "into a top grade Military Complex." The Federal Aviation Administration said last month before Trump's announcement on it becoming a military complex that the arch would not pose a hazard to aircraft, but it should be "appropriately marked with a non-standard eternal flame on top of the structure and floodlight projectors pointed towards the arch to make it noticeable for pilots. An assessment by the National Park Service said the memorial arch could disrupt the historical significance of dozens of nearby sites. The Park Service approved the project despite its assessment. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum announced early last month that excavation work on the site in Memorial Circle would begin within weeks. The Interior Department did not respond immediately to questions on the status of that work. The arch is one of several projects around Washington that Trump has undertaken as he remakes the city from renovating one of its storied public golf courses to threatening to demolish the John F. f7227b2b31e1.text: Police and protesters clashed in Liège, Belgium, on Wednesday as student anger over education costs and school conditions grew, echoing massive protests in neighboring France. Why it matters: The protests are exposing broader anger across Europe over school funding and classroom conditions. Catch up quick: Protests that began in Paris in mid-September as a localized demonstration by high school students have escalated into a massive nationwide movement, with students, parents and teachers' unions demanding more education funding. There have been clashes between French police and protesters in recent days, culminating in a 15-year-old boy's hand being blown off by a police-fired stun grenade. More than 6,500 people — most of them minors —have been arrested since the protests began in France. In Belgium, police have made at least 139 arrests in Liège since the protests began Oct. 1. The big picture: The current wave erupted in France, but education grievances across Europe predate it, with crowded classrooms, teacher shortages, university cuts and soaring education costs fueling protests over government investment in education. In Greece, students called nationwide school actions for Thursday, according to Euronews , including assemblies, walkouts, demonstrations and potentially occupations. In Italy, high-school occupations began in Turin and Rome on Monday under the slogan "Let's do as in France." Italian students cited underfunding, deteriorating school buildings and rising living costs among grievances they share with French students, and a delegation traveled to Paris in solidarity, ANSA reports . In Ireland, thousands of university students demonstrated in Dublin earlier this month, demanding lower fees, more higher-education funding and affordable accommodation, per RTÉ . In Germany, students, teachers, parents and unions rallied in September to demand greater education investment, more teachers and a more equitable school system, according to Tagesschau . In Austria, student groups are preparing fresh demonstrations in mid-October after the country's university association warned of possible cuts of around €1 billion from the next three-year university budget, ORF reports . Between the lines: The education unrest comes as several European governments face mounting pressure to rein in deficits while higher borrowing costs make their debts more expensive to service. France and Belgium are each running budget deficits of more than 5% of their GDP this year, while Austria's is above 4%, according to European Commission forecasts. That squeeze is forcing governments to make difficult choices over public spending. The bottom line: The protests aren't one coordinated European movement, but students across several countries are mobilizing around their shared concerns. Go deeper: The global fiscal reckoning is here

af2d5c2517d5.text: President Trump will attend a summit Thursday meant to empower scientists and position the U.S. as a leader in breakthroughs driven by "super intelligence," according to an announcement shared first with Axios. Why it matters: The Trump administration is looking for industry to step in amid its cuts to government funding for science research and development. Driving the news: The White House is announcing more than $1 billion in industry commitments for the Genesis Mission from AMD, OpenAI, Anthropic and others. The White House is also announcing a compute hub of more than 14 institutions across 10 southeast states, and a $1 billion investment in Georgia for student and faculty compute access. The National Science Foundation and the Energy Department will invest more than $100 million in AI-driven science tools. Leading scientists and "innovators" will attend the summit, the White House says. Zoom in: The summit was inspired by a July report from White House Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios. It highlights industry's increasing role in driving research and development, plus new mechanisms for funding and organizing research. Catch up quick: Trump last November launched the Genesis Mission, which sets ambitious deadlines to accelerate scientific discovery. In July, the White House announced that the effort would be expanded to more than 15 federal agencies. Last week, the White House held another AI summit that focused on the rollout of America.gov, which aims to streamline government services using AI.

c941dfee3ef8.text: The Pentagon instructed U.S. Central Command several days ago to conclude preparations for resuming major combat operations in Iran , U.S. officials said. Why it matters: The directive didn't include a specific date for launching strikes, and President Trump hasn't made any final decisions. But U.S. and Israeli sources say it could happen before the U.S. midterm election and possibly the Israeli elections a week earlier. The big picture: If major combat operations resume, they're expected to include massive bombing of Iranian energy, infrastructure and nuclear targets, sources say. Resuming the war in the next three to four weeks could influence the midterm elections, in part because oil prices might rise in response. "The Department's job is to develop and present military options to the President," a Pentagon official told Axios. A White House official said Trump has all options available at any time. "The U.S. is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing. Iran has been decimated, and things will go one of two ways: the easy way or the hard way," the official said. "President Trump holds all the cards and will do whatever is best for the United States." The Atlantic reported earlier Wednesday that Trump is weighing striking Iran before the midterm election. Driving the news: On Friday, Trump's national security team met at Camp David for several hours to discuss the war and other issues. An Israeli official told Axios that part of the meeting focused on a possible resumption of major combat operations in Iran. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said after the meeting that it focused on "long-term" foreign policy planning. Negotiations between the U.S. and Iran haven't made any progress. Qatari mediators are still waiting for an Iranian response to a U.S. counterproposal that included demands for nuclear concessions. "The discussion about possible resumption of major combat operations in Iran has increased. The chances of it happening before the elections is not high but we don't rule it out. After the midterms the chances of it happening increase significantly," a second Israeli official said. Behind the scenes: President Trump spoke Wednesday with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. It was their second call in days , after barely speaking for many weeks. A U.S. official said Trump and Netanyahu spoke about "remembrance and respect for the victims of the October 7 massacre." The call took place after Netanyahu held a meeting with his national security team about Iran, the first Israeli official said. Netanyahu spoke to Rubio on Monday. If major combat operations resume, they will most likely be with the U.S. and Israel working in tandem and with the Israeli military participating. The two Israeli officials said the Iranian regime is desperate and paranoid, which might lead it to strike first. They said the Iranians have suffered two surprise attacks and don't want to experience a third. Between the lines: Resumption of the war could also affect the Israeli elections, since Iran would likely fire hundreds of ballistic missiles at the country in retaliation. A renewed escalation — or even a heightened state of tension or emergency — could benefit Netanyahu politically and prevent his opponents from attacking him in the final stretch of the campaign.

f000a14dc742.text: Anger and backlash are building at Cornell University this week over the way the school handled an alleged gang rape in 2024. The case has renewed questions about how sexual assault allegations are investigated on college campuses and by law enforcement. Geoff Bennett discussed more with Deborah Tuerkheimer, a former prosecutor and author of "Credible: Why We Doubt Accusers and Protect Abusers." Amna Nawaz: Anger and backlash are building at Cornell University this week over the way the school handled an alleged gang rape in 2024. Geoff Bennett: Today, students staged a seven-hour sit-in and launched what they're calling an economic blackout, halting all spending on campus, including with any university operations. That follows a rally earlier this week that drew thousands of students, faculty, and community members demanding justice for Jane Doe, who says she was sexually assaulted by multiple men at Cornell's Chi Phi fraternity two years ago. Saya Taylor, Cornell Protester: Jane Doe deserved an administration that delivered a fair and proper judicial process. Jane Doe deserved a police department that would actually follow up on her case. Instead, she was silenced, her rapists free to walk the grounds of Cornell under a system that chose the university over the student. Geoff Bennett: Yesterday, Cornell announced former federal prosecutor Sally Yates will lead an independent review of the university's handling of the case. And, late last week, Governor Kathy Hochul appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James a special prosecutor. The local district attorney did not pursue charges back in 2024. The case has renewed questions about how sexual assault allegations are investigated on college campuses and by law enforcement. Northwestern Law Professor Deborah Tuerkheimer is a former prosecutor and author of "Credible: Why We Doubt Accusers and Protect Abusers." She joins us now. Thank you for being with us. Deborah Tuerkheimer, Northwestern Pritzker School of Law: Thank you for having me. Geoff Bennett: New York data shows that most campus sexual assault cases never reach law enforcement, never result in serious discipline. And yet we know that Jane Doe pursued many of the avenues available to her. There was a Title IX investigation. There was a police report. Of course, there's now a civil lawsuit. When you look at how this case was handled, what should have happened differently? Deborah Tuerkheimer: Well, from the beginning, the criminal investigation really never got off the ground. From what we have been able to tell, there was no effort to build a relationship with Jane Doe. There was no effort to take into account the impact of trauma and the way that traumatic memories are really stored and retrieved and encoded differently than other types of memories. There was very little effort then to gather the kind of corroborative evidence that would give investigators a sense of whether charges were viable. Instead, what we saw is that, from the very beginning, the investigation was dismissed, and Jane Doe was too. Geoff Bennett: And Cornell handled this through Title IX, even though the allegations included serious crimes. At what point should a university turn a case like this directly over to law enforcement? Deborah Tuerkheimer: Well, the choice of whether to take a case to law enforcement really belongs to a victim. In this case, as you said, Jane Doe did seek to pursue both a criminal prosecution and also her Title IX complaint, and that is absolutely within the right of someone who's been the victim of sexual assault. So, often, the proceedings proceed parallel, and they can happen at the same time. One can happen before the other. But, again, here, we saw only the Title IX proceeding go forward, and the criminal case never got off the ground. Geoff Bennett: And New York law has come under scrutiny too, as you well know, over how voluntary intoxication affects sexual assault prosecutions. How does that complicate questions of consent and prosecution? Deborah Tuerkheimer: Well, New York has a provision of its rape law that says that a person who is mentally incapacitated or temporarily unable to control or appraise their conduct due to alcohol or drugs is not able to consent, but only if those drugs or alcohol were administered without the consent of the victim. So that's what's called the voluntary intoxication loophole. About 19 states do treat voluntary intoxication and involuntary intoxication differently. And what it means is that someone who's voluntarily ingested alcohol or drugs is deemed not to be a victim, unworthy of the law's protection. Geoff Bennett: You have written extensively about consent, the skepticism directed at victims, the institutions that can protect the accused. How does the Cornell case fit into that broader pattern that you have researched and written about? Deborah Tuerkheimer: Well, sadly, these dynamics are familiar, all too familiar. And I say sadly, but also maddeningly. In cases across the country every day, victims are met with undue skepticism. They're met with blame. They're met with disregard. I call this the credibility discount, and we see it all the time. It's ubiquitous. Geoff Bennett: And we should say, the names and images of the seven men who have been accused have been spread widely across social media. Their names have, in some cases, been reported, even though none have been criminally charged. And we have seen cases, including the Duke lacrosse case, where men accused of sexual assault were ultimately exonerated. So, what protections are owed to the accused? Deborah Tuerkheimer: Well, in criminal court, the a criminal defendant has the highest level of protection, and that's appropriate because of the consequences that can ensue. And, on campus, there are also protections that are due to a respondent. I think what we're seeing in this case is that the credibility discount means that investigators aren't even doing their job. They'

The market odds of a rate increase at the US Federal Reserveâs October meeting sank Wednesday after the central bank published minutes of its September meeting, though Fed watchers priced in a December hike.
While the Fedâs policymakers voted unanimously to raise interest rates last month, they were divided over the rationale for doing so.
Some sought to head off demand-driven inflation while others wanted to curb energy and AI-driven price shocks.
Last weekâs cooler-than-expected jobs report, along with a rise in bond yields, bolstered the case for a pause: âThe long end of the yield curve has already gone up, and thatâs the end that matters to the economy,â a former Philadelphia Fed president told The Wall Street Journal.

d365005b900b.text: By — Adriana Morga, Associated Press Adriana Morga, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/education/student-loan-borrowers-have-more-time-to-reduce-interest-rates-heres-what-to-know Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Student loan borrowers have more time to reduce interest rates. Here's what to know Education Oct 7, 2026 7:25 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — Student loan borrowers now have until the end of 2026 to enroll in auto pay and have their interest rate reduced by 1%. The original deadline was Sept. 30, but the U.S. Department of Education extended it to give borrowers more time to enroll. The rate reduction will last through June 2028. Borrowers who currently use auto pay already receive an interest-rate discount of 0.25%, so the new reduction takes off just 0.75%. This temporary benefit is meant to support borrowers, along with those who are returning to repayment, and ensure they can stay on top of the new Repayment Assistance Plan that requires on-time payments, according to the Education Department. READ MORE: Why experts say this moment is ripe for student loan scams The interest reduction can benefit borrowers who have large balances and are on fixed payments, said Lesley J. Turner, associate professor of public policy at the University of Chicago. "For a limited time, borrowers are now able to get a full percentage point reduction in their interest rate if they sign up for auto debit," Turner said. "So this is a quadrupling of the earlier benefit. It's a pretty big benefit, especially for borrowers who have large balances." Since the interest reduction was announced this summer, nearly 2 million borrowers have enrolled in auto pay. Around 9 million Americans are in default on their federal student loans as of June, according to the Education Department. Hundreds of thousands more are behind on loan payments and at risk of default this year. If you're looking to enroll your student loans in auto pay, here's what you need to know: If you're new to auto pay, enroll by the end of the year In order to get the 1% interest reduction, you must enroll in auto pay by Dec. 31. First, log in to your student loan servicer account and select auto pay. You'll need to enter your bank information to automatically withdraw the monthly payment from your checking or savings account. Even without the rate reduction, auto pay is a good way to stay on top of your student loans, Turner said. "We all know life gets busy and if you have to log in every month and manually make your payment there may be a chance that you forget and then you end up having your loans go delinquent," she said. If you're already enrolled, you already have the reduction Borrowers who were enrolled in auto pay before the announcement in July have had their interest rate automatically reduced by 1%, according to the Education Department. If you're currently in default, consolidate your loans If your student loans are in default, you must log in to studentaid.gov and consolidate your eligible loans in order to sign up for auto pay. READ MORE: As student loan defaults rise, experts worry about what's next Involuntary collections on federal student loans remain on hold. The Trump administration announced earlier this year that it is delaying plans to withhold pay from student loan borrowers who default on their payments. Borrowers are considered in default when they are at least 270 days behind on payments. The online application for loan consolidation is available at studentaid.gov/loan-consolidation. If you have multiple federal student loans, you can combine them into a single loan with a fixed interest rate and a single monthly payment. The consolidation process typically takes around 60 days to complete. You can only consolidate your loans once. If your student loans are in default, you can also contact your loan holder to apply for a loan rehabilitation program. Through this program, borrowers are enrolled in a reduced payment plan and, after five successful payments, wage garnishment ends. Borrowers can find more information about loan rehabilitation here. e97efaded06d.text: By — Bob Thomas, Associated Press Bob Thomas, Associated Press By — Jake Coyle, Associated Press Jake Coyle, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/arts/eva-marie-saint-star-of-on-the-waterfront-and-north-by-northwest-dies-at-102 Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Eva Marie Saint, star of 'On the Waterfront' and 'North by Northwest,' dies at 102 Arts Oct 7, 2026 7:19 PM EDT LOS ANGELES (AP) — Eva Marie Saint, the pale, willowy actor who won an Academy Award for her first movie, "On the Waterfront," and starred opposite Cary Grant in the Alfred Hitchcock thriller "North by Northwest," has died. She was 102. Saint, whose acting work lasted well into her 90s, died at her home in Los Angeles on Tuesday, confirmed family representative Jeff Sanderson. Saint had one of the most spectacular debuts in Hollywood history, as the love interest of Marlon Brando's tormented Terry Malloy in "On the Waterfront," and her first trip to the Academy Awards was memorable too. Pregnant with her first child, Saint accepted her Oscar from Frank Sinatra and smilingly murmured a unique winner's speech: "I think I may have the baby right here." (Her son, Darrell, was born two days later.) The award for the 1954 classic made her an instant star, but she soon astonished Hollywood with a firm independence that would mark her career. She refused offers of studio contracts and declined chances to follow up on her great success, explaining that she was taking time off to become acquainted with her new son. (A daughter, Laurette, was born in 1958.) A curated career In her first decade in Hollywood, Saint appeared in a mere seven films. She declined such top-level productions as "The Man in the Gray Flannel Suit" with Gregory Peck, "Summer and Smoke" with Laurence Harvey and "The Rainmaker" with Burt Lancaster. She credited her husband, TV and stage director Jeffrey Hayden, with persuading her to star in Hitchcock's "North by Northwest," the classic 1959 thriller in which Saint plays a spy who seduces Grant, but ends up falling for him. "I vividly remember him saying, 'Honey, I think you should find a quiet spot. I'll take care of the children and I want you to really think about this and reread this script,'" she told Vanity Fair in 2014. "He was so right. And that's what husbands are for." Instead of being put off by her selectivity, studios continued offering her starring roles in such films as "Exodus" (with Newman), "Raintree County" (Elizabeth Taylor, Montgomery Clift) and "All Fall Down," with Warren Beatty. She turned more to television in the 1970s and enjoyed renewed popularity in the 1980s as the mother of Cybill Shepherd in the hit sitcom "Moonlighting" and as Tom Hanks' mother in the film comedy "Nothing in Common." She won an Emmy for the 1990 miniseries "People Like Us," and had roles in such 21st century movies as "Because of Winn-Dixie," "Superman Returns" and "Winter's Tale," adapted from Mark Helprin's novel of the same name. In 2021, she played Marisa Tomei's aunt in the brief audio play "The Bus Ride," part of "The Pack Podcast." Saint was married to Hayden for 65 years, until his death in 2016. That was her real name When Saint emerged in the public consciousness, many believed her theatrical-sounding name must have been invented. She was born with it on July 4, 1924, in Newark, New Jersey. The family moved to Delmar, a small town near Albany, New York, where her father was a Goodrich Rubber Co. manager. Eva's goal was to become a third-grade teacher like her mother, but at Bowling Green State University in Ohio she tried out for a play and won the leading role. After graduation, she lived with her parents and began hunting for acting jobs in Manhattan. After a fruitless year, she landed a two-line role as a telephone operator on a radio drama and soon was working steadily on soap operas and nighttime dramas, appearing for two years as Claudia on "One Man's Family." Network television was booming in the early 1950s, and her looks and dramatic sense made her a favorite with casting people and producers. She credited Lee Strasberg with helping her overcome shyness A critical turn in Saint's career came when she auditioned before Elia Kazan and was accepted into the Actors Studio, which shaped a generation of method-actor stars. She credited acting coach Lee Strasberg with helping her overcome her shyness. "Lee Strasberg, when he got to know me a little bit, gave me a scene to do where I had to cry in front of my peers," she told The Santa Barbara Independent in 2009. "I worried about it, I worked on it, I tried to use what I was learning at the studio. I finally did the scene, and I cried, and my peers were crying with me. It was just an incredible moment for me." Saint was rejected for the single female role in the play "Mister Roberts," but was hired to understudy the actor chosen, Jocelyn Brando, Marlon's sister. In six frustrating months Saint never got to substitute for Brando. She finally made it to Broadway in "A Trip to Bountiful," which she had played on television. Kazan invited her to try out for the female lead in "On the Waterfront" by improvising a scene with Brando. She was told to try to stop a young man from entering her apartment. She told the Los Angeles Times in 2001: "All I know is that Marlon got in the door and turned on the music. We started dancing. He flicked my skirt. Kazan saw the sparks fly, and that's how I got the part." Thomas, a former Associated Press Hollywood correspondent who died in 2014, was the primary writer of this obituary. The Court of Appeals in New York has heard arguments from both lawyers for families of 9/11 victims and the government of Saudi Arabia as it decides whether the families' long-running legal case against the Middle Eastern country can move to trial.
Almost 3,000 people were killed on 11 September 2001 after hijackers seized four US passenger jets and crashed them into the World Trade Center in New York, the Pentagon, and a Pennsylvania field, following resistance from passengers.
The families allege that a Saudi government employee, Omar al-Bayoumi, knowingly supported two of the hijackers and that he was working with a network of officials linked to the Saudi Ministry of Islamic Affairs.
Bayoumi, who is now retired from government work, has denied knowing the two men were hijackers or that he had any involvement in 9/11, while Saudi Arabia has said that any allegation that it or its officials are complicit in 9/11 is categorically false.
The Kingdom has argued that, as a foreign sovereign state, it has immunity from prosecution in US courts.
The families, who first filed the lawsuit in 2002, spent several years lobbying US Congress to pass an amendment to the foreign sovereign immunity law to allow the case to go ahead.
In 2016, Congress passed the Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act (JASTA), which allows civil claims against a foreign state or official for injuries, death, or damages from an act of international terrorism.
In August 2025, the Manhattan District Court ruled that the 9/11 families had presented enough evidence to meet the terms of the act and the case was allowed to proceed towards a trial.
Saudi Arabia on Wednesday asked the Court of Appeals to reverse that decision.
Counsel Gregory Rapawy argued core issues of fact â including the central question of the nature of Bayoumi's employment by the Saudi state â had not been decided and needed to be done so before the country could be stripped of immunity.
9/11 families' lawyer Gavin Simpson argued that the District Court had already found that Bayoumi's actions "were not just acts of a good Samaritan or an innocent participant".
"He was, in fact, following Saudi Arabia's instructions when assisting the hijackers," said Simpson, and that these were points that Saudi Arabia had "failed to rebut."
One option the judges seemed to wrestle with was whether to send the case back to the district court to make more concrete findings, which could involve taking testimony from live witnesses.
Asked by Judge Guido Calabresi which witnesses Saudi Arabia could call in that eventuality, Rapawy suggested that if the issue ultimately came down to Bayoumi's credibility, "we would have to see" if he could be called to testify.
As he drew the hearing to a close, Judge William Nardini said "it's a difficult case, and we will take it under advisement", meaning that the panel would issue a ruling at a future date.
Speaking outside the courthouse, Terry Strada, whose husband Tom was killed in the World Trade Center, told the BBC she felt positive about the hearing.
"25 years is an extraordinary time to go without accountability and justice for the murder of your loved one. What we hope is that the judges will uphold [District Court] Judge Daniels' decision and move to a trial."

For Alberta independence supporter Keith Wilson, the western Canadian province is in a league of its own.
With its wealth of rich oil and gas reserves, a significant agricultural sector and a young and skilled workforce, its economy is one to be reckoned with, says Wilson.
The province will hold a referendum on 19 October, giving residents two options: vote to stay in Canada, or vote to move ahead with a formal binding referendum on independence at a later date.
The vote, despite not being a cut and dry "stay or leave", still stands to be among the most consequential in recent Canadian history, and a significant test of national unity.
One key issue has become central to the debate: Would Alberta be richer if it were to become an independent country?
The answer for Wilson is yes.
"Alberta's economy is unique. is fundamentally different than the rest of Canada's - we have the people, the institutions, the infrastructure to excel," he says.
Alberta separatists have long argued that the province has been short-changed by being part of Canada, and that more of the oil and gas wealth would be kept within its borders instead of being shared with Ottawa, delivering it tens of billions in savings.
But many disagree with their accounting.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, who opposes independence, predicts a more sober outcome. She says the province could risk paying C$400bn ($283bn; Â£213bn) in transition costs alone, while bleeding billions more in lost investments and trade due to the political upheaval.
A report commissioned, external by her government released earlier this month calculated the costs of separation as between C$50bn and C$170bn over five years - and a highly unpredictable outlook over the long term.
The report cautions that the to-do list for a newly independent Alberta would be long and costly.
It would have to set up agencies to manage taxes and national security, develop its own constitution, legal and court systems, and pension plans, and negotiate the division of federal assets like national parks and military bases.
Lennie Kaplan, a former finance official in Alberta, says the province would be expected to take on a share of Canada's national debt, among many other fiscal challenges and responsibilities.
A report on Alberta independence by the CanadaWest Foundation, external, a non-profit Alberta-based think tank, estimates that the province could be stuck with additional debt ranging from C$258bn to C$333bn.
With a projected hit to Alberta's GDP and the additional costs, the report estimates separation could hit Albertans' bottom line and reduce their disposable income by 5.8% on average.
"Why do we have to create all this uncertainty that might impact and impair the province's fiscal position going forward? Why wouldn't we just work within Canada to address these issues?" Kaplan asks.
Opinion polling indicates that around 20% to 25% of Albertans plan to vote in favour of moving ahead with a binding separation referendum, with higher support among younger, rural and conservative voters.
Behind the separatist push is the belief that Alberta is misunderstood and overlooked by decision-makers in Ottawa. For decades, that sentiment fuelled a sense of "western alienation" in the prairie province.
Once a fringe movement, a number of factors pushed it to the forefront of Alberta politics.
There was anger over environmental and political pushback that killed proposed pipelines from landlocked Alberta to coastal waters.
A decade of Liberal government in Ottawa has also caused frustration in reliably conservative Alberta. And, in addition, there is also leftover distrust of the federal government over what some Albertans saw as excessive lockdowns during the Covid-19 pandemic.
Over the past year, separatist organisers held townhalls across the province to gauge interest from the public. They then launched a citizen-led petition to separate earlier this year, which got more than 300,000 signatures.
Smith, the premier, decided earlier this year she would authorise a vote.
Alberta is home to Canada's oil and gas sector, with oil reserves estimated to be the fourth-largest in the world. Crude oil is by far Canada's most profitable commodity, accounting for C$142bn in export value in 2025 alone.
Most of it is sold to refineries in the US.
The province has the highest GDP per capita in the country, and it contributes billions a year to the federal tax pool because of its strong economy.
It has not received any "equalisation" payments - money that so-called "have not", or less wealthy, provinces receive from the federal government - since 1965.
Calculations by Tegan Hill and Nathaniel Li, economists at the Fraser Institute think tank, show that Alberta's total net contribution to Ottawa since 2007 has been C$322bn, or an average of around $17bn per year.
"That's nearly four times that of British Columbia, more than four times Ontario," Hill tells the BBC. "The other seven provinces were net recipients, meaning Ottawa spent or transferred more money to those provinces than it collected."
Hill explains that the amount Alberta contributes to the rest of Canada is one of the main frustrations cited by those in favour of separation.
The sentiment, she says, is that: "We're paying to support these other provinces, and if we just went our own way, we could keep all that wealth for ourselves."
This belief is at the heart of the economic projections from the Alberta Prosperity Project, one of the main groups organising in favour of independence.
In its fiscal plan, released last year, external, they estimate Alberta will save up to C$47bn annually if it stops paying federal taxes.
The plan acknowledges that Alberta's costs would be higher if it were independent because it would have to pay for things like national defence and international diplomacy, estimating those costs to be up to C$31.6bn annually.
This would be in addition to paying for things Alberta as a province already covers

c7d721434418.text: Protests are continuing in France, a day after more than 250,000 people took to the streets across the country to demand education reforms. Demonstrations began in mid-September, fueled by frustrations over classroom sizes and poor building conditions. Special correspondent William Denselow reports from Paris. Amna Nawaz: Well, protests are continuing in France a day after more than 250,000 people took to the streets across the country to demand education reforms. Demonstrations began in mid-September, fueled by frustrations over classroom sizes and poor building conditions. Nearly 500 people were arrested Tuesday, bringing the total to more than 6,000 since the start of the protests. Special correspondent William Denselow reports from Paris. William Denselow: Anger on the streets of Paris, as demonstrators led by high school students continue to give French authorities a failing grade. Marwan, Student (through interpreter): National education is really catastrophic. Personally, in my high school, the roofs are open, there's no heating, the desks are broken. So we work in really precarious conditions. Rayan, Student: The building, the school and the system, we want to change. William Denselow: The government says demonstrations have been hijacked by outside groups, leading to urban violence. Several hundred teenagers have been injured, prompting authorities to suspend the use of stun grenades. Amaima, Student: A boy whose mouth is completely destroyed, et cetera, and many more things. And it's just horrible to see, especially when it's kids who are just trying to fight for their rights. William Denselow: A right to a better education. France tops the list for average class sizes in Europe, with roughly 25 to a class in public schools from ages 11 to 15. Responding to the recent protests, the government promised to make visible changes to the nation's schools. Edouard Geffray, French Education Minister (through interpreter): We must do more and better, notably for high schools. And so the prime minister has entrusted us with a number of initiatives. William Denselow: Initiatives like addressing class cancellations by replacing absent teachers. But that requires substantial investment, no easy task as French public debt hit roughly $4 trillion in June, soaring to 119 percent of GDP. That's the highest level since 1946, after the destruction of World War II. Genevieve Pons, President, Europe Jacques Delors: Times are difficult with oil prices rising. So it's a really difficult moment for the government in France now, because they have to face these real problems with very rapidly shrinking means. William Denselow: For demonstrators, the message is clear. Lawmakers must find a solution. Trade unions joined Tuesday's demonstrations in solidarity with the student movement. It adds further pressure on the French government ahead of next year's presidential elections. Genevieve Pons, president of the Europe Jacques Delors, a Brussels-based think tank, says whoever is elected president next April will be tasked with answering a fundamental question. Genevieve Pons: France will need total, if I may say so, rethinking,because we have to answer this question. Why is it the country where the taxes are the highest and a country where public services have real problems? William Denselow: Existential questions attracting attention from overseas. On Tuesday, President Trump weighed in on social media, claiming the protests were being fueled by out-of-control mass migration and not schools, further stoking an already charged immigration picture here. In response, the French foreign minister said France will write its own story during what's becoming an increasingly challenging chapter in the country's history. For the "PBS News Hour," I'm William Denselow in Paris.
