Watch: Why was the sign at the British consulate in East Jerusalem removed?
Israel said in September it would shut the British consulate, in retaliation for UK sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank which are illegal under international law.
The UK government had made last-ditch efforts to persuade Israel not to close the building ahead of Thursday's deadline, after the Israeli government said it would close the consulate within 30 days of the UK sanctions announcement.

1a816e62cfe6.text:
Mark Zuckerberg was just three minutes into his keynote speech at the company's annual Meta Connect product event last month when his tone turned almost wistful.
"Building is an act of love," he said, glancing down at the ground with his hands in his pockets. "It's how we impart what we believe, and we pour our hearts and our souls into what we make."
Speaking to hundreds of analysts and developers, Zuckerberg proceeded to share news about Meta's latest AI products: its new agentic chatbot Muse, a slew of smart glasses, as well as a Tamagotchi-like AI gadget users can attach to their wrists.
It was a conference focused on new technologies - but still, it's perhaps notable that during a presentation lasting nearly an hour, Zuckerberg did not mention two of his most popular products, Instagram and Facebook, the social media platforms that have helped Meta become a $2tn company.
For much of the past year, Meta has been embroiled in a series of legal actions, accused of deliberately designing products that are addictive to young users.
That has led to the release of internal emails, corporate documents and whistleblower testimony that personal injury lawyers and prosecutors across the country have wielded to make their case.
And Zuckerberg is unpopular: last year, a Pew Research Center poll found that two-thirds of Americans had an unfavourable opinion of him.
His reputation is unlikely to be helped by The Social Reckoning, a film by Aaron Sorkin released this week. It's about whistleblower claims that Meta executives were aware of their products harming young people. Succession actor Jeremy Strong plays Zuckerberg as a "full-on villain", according to a review in the Hollywood Reporter, "stoically arguing that even the slightest gesture of responsibility is anathema where money is concerned".
Some speculate that this is Meta's "Big Tobacco" moment, with a consensus forming against the company, and the social media industry as a whole.
But the truth seems to be more complicated. Despite months of bad press, in the real world Meta's products are doing better than ever. Use of its apps continues to rise, and users are already flocking to its new AI assistant.
It raises the question: can anything really clip Meta's wings? Or is it now something of a 'Teflon' company, with scandals simply bouncing off it?
Meta's 'trust deficit'
It's certainly been a year of bad headlines for Meta.
Last summer, Reuters revealed that Meta allowed its chatbots to "engage a child in conversations that are romantic or sensual", and provide false medical information to users.
Meta has revised those policies and said that such responses should never have been allowed.
And this year, bills have been mounting. In March, a jury gave $6m (Â£4.5m) to a 20-year-old California woman who claimed she suffered mental health harms related to her use of Meta's Instagram and Google's YouTube.
Around the same time, New Mexico became the first state to succeed in a lawsuit against Meta over child safety issues. A jury found the company had failed to warn the public about the dangers its platforms posed to kids. Meta was fined a total of $942m. The judge called Meta a "public nuisance" akin to air pollution.
Meta says it disagrees with the verdicts and is appealing both cases.
In May, Meta was among the social companies that avoided a trial by settling a case brought by a Kentucky school district that claimed their product design had led to a youth mental health crisis. Meta reportedly agreed to pay $9m, the most of any defendant.
And this summer, Meta struck a high-profile $18bn settlement with 48 US states, plus the District of Columbia and three US territories. Meta denied wrongdoing as part of the settlement, and during the five-day trial it maintained that it had worked extensively over the years to make its platforms safer for young users, pouring resources into testing and research. As part of the deal, the firm promised to enact two-hour daily time limits for young users, along with night-time blocks on use, muted notifications during school hours, and other changes.
The company faces other lawsuits too, including one starting later this month in Los Angeles, also related to alleged social media addiction among young users.
Meanwhile, several countries have moved to ban social media for children entirely, starting with Australia last December. Social media companies are broadly disliked, even while their products remain wildly popular. A Reuters/Ipsos survey suggests that 85% of Americans think social media can be addictive for children, and 61% support greater government oversight.
To some, the trust issue feels existential
"Once the public has stopped trusting you, it's kind of a downward spiral," says associate professor Alison Taylor of New York University's Stern School of Business.
"It feels likeâ¦ the trust deficit is so big, I just don't know that they're going to be able to recover."
'Withstanding the blowback'
But despite those high-profile cases, the company reported that the number of people using some of its apps (like Instagram and WhatsApp) has risen 3% year on year and this year's second quarter revenue was up 28% compared with the same period in 2025.
While it has agreed to temper its pursuit of the teen market (which many brands eagerly cultivate to build their future user base), the company has said that teens accounted for less than 1% of its revenue anyway. Competitors TikTok and Google's YouTube are more popular with young users.

5dbca907d8a5.text: More than half a dozen U.S. House districts in California will send a Democrat to Capitol Hill next year no matter what. Party leadership still has a lot riding on the outcome. Why it matters: Most of these Democrat vs. Democrat runoffs — a quirk of California's election system — are between an establishment candidate and an outsider vowing to make leadership's life hell. Democratic Reps. Mike Thompson, Doris Matsui and Jimmy Gomez are all facing well-funded challenges from younger, less establishment-aligned Democrats. There are also several Northern California races that feature a pro-leadership Democrat facing off against a more left-leaning rival. Sought for comment on this story, Justin Chermol, a spokesperson for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), told Axios: "Stop wasting our time with your irrelevant stories that have nothing to do with taking back control of the House of Representatives." 4th District: Rep. Mike Thompson vs. Eric Jones Thompson , a 75-year-old first elected in 1998, faces a challenge from 35-year-old former venture capitalist Eric Jones. "I don't think anyone in Democratic leadership today is really doing their job well," Jones said in an interview with Axios. Asked if he would vote for Jeffries as speaker, Jones replied: "As of today, I wouldn't vote for any member." Jones is trying to cobble together a populist, anti-establishment coalition consisting of both progressives and Republicans. He said he does not identify as progressive, telling Axios he prefers "no labels." He said that, if elected, he will "have the benefit of independence ... of not taking party money, and I'm not going to vote a party line." 7th District: Rep. Doris Matsui vs. Mai Vang Matsui, 85, is seen as particularly vulnerable after finishing second to Mai Vang in the jungle primary election in June. Vang, a progressive Sacramento City Councilmember in her 40s, has positioned herself alongside a new bloc of Democratic Socialists of America (DSA)-aligned candidates including Darializa Avila Chevalier, Chris Rabb and Melat Kiros. She previously signaled to Axios she won't vote for Jeffries as speaker, saying she "cannot support this kind of leadership" and that "we need new leadership and a new direction." 11th District: Scott Wiener vs. Connie Chan The fight between state Sen. Scott Wiener and San Francisco Supervisor Connie Chan to succeed former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi has been particularly bitter. Chan has positioned herself to the left of Wiener, a longtime progressive who has come under fire from the pro-Palestinian movement for being insufficiently critical of Israel. Wiener told Mission Local he looks "forward to electing Hakeem Jeffries speaker." Chan told the outlet that "any candidate for speaker, including Hakeem Jeffries, will have to earn my vote." 14th District: Rep. Aisha Wahab vs. Melissa Hernandez Wahab , a progressive former state senator, defeated Hernandez, the more moderate former mayor of Dublin, California, in an August special election to replace former Rep. Eric Swalwell . The two are now duking it out for a full term. Wahab has already shown her willingness to buck leadership: She defied Pelosi and Jeffries by running in the special election instead of allowing a "caretaker" to run unopposed, according to The Sunday Times . The Wahab and Hernandez campaigns did not respond to questions about whether their candidates would vote for Jeffries as speaker. 34th District: Rep. Jimmy Gomez vs. Angela Gonzales-Torres Gomez has come under fire after the House Ethics Committee opened an investigation into him in August over allegations of sexual misconduct, which he denies. He has been a longtime target of the left, having survived three consecutive primary challenges from Democrat David Kim since 2020 by 2 to 11 percentage points. This time he faces a challenge from Angela Gonzales-Torres, a progressive local neighborhood councilor backed by many of the same left-wing groups that support Vang and Wahab. Gonzales-Torres , asked in an interview with Axios if she would vote for Jeffries as speaker, said she looks forward to "supporting leaders who are not nearly funded by corporate super PACs." Gonzales-Torres, pointing to her support from DSA, said she considers herself part of the "national slate" of progressive insurgents such as Avila Chevalier, Rabb and Kiros. "Right now [what] we are focusing on is winning this election and hopefully getting to be part of utilizing our bargaining power as this incoming class in Congress," she said. The bottom line: The larger the bloc of Jeffries skeptics that arrives on Capitol Hill in January, the worse a time Democratic leadership will have. That could be tempered to a large degree by the size of Democrats' potential majority, but, as Axios previously reported , many red-seat candidates are also maintaining their independence from leadership. Still, few Democrats think Jeffries will ultimately be denied the speakership. The fights that come after are more uncertain.

A former Ukrainian security services officer linked to a bomb attack in Monaco in June that targeted a multi-millionaire says he believed it was ordered by senior members of HUR, Ukraine's military intelligence agency.
In an exclusive interview with the BBC from prison in Kyiv, facilitated by his lawyer, Vitalii Zhykovych has given his own account of the attempted assassination for the first time.
Ukrainian-born businessman Vadym Yermolayev and his 13-year-old son were badly hurt in the blast and his partner suffered catastrophic injuries. Yermolayev later described their survival as "nothing short of a miracle".
Zhykovych describes himself as a "freelancer" for Ukraine's SBU security service and says Anastasia Berezovska, the woman caught on camera planting the bomb in Monaco, was his "agent".
A week after the bombing, Berezovska's body was discovered in the woods west of Kyiv with gunshot wounds to the head.
But Zhykovych insists he did not send her to kill, and nor did he kill her.
He was arrested and accused of her murder together with an active-duty intelligence officer from HUR called Vladyslav Reut.
Reut initially confessed to investigators, and led them to the shallow grave. But days later in court, he changed his testimony to blame Zhykovych.
For a long time, Zhykovych himself stayed silent.
Now, responding to questions from the BBC, he alleges that Reut - who he refers to as "The Boss" - had "proposed the operation" in Monaco against Vadym Yermolayev.
He understood it was an official mission.
"As Reut informed me, this operation [â¦] had been authorised and approved by Reut's superiors, who served in the Main Intelligence Directorate of the Ministry of Defence [HUR]," he says.
Distancing himself from the explosion itself, he alleges that Reut asked to use Berezovska for the bombing and when Zhykovych refused â he says she was not fully trained â Reut agreed to send her for reconnaissance instead.
Reut then communicated directly with Bereszovska without including him, according to Zhykovych, who alleges that Reut also provided her with the explosives.
The BBC asked HUR to comment on the latest claims. The agency has previously said that is it "committed to a full investigation" and providing "comprehensive support" to law enforcement bodies.
The SBU has described Zhykovych in a statement only as a "former law enforcement officer".
Yermolayev was attacked in Monaco as he and his family were returning from an evening meal on the seafront. A surveillance video shows Berezovska walking slightly in front of the group, then leaving the device in a bag on their doorstep.
It detonates just as they get close, apparently shocking even Berezovska with its force.
Yermolayev later said he believed that serving HUR officers, "individuals close to the agency's current and former leadership", were linked to the attack.
He called for "the truth, protection, and justice".
Berezovska was quickly identified as the suspected bomber and on 2 July her image, taken from CCTV footage, was circulated by Interpol.
She had already fled, first driving through Italy and Germany, then taking a bus from Frankfurt to Ukraine.
Before she could be caught and questioned though, she was driven to the woods by Reut and Zhykovych and killed. Each blames the other for her shooting.
The shocking case has prompted intense speculation, including over who may have wanted Yermolayev dead and why, and whether this could have been a state-ordered assassination attempt, a rogue operation or some kind of criminal score-settling.
The businessman himself, who renounced his Ukrainian passport some years ago and now has Cypriot citizenship, has dismissed multiple theories.
They include the idea the attack might be linked to a struggle between organised crime groups involved in highly lucrative scam call-centres in Ukraine.
Earlier this year, a court in Estonia convicted Yermolayev's son, Artur, of defrauding its citizens out of millions of euros through such "offisy", as the scam networks are known in Ukraine.
Vadym Yermolayev told the Ukrainska Pravda newspaper that he "never had anything to do with anything" in the case.
Now Zhykovych has put forward his own theory to us.
He alleges that Reut told him the bombing was in retaliation for "funding the annexation of Crimea", which he understood to mean Yermolayev was paying taxes to Russia from businesses in Russian-occupied Crimea.
"In my view, this constitutes grounds for the operation," he communicated from prison.
Yermolayev has repeatedly denied any remaining business interests linked to Russia.
But might this story be even murkier?
At his most recent custody hearing in Kyiv, surrounded by heavily armed guards, Zhykovych spoke publicly for the first time since his arrest. The BBC were the only media present.
At one point Zhykovych said Reut had in fact told him the attack in Monaco was not "authorised".
"Someone had ordered this target from the civilian side," Zhykovych said, without explaining.
The judge then interrupted, reminding him that he was addressing an open court.
Zhykovych also revealed that Reut originally talked of two targets.
When we asked, he said he could not disclose the second name. Other sources strongly suggest it was a pro-Russian blogger tried and convicted in absentia last year by Ukraine of treason.
As the investigation continues â into both the bombing in Monaco and the murder in Ukraine - Berezovska's family have many questions of their own.
The 39-year-old had been in Germany since early 2022, when she left Ukraine as a refugee with her young son.
Zhykovych now claims she was living a double-life, working with him as an agent "against Muscovy" â meaning Russia.
He said they had met online and told us the pair were working to "repel the armed aggression of the Russian Federation".
Berezovska's husband has told the BBC that the allegation was "nonsense". He believes she was dragged, unwittingly, into the whole affair.

Some people in the US "still hate the look of solar", Kate Collardson acknowledges.
She would know. Collardson handles operations for the Solar Service of Colorado, a solar maintenance and inspection company. She's also held just about every other job in the industry, from installer to instructor.
For those that hate the look of solar panels, an alternative is a solar roof, where the tiles (or shingles) house solar cells, but look much the same as regular tiles.
This is especially important for historic buildings, where heritage rules limit changes to their appearance.
For many people, the first time they'd heard of this product category was in August, when Tesla's website stopped offering solar roofs, external. This followed disappointing sales and a lawsuit over sudden price hikes, external.
Other companies have also pulled out, but Tesla's decision in particular sent shockwaves through the solar roof industry.
Some see it as a death knell for solar tiles; others, as an opportunity.
For instance, the small Swiss company Freesuns is considering expanding to the US.
Deborah Learoyd, Freesuns' CEO and managing director, estimates that the company's sales have grown 20â30% since it was established in 2019.
In general, solar roof components continue to be manufactured in smaller batches. This limits the economies of scale and standardisation, though flexible manufacturing could help somewhat.
Learoyd says that while the unit costs for Freesuns' products are slowly decreasing, "a lot of the cost is actually the fact that every roof is a little bit different. And so it has to be engineered a little bit differently, installed a little bit differently".
Solar roofs typically require collaboration among roofers, solar installers and electricians. And building regulations tend to be more complex than for solar panels.
The additional time and paperwork can take a toll on a roofing business, Collardson explains. "You try to put a roofer into the equation and they're going, 'This is taking forever. I'm losing money. I could have sold 10 roofing jobs in the time that it takes me to sell this one'."
Collardson has to charge more for repair of solar shingles, compared to a standard photovoltaic (PV) setup.
She explains, "With traditional solar, we generally have electronics on the panel and a map that shows us exactly how much each panel is producing." So when something goes wrong, it's easy to spot where.
"With solar shingles, we don't really have the benefit of that mapping; there's no room underneath the shingle for the electronics." Thermal cameras can identify the trouble spots, however.
But then there's the matter of accessing them. "You can remove the one in the middle of the array, but you have to walk on the others, and you really shouldn't walk on them because you're going to create micro-fractures and that's going to cause issues down the road."
Before repair costs are factored in, a solar roof might cost twice as much as a system of solar panels mounted on a roof.
Solar roofs are also less efficient - one reason is that the tiles are just smaller.
Another factor is the energy lost as heat. Since the tiles sit close to the roof, there's less airflow than with standard solar panels mounted on a roof. Heat impairs solar performance.
Coloured tiles are even less efficient, comments Ben Graves, co-founder of UK solar company Sunsave. "The reason why all solar cells are black, and increasingly the whole panel is now black, is because black is the best absorbing colour."
Overall, much more space would need to be devoted to solar roof tiles to produce the same amount of energy.
Sunsave does not offer solar roofs. "Most people in the UK just don't have enough money to pay for it," Graves believes.
While appearance was a bigger factor five years ago, now "the vast majority of consumers are most interested in how much they can save".
But supporters of solar roofs argue that they should not be pitted against standard solar modules on roofs.
"Let's not compare PV roof tiles to a standard PV system, but look at PV roof tiles as generating additional electricity from our roofs instead of just having the roof sit there," urges Martin Heinrich who leads a research group at the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems in Germany.
While standard solar panels have gone from strength to strength, solar roofs have not advanced to the same extent.
One advancement that could especially help solar roofs is matrix shingling technology.
This is a different way of connecting solar cells. The solar cells are cut into narrow strips, layered like overlapping shingles, and connected to each other using electrically conductive adhesive, rather than metal wires.
This means that the electrical current can flow around shaded areas, unlike with standard modules. "If you get like a bird pooping on a part of the cell, the current can go around it," Learoyd explains.
In addition to increasing energy output, this improves the appearance as the silver wires aren't visible.
Another advantage, Heinrich says, is that "since we cut the cells into smaller areas, we can fill out special sizes more easily. You don't have to adhere to the regular pattern size."
Freesuns is an early adopter of matrix shingling technology in building-integrated PV. "We see it as a big opportunity for the future in terms of how we would make our tiles," Learoyd says.
What would also help the company is better software for automated design. This would speed up the design process, since each roofing job is unique.
Learoyd believes this would lower costs and give "the whole construction industry much more confidence in using the product".
Ten years after her own solar roof was installed, and despite the sector's setbacks, Learoyd remains optimistic.
She believes that for people with the means, it will eventually become standard to install a new roof with some sort of embedded solar. "It's just a no-brainer."

Widespread snow driven by a polar vortex is rumoured to be heading for the UK this autumn and winter. But is that really the case?
Headlines have been suggesting it is down to the effects of El NiÃ±o but the truth is much more complicated.
For the rest of the autumn, El NiÃ±o actually increases the chance of wet, mild and potentially stormy weather for the UK.
Later in winter it could shift the odds towards cold and snow, something that can be influenced by changes in the polar vortex but none of this is certain.
What is a polar vortex?
The polar vortex is a ring of strong westerly winds encircling the North Pole every winter, around 10-30 miles (16-48km) above the Earth's surface.
It forms because the air high above the Pole becomes extremely cold and dense in winter. The contrast with warmer air further south drives the very strong stratospheric winds that make up the polar vortex.
This is all going on high up in the stratosphere, far above the troposphere - where our weather actually happens.
A strong polar vortex tends to encourage a strong polar jet stream in the troposphere.
This drives areas of low pressure from west to east, bringing mild air from the Atlantic across the UK with spells of wind and rain. The coldest air is essentially locked away to the north of us.
Sometimes, however, the polar vortex can wobble, weaken or even reverse direction.
Over a period of days and weeks this can work its way down through the atmosphere influencing our jet stream, causing it to weaken, become more bendy or reverse.
It can deliver colder northerly or easterly winds which can bring the UK its coldest winter weather
However, it does not always translate into changes in weather patterns at the Earth's surface.
Equally, periods of a meandering jet stream and cold winter weather often occur without significant changes in the polar vortex.
What does El NiÃ±o have to do with it?
El NiÃ±o - the naturally-occurring climate phenomenon in the Pacific Ocean - is continuing to grow and by some measures is already the strongest on record.
The heat released from the warm Pacific Ocean into the atmosphere impacts weather patterns around the globe.
In autumn it increases the chance of wet and stormy weather in the UK - something that is reflected in the forecasts for this season.
In late winter, the waves of energy released by El NiÃ±o can move upwards through the atmosphere making it more likely that the polar vortex becomes disrupted, increasing the chance of ice and snow.
However, the links are unclear and the evidence is mixed.
The so-called Big Freeze of 2009/2010 was, at the time, the coldest winter in three decades - and coincided with an El NiÃ±o.
However, 2006/2007 was also an El NiÃ±o winter and was unseasonably warm.
The so-called Beast from the East in 2018 actually occurred during a La NiÃ±a year, effectively the opposite of El NiÃ±o.
So while El NiÃ±o is already having big impacts on global weather, and may influence the polar vortex later in winter, snow and ice in the UK is far from guaranteed.
Current forecasts suggest no significant cold or snow is likely in the near future.

40596e3286f7.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/how-moscows-secrecy-about-a-suspected-plague-case-follows-a-soviet-era-pattern Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter How Moscow's secrecy about a suspected plague case follows a Soviet-era pattern World Oct 8, 2026 6:56 PM EDT The Kremlin has long maintained a culture of secrecy when it comes to controlling public information, especially involving accidents — from industrial disasters to health emergencies. The suspicious death last week of a worker at a research lab in Siberia that has fueled global concerns about suspected pneumonic plague is just the latest example of how leaders in Moscow manage the official narrative that often covers up the truth for years. READ MORE: Russia's public health watchdog denies a second infection in suspected pneumonic plague case Russia's public health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, has told the World Health Organization that no case of plague has been registered in the Irkutsk region of southeastern Siberia. In tersely worded statements, the Russian agency said the lab worker contracted pneumonia of "unknown" origin and that tests found no evidence her illness was caused by any of the pathogens she worked with at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East. The WHO urged Russia to share more information to clarify the cause of the severe pneumonia, the pathogen that prompted the public health measures and media reports that a second employee had pneumonia of undetermined cause. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Scarce official information about the worker's death, which unconfirmed reports in Russia blamed on pneumonic plague, follows the Soviet-era patterns of secrecy in dealing with outbreaks of infectious diseases, accidents and other emergencies. Here are other examples of Moscow censoring public health information: The 1959-60 smallpox outbreak In the final days of December 1959, leading Soviet graphic artist Alexei Kokorekin fell ill and died shortly after returning from a trip to India. Doctors initially struggled to identify the cause of death as smallpox, which was considered eradicated decades earlier. Once it became clear, authorities launched a massive effort to contain the outbreak. The KGB meticulously tracked down Kokorekin's contacts, and thousands of people were put in isolation. An Aeroflot flight carrying one of his contacts was contacted before it landed in Paris and ordered to return to Moscow. Authorities halted all travel to and from Moscow and launched an unprecedented effort in which thousands of vaccination teams distributed shots to millions of residents of the capital and the surrounding region. International news outlets reported the massive campaign, but Soviet state media kept silent about it. The outbreak led to 46 confirmed cases and three deaths in Moscow before it was contained in 44 days. A novel and movie based on the outbreak appeared later, but the true details of what happened were hidden from the public until the waning years of the Soviet Union. The 1971 Aral Sea smallpox outbreak During tests of a smallpox bioweapon on a tightly guarded range on Vozrozhdeniya Island in the Aral Sea in August 1971, a research ship accidentally sailed too close to the aerosolized plume of microbes. A marine biologist on the ship contracted smallpox and spread it to several others in the town of Aralsk in what is now part of Kazakhstan, resulting in 10 infections and three deaths. The town was quarantined and more than 40,000 people were vaccinated against smallpox within days, but the public remained unaware of what happened. The incident only became widely known in 2002 when U.S. researchers publicized old Soviet archives. The 1979 anthrax leak On April 2, 1979, anthrax spores were accidentally released from a secret biological weapons lab in Sverdlovsk, the Ural Mountains city that is now called Yekaterinburg. The accident was caused by a worker failing to replace a faulty ventilation filter, resulting in the release of the deadly spores into the air. At least 68 people died in the resulting anthrax outbreak. Soviet authorities officially blamed the deaths on contaminated meat from a street market and the KGB made sure to keep details of the accident under wraps, confiscating medical records. It wasn't until after the 1991 collapse of the Soviet Union that the truth about the outbreak became known under Russian President Boris Yeltsin, a former Communist Party boss in Sverdlovsk. The 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster When the reactor No. 4 exploded at the Chernobyl nuclear power plant in the then-Soviet republic of Ukraine on April 26, 1986, it spewed a radioactive cloud across Europe. Authorities were slow to report the incident and warn the public about the radioactive threat. When Sweden detected the radiation, Moscow initially denied that any accident had occurred. Soviet officials waited for 36 hours before ordering the evacuation of the town of Pripyat near the plant. Five days later, tens of thousands of people were exposed to radioactive fallout as they marched through the streets of Kyiv during the May Day parade. Despite Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev's policy of "glasnost," or greater openness, authorities heavily censored medical data and casualty figures as part of their efforts to conceal the true scale of the disaster. Immediately after the accident, 30 plant workers and firefighters died from acute radiation sickness, and thousands of people later died from radiation-related illnesses. c7ec5583e0fd.text: Millions along the Gulf Coast are on high alert as Hurricane Isaias gains power and moves closer to land. Isaias is now a Category 2 storm, the first hurricane in the Atlantic basin this year. Forecasters are warning of heavy rain, damaging winds, flooding, storm surge and the possibility of tornadoes. Amna Nawaz discussed the latest with National Hurricane Center Director Michael Brennan. Amna Nawaz: Millions of Americans along the Gulf Coast are on high alert due to life-threatening conditions as Hurricane Isaias gains power and moves closer to land. Isaias rapidly intensified overnight from a tropical storm to what is now a Category 2 hurricane, making it the first one in the Atlantic this year. Residents are securing their homes and gathering supplies. Local and state officials are issuing evacuation orders. And forecasters are warning of heavy rain, damaging winds, flooding, storm surges, and the possibility of tornadoes. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said his state will be ready. Gov. Ron DeSantis (R-FL): And I will just say we have got everyone mobilized, the full monty for the storm. We're taking it very seriously. I hope it weakens. I think there's conditions where it could. But our assumption is that it's going to hit strong as a probably lower-end category 3. Amna Nawaz: Joining us now is Michael Brennan. He's director of the National Hurricane Center. So, Michael, knowing the path could still change here, let's just start with the latest you know on the potential path of this hurricane and when it could make landfall. Michael Brennan, Director, National Hurricane Center: Well, the storm has strengthened over the last several hours, now a Category 2 hurricane on the Saffir-Simpson scale. It's going to continue to move off to the northeast over the next several hours overnight and then turn more towards the north. Right now, we're thinking that the center is going to make landfall somewhere in the Alabama or Florida Panhandle coastline, but where the exact center crosses land is not as important as the impacts. You're going to see impacts all along the Northern Gulf Coast from this system. Amna Nawaz: You mentioned how rapidly it intensified. It's already a Category 2. Is there any way to tell just how powerful this storm could be when it makes landfall? Could it possibly reach Category 3 or more? Michael Brennan: Over water, yes. There's a small window of opportunity for it to continue to intensify tonight, potentially taking it close to Category 3 strength overnight. But we think weakening will commence later tonight or tomorrow as it approaches the coastline. So we're really looking at maybe a Category 1 or 2 as it makes its approach, final approach, to landfall. But, regardless, a lot of people get really hung up on the intensity and the categories. I think the hazards are largely baked at this point, meaning that, no matter what intensity the storm comes ashore as, the hazards are largely going to be unchanged, We're going to see a lot of storm surge, rainfall, flooding, and potential for strong, impactful winds moving inland over some of these Southern Tier states with long-duration power outages. Amna Nawaz: We know those residents are being urged to prepare. What kind of preparations should they be making? How far inland should they be preparing, and when and how do people make that decision to evacuate? Michael Brennan: So, first and foremost, I'm glad you mentioned the evacuations. There are a number of mandatory or recommended evacuations along the Northern Gulf Coast here, especially coastal Alabama, portions of Mississippi and even Florida Panhandle. If you've been ordered to evacuate, you need to go ahead and do that right away. Don't assume that you'll have the entirety of tomorrow to make necessary preparations or evacuate. You can see in the satellite imagery here the conditions are already spreading well out in front of this storm, so we're not going to have all day tomorrow to prepare or evacuate if ordered to do so. Amna Nawaz: That is Michael Brennan, director of the National Hurricane Center, joining us tonight. Michael, thank you for your time. Michael Brennan: Thank you.

The challenge is acute in places like Texas, where Trump traveled on Wednesday for the second time in a week to stump for Republican Ken Paxton's Senate campaign. The state hasn't elected a Democratic senator since 1988, yet MAGA Inc. has spent more than $22 million in the past month, according to the ad tracking firm AdImpact. WATCH: Trump speaks at rally for Senate candidate Ken Paxton in San Antonio Another group, Texas PAC, which is aligned with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, has spent more than $83 million on advertising in the past month, an extraordinary amount to protect what's normally a safe Republican seat. One of those advertisements, which featured Paxton's estranged wife saying she's supporting the full Republican ticket, aired across the United States last weekend during a football game between the Dallas Cowboys and the Houston Texans. Candidates are charged a lower advertising rate than outside groups, so the late infusion of super PAC cash has come at a steep price. MAGA Inc., which is running ads primarily on streaming services, has been charged roughly $894 per airing, according to AdImpact, while Texas PAC has been charged roughly $809 for a mix of broadcast and streaming. That compares with about $290 for Democratic nominee James Talarico's campaign, also on broadcast and streaming. Those averages mask some of the more glaring disparities. For example, during a football game last month, Texas PAC was charged $450,000 to air a single spot in the Austin market. Talarico's campaign paid $50,000 for a spot during the same game in the same market, according to AdImpact. Elections are a referendum on the power of money The 2026 campaign is shaping up as a referendum on the power of money in American politics. Democrats freely acknowledge their disadvantage, relying instead on anti-Trump sentiment among voters and targeted messaging on issues like corruption. Some Republicans, meanwhile, are open about the challenge of trying to spend their way out of a tough campaign at this late stage. Neil Newhouse, a longtime Republican pollster, echoed concerns that his party was deploying its cash too late. "After the votes are counted, I think we're going to find the most effective advertising in terms of communicating message and moving voters and poll numbers, the most effective time was advertising that happened well before Labor Day, not after it," he said. "A million dollars of advertising in October is a drop in the bucket." Thune's group began pulling back in North Carolina last week, a sign of the party's challenge in the Senate race there. The state's outgoing Sen. Thom Tillis has been increasingly vocal about his party's vulnerabilities and recently said that, even with a strong cash advantage, "in the last month, you pretty much have to place your bets." "If we have endless resources, then we should spend endlessly in every state," he said. "Absent endless resources, you've got to make data-driven decisions about where you can win." The midterms mark the first national election since the Supreme Court in June erased limits on how much political parties can spend in coordination with candidates for Congress and president, injecting even more money into a political system already awash in cash. Money alone doesn't translate into victory There's plenty of evidence that money alone doesn't translate into victory. Democrat Kamala Harris entered the final stretch of the 2024 campaign with significantly more money than Trump but went on to lose every critical swing state and the White House. ba3a2e6b4197.text: Christa Pike, the Tennessee woman who survived a botched execution, has reportedly taken a few steps in her hospital room six days after she received two lethal injections. Justice correspondent Ali Rogin discussed questions surrounding the state of capital punishment with Austin Sarat, author of "Lethal Injection and the False Promise of Humane Execution." Amna Nawaz: Christa Pike, the Tennessee woman who survived a botched execution, has reportedly taken a few steps in her hospital room six days after she received two lethal injections. Pike was convicted of the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer, and it's now unclear how that case will proceed. Justice correspondent Ali Rogin has more on the questions surrounding the state of capital punishment. Ali Rogin: In response to the failed execution attempt, the governor has paused all pending executions through the end of the year, and a judge has ordered Tennessee to preserve evidence of what went wrong. To discuss, we're now joined by Austin Sarat, author of the book "Lethal Injection and the False Promise of Humane Execution." Austin Sarat, thank you so much for joining us. You have been covering executions and failed executions for a long time. How unique, if at all, is what happened to Christa Pike and how often do executions either fail or get botched like this? Austin Sarat, Author, "Lethal Injection and the False Promise of Humane Execution": What happened to Christa Pike was shocking but not surprising. To anyone that's followed the American death penalty, we know that executions are frequently botched, and the method of execution which is least reliable, most frequently botched, lethal injection. But I don't think anyone was prepared for an execution in which the lethal drugs actually reach the condemned person, and that person lives to tell about it. So it's really an unprecedented event in the recent history of capital punishment. Ali Rogin: It certainly also seems unprecedented in terms of what policymakers do now. What options are the leaders in Tennessee who would make these decisions thinking through right now in terms of, do they try again? How does Christa Pike's legal status change? Austin Sarat: Well, the first thing that they are doing, as Governor Lee has announced, is, they're going to do an investigation to try to find out what actually went wrong in the execution chamber. Next, the governor will have to make a decision about whether or not that this governor wants to commute Christa Pike's sentence. If the governor doesn't do that, and the state decides to go forward with a second execution attempt, we will be entering somewhat uncharted territory. A second execution is very rare in the United States. It happened in 1947 in the state of Louisiana. It's happened a couple of times in Alabama more recently. And the arguments will be made, and I think they're persuasive arguments, that to subject Christa Pike to a second execution attempt would be a cruel punishment, in violation of the Eighth Amendment, and would be a form of double jeopardy prohibited by the Constitution of the United States. Ali Rogin: In your research, you have found that lethal injection fails more often than any other method in American history, including hanging and the electric chair. Why is that? Austin Sarat: Well, no method of execution is foolproof. Every method of execution that we have used in the United States, whether it's hanging, the electric chair, the gas chamber, now lethal injection, has run into problems. Lethal injection runs into more problems because, paradoxically, it's a very complicated way to try to put someone to death. You have to find a usable vein. You have to secure an I.V. You have to make sure that the drugs that you are using are up to date and potent. So it's not surprising that a complicated procedure like lethal injection would run into problems of the kind that it has. And, of course, the problems of lethal injection have not been helped by the desire of states, including the state of Tennessee, to keep what happens in the execution chamber as secret as possible, so that the problems of lethal injection, when they occur, often don't make the headlines that Christa Pike's execution attempt made. Ali Rogin: And certainly this execution attempt has made a lot of headlines, but you have opined that it's not likely to change the dial in terms of public perception around the death penalty. Where is public sentiment today and why don't you think something like this might shift it? Austin Sarat: I think the United States is in a period of national reconsideration of capital punishment. Support for the death penalty is down from what it was three decades ago, and even people who support capital punishment tend not to support it as intensely as they once did. The number of death sentences in this country is way down from what it was three decades ago. And if we look at the states that have the death penalty, many of them that have it on the books don't use it in practice. They don't execute anyone. Ali Rogin: Austin Sarat, expert on the death penalty and capital punishment, thank you so much for joining us. Austin Sarat: My pleasure. Thanks for having me.

97745f8091d4.text: Israel is barreling toward elections in less than three weeks, which could extend Benjamin Netanyahu's already-record tenure as its leader. The Trump administration has worked in near lockstep with Netanyahu since the president’s return to office. Amna Nawaz discussed what Israeli voters are considering with Dan Shapiro, the U.S. ambassador to Israel during the Obama administration. Amna Nawaz: Israel yesterday observed the solemn and terrible anniversary of the October 7 attacks. The nation is now barreling toward elections in less than three weeks, which could extend Benjamin Netanyahu's already record tenure as Israel's leader. The Trump administration has worked in near lockstep with Netanyahu since the president's return to office. But an exclusive in today's New York Times reports that a top official in the U.S. Embassy is often rewriting cables that alter the picture on the ground in Israel, Gaza, and the West Bank. To explore that and the wider picture in Israel, I'm joined now by Ambassador Dan Shapiro, who served as an American envoy to Israel during the Obama administration. Ambassador, welcome back to the "News Hour." Thanks for joining us. Daniel Shapiro, Former U.S. Ambassador to Israel: Thanks for having me on. Amna Nawaz: So I want to start with that New York Times exclusive in which they said they talked to 15 U.S. officials, reviewed dozens of cables and documents and internal communications. And the characterization there is that this top aide was altering information making its way back to Washington in a positive light, in other words, not reflecting accurately some of the things that were making their way up in memos and getting that to D.C. What's your reaction to that reporting? Daniel Shapiro: Well, I don't know the details of this particular case. What I can tell you is that my experience as an ambassador and with an embassy staff is that what Washington policymakers need is clear and unvarnished reporting about what's happening in the country you're serving in. That means that, in a case like Israel, Israel is a security partner and there are aspects of the things that happen in Israel that certainly serve U.S. interests. Certainly, with the case of the current government, which includes very extreme members of the Israeli political system, advocates for mass settlement expansion in the West Bank, people who are looking away from a wave of violence by extremist Jewish settlers against Palestinian civilians, that should also be part of the reporting. So, that's, I think, what an embassy's obligation is, an ambassador's obligation is and those who work for the ambassador. Amna Nawaz: One of the pieces of information The New York Times cites specifically is a memo that staff members in the embassy drafted about Israel expanding some of its West Bank settlements very quietly. They say, according to sources, that memo never made it to Washington. And I should share with you what the ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, said in response to their reporting. He called it a hit piece. He said: "I personally and categorically refute the elements of this proposed story," as he put it. I have to put to you, since you have served in the role. Some will say, isn't it the ambassador's job to gatekeep that information, to edit cables before they go back to D.C.? Do you have any concerns about this reporting? Daniel Shapiro: A good embassy and ambassador gives clear and unvarnished reporting, but there's always judgment calls. And, in the end, the embassy's reporting should reflect what the ambassador believes and the views that he wants to share with the Washington policymakers. Amna Nawaz: As we noted, we're now speaking the day after Israel marked three years since those Hamas terrorist attacks, and we know the shadow of those attacks has loomed large over these upcoming elections. You're there on the ground. We know Netanyahu's faced a lot of questions about what he knew before the attacks. How big a role are those attacks playing in this election? Daniel Shapiro: Yes, I have been here just about 24 hours, and it's very clear that this is the central issue in the closing phase of this election. Who bears responsibility for the October 7 attacks? The opposition candidates led by Gadi Eisenkot as part of a coalition of parties are saying that Netanyahu was asleep at the wheel, had policies that underestimated what Hamas' intentions and capabilities were in Gaza, didn't respond in real time, nor were they prepared before the case for that -- attacks. And they are making that case to try to cement the case against Netanyahu continuing in office. Netanyahu, for his part, and his allies are saying, no, it was the fault of security and intelligence chiefs, generals in the military. They were the ones who were asleep at the switch. They did not share information with him. They didn't wake him on the morning of the attack in time to make key decisions. And he is trying to rally his traditional supporters to say he's still the person that can be trusted to deal with the various security threats that Israel still faces. It looks like it's a very close election, and it may be that neither side will really be able to form a coalition government coming out of it, in which case it's entirely possible that Netanyahu will remain in office as a caretaker while another election is run a few months from now. Amna Nawaz: We have seen Netanyahu say that he has no greater partner than U.S. President Trump, but we did see President Trump sort of sidestep a question recently about endorsing Netanyahu. What have you noticed about relations between the two? Have they taken a hit recently? Daniel Shapiro: They certainly have cooled. There was certainly a period earlier this year when it was fully expected, and I know Netanyahu was expecting it, that President Trump would give him a fulsome endorsement. But this election cycle, 12 pastors, seminarians and former clergy ran as Democrats, with about half securing nominations. Lisa Desjardins discussed more with NPR religion correspondent Jason Derose, who recently spent time on the campaign trail with several of these candidates. Amna Nawaz: Well, with just a few weeks to go until Election Day, Democrats are hoping to flip some seats in deep red states. And some are doing that by talking about religion. Our Lisa Desjardins has more. Lisa Desjardins: Fusing faith in politics is almost a no-brainer for many Republicans hoping to hold public office. But this election cycle, 12 pastors, seminarians, and former clergy ran as Democrats, with about half managing to secure their nominations. Coming from the pulpit to the political stage, these candidates have used their experience as religious leaders to talk about their call to run. James Talarico (D), Texas Senatorial Candidate: I want to speak to you this morning, not as a candidate, but as a fellow Christian. Frederick Haynes III (D), Texas Congressional candidate: But this Republican Party has demolished and torn down. It's time for us to reconstruct this nation and make it truly one nation under God, indivisible, with liberty and justice for all. Adam Hamilton (D), Kansas Senatorial Candidate: Jesus himself, there were times he turned over the money changers' tables in the temple, and he still taught us to love our neighbor and even love our enemy. Lisa Desjardins: For more, we are joined by NPR's religion correspondent, Jason DeRose, who recently spent time on the campaign trail with several of these candidates. Thank you for joining us, Jason. Jason DeRose, NPR Religion Correspondent: Happy to be here. Lisa Desjardins: This is a small, but noteworthy group. On the ballot in November, there will be five Democrats in congressional races who are clergy or in training to be clergy. Of those candidates, four of them are in competitive races that could determine the fate of the House or the Senate. Now, we have seen Republican clergy run before. We have seen that this year also, but what's new here is this Democratic cohort. Why do you think this is emerging now? Jason DeRose: Well, for many years, as you said, Republicans really had the market cornered on this. And I think that Democrats finally figured out a way to have clergy, the people best trained and most trained and most used to talking about their faith and how it -- how they use it in public life. And these people emerged through state legislatures. Three of these candidates serve in state legislatures right now. So they realized, this is our moment, I think. I don't think there was a big campaign to get them to run, say, from the Democratic Party. It was much more -- these were people serving their neighbors in state legislatures who said it's now time for a larger stage. Lisa Desjardins: There is news regarding one of these candidates. That's Adam Hamilton in Kansas. The Cook Political Report rated that Senate race in Kansas a toss-up, which is rather incredible for a state that has not voted for a Democrat for Senate in decades. What can you tell us about that race? What does it tell you about what's happening? Jason DeRose: Well, what's interesting to me there is that, when I first started this reporting, it was a pretty solidly Republican race, and this has moved very quickly from solidly red to leans red and now to toss-up, a very big deal. Hamilton is the pastor of a very large, one might call it a megachurch, a Methodist megachurch. He's written many, many books. But he was actually a Republican for many years who, in fact, thought of running as an independent, but decided to run as a Democrat. And it seems to be working out for him, becoming a toss-up. Lisa Desjardins: How do these candidates thread this needle -- we have separation of church and state here -- between talking into a secular crowd and then also speaking of their faith to a religious one? Jason DeRose: Well, it's a really difficult needle to thread for clergy because they're so used to talking about their faith. But, again, these people, some of them have spent time in legislatures talking about their -- how their faith influences their politics, but not how it dictates their politics. And I think that, for James Talarico in particular, he came to prominence talking out against Christian nationalism while being a seminarian, while being a politician. So he's figured out how to do it as well. I think part of what he says and part of what Sarah Trone Garriott in Iowa and Lindsay James in Iowa also do is, they say that their faith influences their politics, it doesn't dictate their politics, and they don't dictate other people's faith. Hall, Associated Press By — Kim Chandler, Associated Press Kim Chandler, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/christa-pikes-attorneys-say-she-is-walking-with-help-and-eating-after-failed-execution-attempt Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Christa Pike's attorneys say she is walking with help and eating after failed execution attempt Nation Oct 8, 2026 8:35 PM EDT NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Christa Pike has begun walking and eating again at a hospital a week after surviving Tennessee's attempt to execute her with lethal drugs, her attorneys said Thursday. Pike, 50, survived two doses of pentobarbital as the state sought to giver her a lethal injection eight days ago for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. The drug didn't kill her, and her arms were left burned and blistered, according to her lawyers. For the first few days of her hospitalization, Pike was unconscious and on a ventilator. WATCH: Botched execution reignites debate surrounding death penalty Her first steps on Wednesday were "limited" and she required some assistance as she walked on Thursday, her lawyers said in a statement. She is also regaining mobility in her arms, and she was able to eat for the first time. But the lawyers warned uncertainty remains about her physical recovery and her legal standing after the attempt to carry out her death sentence. Questions remain about Pike's recovery and legal case The failed execution on Sept. 30 has renewed scrutiny of how states carry out the death penalty. Texas on Wednesday carried out the first execution in the U.S. since the Tennessee attempt. "While her physical recovery has been remarkable, significant questions remain about the long-term effects of what she endured," her attorneys said in Thursday's statement. "Christa is dealing with the profound psychological trauma of having survived a failed execution, including the terror, pain and uncertainty of believing she was about to die." Pike regained consciousness Tuesday and was able to speak after awakening, they said. They initially described her as "confused" soon after regaining consciousness, and said Thursday that she continued to struggle with concentration and memory. Doctors say it is too early to assess the long-term impacts, the attorneys added. It also remains unclear whether Tennessee will try to execute her again. Her attorneys have said that they will urge Republican Gov. Bill Lee to commute her death sentence to life in prison without parole. "She should never be subjected to another execution attempt," they said in the statement. What went wrong with the execution remains unclear Lee has since postponed the state's only other scheduled execution this year and ordered a review of why the execution failed. The state's prison chief resigned after the execution attempt. Medical and lethal injection experts have focused on whether a problem with the IV line caused the drug to pool in her tissue instead of entering her bloodstream. READ MORE: The latest on Christa Pike's case and Tennessee's previously botched executions Pike's attorneys wrote in a court filing that "apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed." State officials have offered no explanation of what occurred. As the process got underway Pike was asked if she had a final statement and she spoke of being at peace. About five minutes later, she raised her head and said her arm hurt. Later, she appeared to lose consciousness but could be heard breathing heavily until media witnesses were escorted from the witness room nearly 90 minutes into the execution. An ambulance took her to a hospital. Chandler reported from Montgomery, Alabama. Associated Press writer Safiyah Riddle in Los Angeles contributed. Few details were immediately available about the shooting, which happened around 4 p.m. The person who was shot was conscious and being treated at a hospital, the New York Police Department said in a post on X, noting that its officers didn't witness the shooting and weren't involved. READ MORE: New ICE guidance bans high-speed car chases and sets tighter rules for traffic stops, memo shows Messages seeking further information were sent to federal authorities. An FBI spokesperson said an evidence response team was responding to the scene "to support our partners at the Department of Homeland Security," but offered no other details. The shooting happened in the Marble Hill neighborhood, a small part of Manhattan attached to the Bronx. Pedro Almaraz, an employee at a nearby restaurant, said he heard about three or four gunshots and saw a man on the ground surrounded by several officers wearing face masks and vests with Department of Homeland Security branding. Witnesses, he said, were screaming. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, a Democrat, said in a post on social media that she had been briefed on the shooting. "We expect federal authorities to provide a full and transparent accounting of the circumstances surrounding this incident. New Yorkers deserve to know exactly what happened and why," she said. Videos and photos posted by bystanders on social media showed a man sitting on the ground with his hands behind his back, in the immediate aftermath of the shooting. Another video shows New York City police officers picking up an apparently injured man and carrying him into a police vehicle. Nearby, a damaged car sat blocking the roadway with small holes in two of its windows. The videos show agents wearing Immigration and Customs Enforcement badges on the scene, including one carrying a rifle. "This is an unconscionable and incredibly serious situation," Mayor Zohran Mamdani said on X. "I have called the President; when we speak I will demand that he ends all ICE enforcement actions in our city. I will not stand by while ICE agents terrorize our communities." A new report paints a dark picture of the state of global wildlife—but also highlights flickers of light where some populations are on the upswing.
Over the past half-century, populations of thousands of vertebrate species across the globe have decreased in size by 73 percent on average, according to the “Living Planet” report published Wednesday by the nonprofits World Wildlife Fund and the Zoological Society of London. A number of factors contributed to this precipitous decline, including habitat loss, overexploitation and climate change.
However, a closer look at certain regions and biomes offers reasons for hope, the report’s authors say. Roughly half the populations they studied are stable or even increasing. Though these gains are outweighed by the greater magnitude of losses elsewhere, they show that concerted conservation efforts have made a difference for species such as green sea turtles and bluefin tuna, according to lead author Rebecca Shaw, the chief scientist at the World Wildlife Fund.
“The report focuses on hope because even though the headline statistic is really, really stark … what we see underlying the statistic is some real movement in some species,” Shaw said.
Despite these successes, the report stressed the importance of tackling biodiversity loss at a global scale by changing the three major systems driving extinction: food, energy and finance.
Species Losses By the Numbers
The “Living Planet” reports are released roughly every two years. The latest taps into data from tens of thousands of populations of 5,790 vertebrate species across the animal kingdom—from Laysan albatross to ring-tailed lemurs.
Rather than tallying the total number of animals lost or gained, the researchers measured changes in relative abundance of populations. That means a small population of monkeys that has dropped from 200 to 100 would have experienced the same 50 percent loss as a large colony of 20,000 bats that has dipped to 10,000.
This method allows researchers to compare data from different populations and better track overall trends, said Louise McRae, a research fellow at the Zoological Society of London who works on the Living Planet Index that informs the report.
“The reason we do that is so that we can get a good picture of what is happening across different species by giving them equal weight within this index,” she said. “We’re getting a better signal of the health of the environment.”
So while the new report does not mean there are 73 percent fewer wild vertebrate animals in total today than in 1970, it does show populations the report monitored are plummeting on average. However, diving deeper into the numbers reveals the varied stories playing out for wildlife around the world.
By geography, monitored species populations have faced the most significant decline in Latin America and the Caribbean, with an average 95 percent decrease from 1970 to 2022. In that same timeframe, North America and the combined regions of Europe and Central Asia have seen around 25 percent declines, though the authors pointed out that development in those areas had already had large-scale impacts on nature prior to 1970. Declines in Africa and the Asia and the Pacific region were 80 percent and 49 percent, respectively.
The researchers also broke the numbers down by biome. Freshwater species were the clear losers, seeing an overall decline of 85 percent—significantly more than terrestrial or marine species, though these vertebrates are also seeing major losses.
The report attributed the nosedive in freshwater species to a number of factors, including pollution, overharvesting and habitat loss caused by infrastructure such as hydropower dams. Impacted species included in the report range from migratory fish such as Chinook salmon in the Western United States to the Amazon pink river dolphin in Brazil, which plummeted by 65 percent between 1994 and 2016 alone in the Mamirauá Sustainable Development Reserve in the state of Amazonas.

For terrestrial species, habitat loss and degradation drove much of the biodiversity decline, while marine life faced major threats from overfishing.
Viorel Popescu, an associate research scientist at Columbia University who wasn’t involved in the report, said it’s valuable to bring these “huge amounts of data” that are largely invisible to most of the public “to the forefront.” But he added that the report may be an underestimate of total biodiversity losses, given that it only focuses on vertebrate species the authors analyzed. Other scientists have echoed this critique.
Popescu pointed to the collapse of many populations of insects, which make up roughly three-quarters of all known animal species on Earth. In fact, beetles alone account for 25 percent of all animal species.
“Those declines could be even more drastic,” Popescu said.
Good News and Bad News
The report also pointed to bright spots around the world. For example, in 2025, the green sea turtle became the first marine turtle to be downlisted by the nonprofit International Union for Conservation of Nature, which means populations increased enough around the world for the animal to no longer be considered endangered.
But this recovery didn’t happen overnight. According to the report, a roughly five-decade coordinated conservation effort launched across more than 80 countries helped populations rebuild through protecting nesting females and eggs, beach management, lighting regulations, turtle excluder devices and other bycatch reduction measures to help reduce sea turtle entanglements in fishing gear.

(AP) — After more than 10 months at sea, thousands of sailors Thursday poured out of the the USS Lincoln on San Diego Bay to thunderous cheers, streaming tears and emotional hugs, marking a homecoming that included new dads who met babies born while they were away on a historic deployment supporting the Iran war. WATCH: Hegseth welcomes return of USS Lincoln after long, troubled deployment The reunion followed an emotional rollercoaster for families who described crying and losing sleep after hearing reports of supply shortages and deteriorating mental health among the crew during the deployment that spent a record 265 days of uninterrupted time at sea. Many said they only could communicate with family via the occasional email or rare WhatsApp calls. Abel Ramirez, 20, was glad to have that all behind him. He walked off the carrier with a big grin, overjoyed that his first deployment was over. "It feels amazing," he said while headed out to search for his parents who traveled from Texas. "There was a certain point when I never thought I would come off." Cassity Garduque, 14, waved as her mom in her sailor uniform frantically waved back from the top deck after the ship docked at the pier. "It feels really overwhelming," she said about being seeing her mom again. "She missed most of my seventh grade and my birthday." She added that she's happy her mom won't be eating ramen almost every day and can celebrate with her now. Capt. Daniel Keeler, the ship's commander, said most of the crew was on their first deployment and that the issues they faced were normal for such a long deployment, adding everyone had access to four meals a day. "It's a floating city as you can see and at any moment there might be a clogged toilet," he said. The Navy has downplayed problems on the carrier The Navy initially downplayed any problems during the deployment, and President Donald Trump commented in August that the Lincoln's lengthy deployment was "not nearly long enough." WATCH: Trump says USS Lincoln's deployment was 'not nearly long enough' Navy leaders eventually acknowledged there were some issues aboard. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth flew out to the Lincoln on Wednesday to give the crew the Presidential Unit Citation, the highest honor a unit can receive. Hegseth told the crew that "what makes the U.S. military and the U.S. Navy and all these sailors different is that you adapt and that you're resilient and you overcome — you finish the mission nonetheless." Hegseth pushed back against what he said were efforts to turn the "Lincoln into some sort of a symbol, a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission." USS Lincoln crew looks forward to family and favorite meals The Lincoln, which set a record for uninterrupted time at sea, is the second carrier to endure an unusually long deployment during the Iran war and to receive the Presidential Unit Citation afterward, typically reserved for significant achievement in combat. The crew of the USS Gerald R. Ford returned in May from a 326-day deployment — the longest for an aircraft carrier in the past 50 years and a record in the post-Vietnam War era. The Lincoln's deployment of 322 days was just shy of that. Among the first to depart the carrier at the naval base in Coronado were 64 fathers meeting their babies for the first time, the Navy said. With the airwing included, there were 122 new dads, Keeler said. Waiting for the Lincoln to bring her husband home, sailor Kathy Monterrosa held her 6-month-old daughter, Sarahi, outfitted in a tiny blue and white sailor dress. "She's our deployment baby," said Monterrosa, of Virginia Beach, Virginia. It was tough to hear about the ship's conditions while she was pregnant, she said. "I was crying a lot and worried. I wasn't sure if he was OK or not," she said. When she finally heard from her husband, he told her it was "pretty bad," but now she said she feels blessed to have her family home. Sailor Steven Rivas beamed as he held is 7-month-old daughter. "I couldn't grasp the reality of it," he said about coming home. He became overwhelmed as they pulled into the bay, "seeing everyone and knowing my family was waiting for me," Rivas said, his voice shaking as his eyes teared up. Alma Solano Velez said her husband gave his family an extensive list of the foods he has been craving over the past 10 months: oxtail, barbecue chicken, broccoli and shrimp empanadas to name a few. He had told his wife about "the lack of food and showers" on board and was looking forward to seeing their daughter, who turned 4 while he was away, she said. The carrier left San Diego in November and arrived in the Middle East in January. U.S. and Israeli forces launched airstrikes against Iran on Feb. 28. In August, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said the Lincoln maintained adequate food supplies, but because combat operations limited resupply opportunities, meal options were reduced for a short time. After more than 10 months at sea, the Lincoln's crew got a stop in Thailand early last month on the way back from the Middle East. Long deployments can tax service members Extended naval deployments can wear on service members who are away from home for long periods and increase strain on the ship and its equipment. The Navy told lawmakers that eight sailors attempted suicide during the record-setting deployment, though experts say that number is low in a strike group of 6,000 sailors over 10 months. f2a962f42b36.text: By — Josh Funk, Associated Press Josh Funk, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/army-calls-for-safety-fixes-after-finding-systemic-failures-behind-dc-midair-collision Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Army calls for safety fixes after finding systemic failures behind DC midair collision Nation Oct 8, 2026 7:46 PM EDT The U.S. Army found systemic safety breakdowns behind last year's midair collision between an American Airlines jet and a Black Hawk helicopter near Washington, D.C., and recommended changes to prevent future tragedies. WATCH: NTSB investigators say DCA midair collision followed years of ignored warnings The Army report — completed in May and released publicly Thursday after months of pressure from the victims' families — identified failures involving air traffic control, helicopter routes, training and safety practices. The Associated Press obtained a copy of the report hours before it was released. The deadliest plane crash on U.S. soil in over two decades happened when the helicopter collided with the descending airliner as it approached the runway, sending both plummeting into the icy Potomac River and killing 67. The Army report highlighted how the air traffic controller at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport could have prevented the crash, but it also acknowledged the military's own failings and other contributing factors. Families demand answers from the Army Tim Lilley, a former Army Black Hawk pilot whose son Sam Lilley was the airliner's first officer, said the report leaves important questions unanswered. Parts were redacted, and responsibility for the Army's failures was assigned broadly rather than to individuals. "The Army owes the families and the American public a full accounting of how these risks were allowed to persist, who was responsible for the decisions that allowed them to persist and what will be done to make sure this never happens again," said Lilley, now a commercial jet captain. The Army acknowledged that in a statement Thursday. "We recognize the families' need for answers and remain committed to transparency regarding the Army's review," it said. Report identifies key factors in the crash While the report largely reinforces the National Transportation Safety Board's conclusions, the civilian investigation was broader and emphasized years of missed warnings by the Federal Aviation Administration along with a weak military safety culture. The Army faulted the air traffic controller for not giving the helicopter crew more precise information about the approaching jet and for not warning the jet's pilot about the helicopter. After the crash, the FAA prohibited controllers from relying on pilots to maintain visual separation in busy airspace. The report recommended looking beyond Washington to examine military helicopter operations in other major cities for similar risks. An Army official said the review of helicopter flights in other cities, including Los Angeles and the Seattle-Tacoma region, is ongoing. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the situation publicly. The lieutenant general who authored the report cited "breakdowns across all layers of conflict management" but singled out two failed radio transmissions that contributed to the helicopter crew not identifying the jet. The military pilots' night-vision goggles also restricted their view and made it hard to spot the plane amid the city lights. The poorly designed helicopter route allowed a scant 75 feet (23 meters) of vertical separation between a helicopter and a plane landing on the airport's secondary runway, assuming helicopters stayed near the riverbank, which the route didn't require. This did not allow enough separation to account for the accepted level of error in a Black Hawk's altimeter, and the NTSB found the helicopter was flying nearly 100 feet (30 meters) higher than its instruments read. NTSB says the Army is making safety changes The NTSB said in a letter to the Army last week that it was pleased with the Army's progress on seven of its eight safety recommendations. That contrasts with the FAA's failure to implement roughly a third of the recommendations aimed at the agency. The Army said it has strengthened helicopter crew training, and has inspected and reconfigured 3,585 helicopters after discovering the crashed Black Hawk's ADS-B Out system, which broadcasts its location, hadn't been working for some time. The military is also improving its monitoring of safety risks and working with the FAA to share information about close calls. Victims' families push Congress for safety reforms Families of the crash victims said the Army's findings strengthen their case for legislation requiring aircraft to have technology that helps pilots detect nearby traffic. "It's a simple concept anyone can understand: aircraft should be able to see each other in the sky. The technology is proven. All that's required is the political will to do the right thing," the Families of Flight 5342 group said in a statement Thursday. "We have waited long enough. We waited for the NTSB. We waited for the Army. Both investigations are complete, and both make clear that collision avoidance technology must be part of the solution. There is nothing left for Congress to wait for," they said. The House and Senate have passed separate aviation safety bills but have yet to agree on a final version. Associated Press writer Konstantin Toropin in Washington contributed. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue.
